anchor: We now move to the temporal dimension... K=K(t), Policy=P(t), Architecture=A(t), DecisionModel=M(t), Authority=Auth(t), SystemState=S(t)
statement: All core KnowledgeOS objects (Knowledge, Policy, Architecture, DecisionModel, Authority, SystemState) that had been treated as time-independent are reframed as functions of time t; the central question becomes 'what was true, known, permitted, and decidable at a particular point in time?'

anchor: 83.1 — Time is part of meaning ... Claim(ServiceX,PostgreSQL,t) ... Truth(C,t) is more fundamental than Truth(C)
statement: A claim like 'Service X uses PostgreSQL' is incomplete without a time parameter; Truth(C,t) is proposed as more fundamental than the timeless Truth(C).

anchor: 83.2 — Experiment 1: timeless fact ... Database=PostgreSQL ... Expected: TemporalContextMissing. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: a system storing only 'Database=PostgreSQL' cannot determine when this was true; expected outcome TemporalContextMissing; result PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: A timeless fact lacks temporal context
experiment.setup: System stores Database=PostgreSQL with no time parameter
experiment.method: Ask when the fact was true
experiment.interpretation: Confirms need for explicit temporal interpretation

anchor: 83.3 — Event time versus observation time ... t_e=10:00 ... t_o=10:30 ... EventTime≠ObservationTime
statement: Distinguishes EventTime (when an incident occurred, e.g. 10:00) from ObservationTime (when KnowledgeOS learned of it, e.g. 10:30); asserts EventTime ≠ ObservationTime as fundamental.

anchor: 83.4 — Experiment 2 ... System records only timestamp=10:30 ... cannot determine whether the underlying event occurred at 10:00 or 10:30. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: a system recording only a single timestamp=10:30 cannot determine whether the underlying event occurred at 10:00 or 10:30; result PASS.

anchor: 83.5 — Processing time ... a third time t_p ... EventTime ≠ ObservationTime ≠ ProcessingTime. For distributed systems, this distinction is essential.
statement: Introduces a third temporal axis, ProcessingTime (t_p, when the system processed the observation), giving a three-way distinction EventTime ≠ ObservationTime ≠ ProcessingTime, essential for distributed systems.

anchor: 83.6 — Experiment 3 ... Event:10:00. Observed:10:30. Processed:10:31. System collapses all three into 10:31. Expected: TemporalInformationLoss. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: collapsing event(10:00)/observed(10:30)/processed(10:31) times into a single timestamp (10:31) is expected to produce TemporalInformationLoss; result PASS.

anchor: 83.7 — Validity interval ... A fact may hold over [t_start,t_end). Policy_A is valid from 2026-01-01 until 2026-07-01. Valid(Policy_A,t) is true only within that interval.
statement: Defines a validity interval [t_start, t_end) over which a fact/policy holds; Valid(Policy_A, t) is true only within that interval, illustrated with Policy_A valid 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-01.

anchor: 83.8 — Experiment 4 ... Policy A: [2026-01-01,2026-07-01). Decision: 2026-08-01. System applies Policy A. Expected: PolicyExpired. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: applying Policy A (valid until 2026-07-01) to a decision dated 2026-08-01 is expected to be flagged PolicyExpired; result PASS.

anchor: 83.9 — Open-ended validity ... t_end=∞ ... 'This architecture principle is currently effective.' But 'currently' itself changes with time. Therefore the underlying record should still have an explicit temporal interpretation.
statement: Notes that some facts have open-ended validity (t_end=∞), e.g. 'this architecture principle is currently effective'; warns that 'currently' itself changes with time, so even open-ended facts need explicit temporal interpretation.

anchor: 83.10 — Experiment 5 ... EffectiveFrom=2026-01-01. No end date. Expected: may reasonably mean ValidFrom(2026-01-01,∞) until superseded, depending on domain semantics. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 5: a record with EffectiveFrom=2026-01-01 and no end date may reasonably be interpreted as ValidFrom(2026-01-01,∞) until superseded, domain-semantics dependent; result PASS.

anchor: 83.11 — Valid time versus transaction time ... Valid time: when something is true in the modeled world. Transaction time: when the system recorded it. V(C) ... T(C) ... These can differ.
statement: Introduces the classic temporal-database distinction between Valid time V(C) (when something is true in the modeled world) and Transaction time T(C) (when the system recorded it), noting these can differ.

anchor: 83.12 — Experiment 6: late-arriving knowledge ... Incident occurred V=10:00. KnowledgeOS records it T=10:30. Expected: Both timestamps remain available. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6 (late-arriving knowledge): incident occurs at valid time 10:00 but is recorded (transaction time) at 10:30; expected both timestamps remain available; result PASS.

anchor: 83.13 — Why this matters ... KnownAt(10:15)=False. Even though TrueAt(10:15)=True. This is a profound distinction.
statement: Illustrates why the V/T distinction matters: a deployment decision at 10:15 occurs after the incident (event at 10:00) but before KnowledgeOS learns of it (10:30), so KnownAt(10:15)=False while TrueAt(10:15)=True — called 'a profound distinction'.

anchor: 83.14 — Experiment 7 ... F=True at 10:00. System learns F at 10:30. Decision occurs at 10:15. Expected: at decision time Truth(F)=True but Known(F)=False. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: formalizes the 83.13 scenario — at decision time (10:15), Truth(F)=True but Known(F)=False; result PASS.

anchor: 83.15 — Truth and knowledge are different temporal predicates ... TrueAt(C,t) and KnownAt(C,t). They must not be conflated. This is one of the most important results of Step 83.
statement: States as one of the step's most important results that TrueAt(C,t) and KnownAt(C,t) are distinct temporal predicates that must not be conflated.

anchor: 83.16 — Authorization is also temporal ... AuthorizedAt(A,X,t). An agent may have authority t1≤t<t2. Before t1: not authorized. After t2: not authorized.
statement: Extends temporal predicates to authorization: AuthorizedAt(A,X,t) holds only within an interval [t1,t2) during which agent A has authority X.

anchor: 83.17 — Experiment 8 ... Agent authority expires at 12:00. Agent acts at 12:05. System checks only whether the agent ever had authority. Expected: Incorrect. Result: PASS. Authority must be evaluated at action time.
statement: Experiment 8: checking only whether an agent 'ever had' authority (rather than at the specific action time of 12:05, after expiry at 12:00) is expected to be Incorrect; result PASS; concludes authority must be evaluated at action time.

anchor: 83.18 — Temporal decision validity ... D=(DecisionContent,DecisionTime,KnowledgeState,DecisionModel,Policy,Authority). This lets us reconstruct the decision context.
statement: Redefines a Decision D as a tuple (DecisionContent, DecisionTime, KnowledgeState, DecisionModel, Policy, Authority) to enable full reconstruction of decision context.

type_signature.domain: DecisionContent x DecisionTime x KnowledgeState x DecisionModel x Policy x Authority

anchor: 83.19 — Experiment 9 ... Historical decision exists. Current policy has changed. System evaluates historical decision using current policy. Expected: HistoricalMisinterpretation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: evaluating a historical decision using the current (changed) policy instead of the policy valid at decision time is expected to produce HistoricalMisinterpretation; result PASS.

anchor: 83.20 — Temporal replay ... Replay(D,t_D) using artifacts valid at t_D. Not Replay(D,t_now).
statement: States the correct replay operation is Replay(D, t_D) using artifacts valid at the decision time t_D, not Replay(D, t_now).

anchor: 83.21 — Experiment 10 ... Decision made in 2025. Policy changed in 2026. Replay in 2026. Expected: use Policy_2025, not Policy_2026. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: replaying a 2025 decision in 2026 (after a policy change) must use Policy_2025 not Policy_2026; result PASS.

anchor: 83.22 — This is historical epistemic reconstruction ... K_t ... World truth Truth_t. Organizationally accepted knowledge K^org_t. Agent's knowledge K^A_t. KnowledgeOS recorded knowledge K^sys_t. These are different.
statement: Decomposes 'what did we know at time t' (K_t) into four distinct notions: world truth Truth_t, organizationally accepted knowledge K^org_t, an individual agent's knowledge K^A_t, and KnowledgeOS's recorded knowledge K^sys_t — all distinct.

anchor: 83.23 — Experiment 11 ... engineer knew about a defect at 09:00. Organization formally accepted the defect at 11:00. KnowledgeOS recorded it at 11:05. Expected: these three knowledge states remain distinguishable. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: an engineer's individual knowledge (09:00), organizational acceptance (11:00), and system recording (11:05) of a defect must remain distinguishable as three separate knowledge states; result PASS.

anchor: 83.24 — Knowledge has temporal provenance ... When was it true? observed? accepted? superseded? This is much richer than created_at.
statement: Proposes that a claim's temporal provenance should record when it was true, observed, accepted, and superseded — much richer than a single created_at field.

anchor: 83.25 — Experiment 12 ... System has only created_at=11:05. But cannot determine valid_from. Expected: TemporalSemanticsIncomplete. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: a system storing only created_at cannot determine valid_from; expected TemporalSemanticsIncomplete; result PASS.

anchor: 83.26 — Temporal causality ... CauseTime and EffectTime. Normally a causal relationship should respect temporal ordering: t_cause ≤ t_effect.
statement: Introduces CauseTime and EffectTime and the ordering constraint that a causal relationship should respect t_cause ≤ t_effect.

anchor: 83.27 — Experiment 13 ... System claims Event_B caused Event_A. But t_B>t_A. Expected: CausalTemporalContradiction. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: claiming Event_B caused Event_A while t_B > t_A violates temporal ordering; expected CausalTemporalContradiction; result PASS.

anchor: 83.28 — But be careful. A later observation can reveal an earlier cause ... ObservationTime does not determine EventTime.
statement: Warns that a later observation (e.g. in 2026) can establish that an event occurred earlier (e.g. 2025); therefore ObservationTime does not determine EventTime — the 83.27 ordering constraint applies to event/cause times, not observation times.

anchor: 83.29 — Experiment 14 ... Evidence discovered in 2026 shows a deployment failure occurred in 2025. Expected: Valid, provided the evidence supports the historical claim. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: evidence discovered in 2026 establishing a 2025 deployment failure is Valid provided it supports the historical claim (tests the 83.28 distinction); result PASS.

anchor: 83.30 — Temporal uncertainty ... t∈[10:00,10:15]. Then EventTime is an interval rather than a point.
statement: Extends EventTime to interval-valued uncertainty: t ∈ [10:00,10:15] when the exact time is unknown.

anchor: 83.31 — Experiment 15 ... Deployment occurred sometime between 10:00 and 10:15. System records 10:07:32 as exact. Expected: FalseTemporalPrecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: recording a fabricated exact timestamp (10:07:32) for an event only known to lie within an interval [10:00,10:15] is expected to be flagged FalseTemporalPrecision; result PASS.

anchor: 83.32 — Interval reasoning ... A=[10:00,10:15], B=[10:10,10:30]. The temporal ordering may be uncertain. We cannot automatically claim A<B. There is overlap.
statement: Shows that with overlapping intervals A=[10:00,10:15] and B=[10:10,10:30], ordering A<B cannot be automatically claimed.

anchor: 83.33 — Experiment 16 ... System claims A definitely preceded B. But intervals overlap. Expected: OrderingUndetermined. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: claiming A definitely preceded B despite overlapping intervals is expected to be OrderingUndetermined; result PASS.

anchor: 83.34 — Temporal Allen relations ... before; after; overlaps; during; starts; finishes; meets ... TemporalRelation ≠ simple timestamp comparison.
statement: Names Allen's interval algebra relations (before, after, overlaps, during, starts, finishes, meets) as the vocabulary needed for interval-based temporal reasoning, concluding TemporalRelation ≠ simple timestamp comparison.

anchor: 83.35 — Event sourcing connection ... S_t = Fold(Event_1,...,Event_k). This allows historical reconstruction where the event history is sufficient.
statement: Connects the temporal model to event sourcing: state at time t, S_t, is a Fold over Event_1..Event_k, allowing historical reconstruction when event history is sufficient.

anchor: 83.36 — Experiment 17 ... Current architecture A_5. Historical architecture A_3. Event history A_1→A_2→A_3→A_4→A_5. Expected: Reconstruct(A_3). Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: given event history A_1..A_5, the historical architecture state A_3 should be reconstructable; result PASS.

anchor: 83.37 — But event history is not automatically truth ... If events were incomplete or corrupted, ReconstructedState may still be wrong. EventSourcing ≠ GuaranteedTruth.
statement: Warns that event sourcing does not guarantee truth: if the event log is incomplete or corrupted, the reconstructed state may still be wrong (EventSourcing ≠ GuaranteedTruth).

anchor: 83.38 — Experiment 18 ... An undocumented manual production change occurred. Event log contains no corresponding event. Expected: EventHistoryIncomplete. Result: PASS. This brings us back to observability.
statement: Experiment 18: an undocumented manual production change with no corresponding log event is expected to be flagged EventHistoryIncomplete; result PASS; the file notes this connects back to observability.

anchor: 83.39 — Temporal provenance chain ... Claim_C supported by Evidence_E observed at t_E. The claim becomes accepted at t_A. It becomes superseded at t_S. t_E, t_A, t_S are different temporal dimensions.
statement: Defines a temporal provenance chain for a claim: evidence observed at t_E, claim accepted at t_A, claim superseded at t_S — three distinct temporal dimensions of a single claim's lifecycle.

anchor: 83.40 — Experiment 19 ... System has only updated_at. Expected: it cannot reconstruct the full epistemic lifecycle. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: a system storing only updated_at cannot reconstruct the full epistemic lifecycle (t_E, t_A, t_S); result PASS.

anchor: 83.41 — Temporal supersession ... K_1 accepted from t_1. Later K_2 supersedes it at t_2. K_1 should remain historically valid for the relevant interval rather than being physically erased.
statement: States that when K_2 supersedes K_1 at t_2, K_1 should remain historically valid/queryable for its original interval rather than being physically erased.

anchor: 83.42 — Experiment 20 ... System replaces K_1 with K_2. No historical relation remains. Expected: HistoricalProvenanceLoss. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: physically replacing K_1 with K_2 with no retained historical relation is expected to produce HistoricalProvenanceLoss; result PASS.

anchor: 83.43 — Temporal contradictions ... C_1: A=True valid [t1,t2]. C_2: A=False valid [t3,t4]. If intervals don't overlap, there is no contradiction.
statement: Defines temporal contradiction conditions: two claims C_1 (A=True on [t1,t2]) and C_2 (A=False on [t3,t4]) are not contradictory if their validity intervals don't overlap.

anchor: 83.44 — Experiment 21 ... C_1:[2025,2026], C_2:[2026,2027]. Assume half-open intervals. Expected: No temporal contradiction if the boundary is modeled consistently. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: adjacent half-open intervals [2025,2026) and [2026,2027) produce no temporal contradiction if boundaries are modeled consistently; result PASS.

anchor: 83.45 — Overlapping contradiction ... C_1:[2025,2027], C_2:[2026,2028]. Then [2026,2027] contains contradictory claims. Expected: TemporalConflict. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment: overlapping intervals [2025,2027] and [2026,2028] with contradictory claims A=True/A=False produce a genuine TemporalConflict in the overlap [2026,2027]; result PASS.

anchor: 83.46 — But perhaps both are scoped differently ... C_1: Service_A and C_2: Service_B. Therefore contradiction requires matching Subject + Predicate + Scope + Time. This reinforces our semantic identity model.
statement: Corrects the 83.45 contradiction condition: apparent temporal contradictions may not be real contradictions if the claims are scoped to different subjects (e.g. Service_A vs Service_B); true contradiction requires matching Subject + Predicate + Scope + Time, reinforcing the project's semantic identity model.

anchor: 83.47 — Temporal policy conflicts ... P_1 effective until t_1 and P_2 becomes effective at t_1. This is clean. But if P_1 and P_2 overlap with incompatible rules, we need conflict resolution.
statement: Notes clean policy succession (P_1 ends when P_2 begins) is unproblematic, but overlapping policies with incompatible rules require conflict resolution.

anchor: 83.48 — Experiment 22 ... Two policies both claim Effective=True for the same scope and time. They impose incompatible constraints. Expected: PolicyConflict. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: two simultaneously-effective, same-scope policies with incompatible constraints are expected to produce PolicyConflict; result PASS.

anchor: 83.49 — Temporal precedence ... P_new supersedes P_old. But that precedence must itself be defined. We cannot simply assume Newest = Correct.
statement: Warns against the naive assumption 'Newest = Correct' for resolving policy precedence; precedence rules must themselves be explicitly defined.

anchor: 83.50 — Experiment 23 ... New policy is published but not approved. Old policy remains effective. System applies newest policy automatically. Expected: Rejected. Result: PASS. This combines temporal reasoning with governance state.
statement: Experiment 23: a system automatically applying the newest (published-but-unapproved) policy over the still-effective old policy is expected to be Rejected; result PASS; combines temporal reasoning with governance state.

anchor: 83.51 — Time-dependent authority ... Auth(A,X,t,c). For example A may approve production changes only during an assigned period and within a specific scope.
statement: Extends authority to a 4-ary conditional predicate Auth(A,X,t,c): agent A's authorization for X at time t may additionally depend on condition/scope c.

type_signature.domain: Agent x Action x Time x Condition

anchor: 83.52 — Experiment 24 ... Agent has permanent technical access. Its organizational authority expires. Expected: TechnicalAccess=True but GovernanceAuthority=False. Result: PASS. This is an important security/governance distinction.
statement: Experiment 24: an agent retaining permanent technical access after organizational authority expires must show TechnicalAccess=True but GovernanceAuthority=False — an important security/governance distinction; result PASS.

anchor: 83.53 — Temporal decision model ... M_1→M_2. Decision at t1 uses M_1. Decision at t2 uses M_2. Historical decisions retain their original model.
statement: States that when the decision model itself changes over time (M_1→M_2), historical decisions must retain and be interpreted under their original model, not the current one.

anchor: 83.54 — Experiment 25 ... Model changes on Monday. System recomputes Friday's historical decision using Monday's model. Expected: HistoricalIntegrityViolation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: recomputing a Friday historical decision using a decision model that only changed the following Monday is expected to be a HistoricalIntegrityViolation; result PASS.

anchor: 83.55 — Temporal architecture ... A_1→A_2→A_3. A dependency compliant under A_1 may be prohibited under A_3. Compliance = Compliance(Implementation,Architecture_t).
statement: Reformulates architectural compliance as a function of time: Compliance = Compliance(Implementation, Architecture_t), since architecture itself evolves (A_1→A_2→A_3) and a dependency compliant under an earlier architecture may become prohibited later.

anchor: 83.56 — Experiment 26 ... Implementation hasn't changed. Architecture rule changes. Expected: ComplianceStatus may change even though implementation remains identical. Result: PASS. A governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change.
statement: Experiment 26 (called extremely important): an unchanged implementation can flip compliance status purely because the architecture rule changed — a governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change; result PASS.

anchor: 83.57 — Architectural drift therefore has multiple causes ... ImplementationChange or ArchitectureChange or PolicyChange. DriftCause must be temporally attributable.
statement: Generalizes 83.56: architectural drift/violations can result from ImplementationChange, ArchitectureChange, or PolicyChange, and the DriftCause must be temporally attributable to the correct one.

anchor: 83.58 — Experiment 27 ... Implementation remains unchanged. New architecture makes an existing dependency forbidden. Expected: ImplementationChange=False, ArchitectureChange=True, Violation=True. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: confirms attribution of a new violation to ArchitectureChange=True (not ImplementationChange) when only the architecture rule changed; result PASS.

anchor: 83.59 — Temporal causality of governance ... Cause_world, Cause_knowledge, Cause_policy, Cause_architecture. This gives us a much richer explanation of why a decision or violation occurred.
statement: Introduces four distinguishable causal categories for governance outcomes: Cause_world, Cause_knowledge, Cause_policy, Cause_architecture, enabling richer explanation of decisions/violations.

anchor: 83.60 — Historical question ... Q(t) = What was true, what was known, what was governed, and what was authorized at time t? This is much more powerful than 'What is the current state?'
statement: Formulates the central KnowledgeOS historical query Q(t): what was true, known, governed, and authorized at time t — argued to be far more powerful than a mere current-state query.

anchor: 83.61 — Experiment 28: historical reconstruction ... Why was deployment D approved on 2026-04-10? KnowledgeOS retrieves Knowledge, Policy, Architecture, DecisionModel, Authority at 2026-04-10. Expected: HistoricalRationaleReconstructable. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: retrieving Knowledge/Policy/Architecture/DecisionModel/Authority all as of 2026-04-10 to answer 'why was deployment D approved' is expected to make the historical rationale reconstructable; result PASS.

anchor: 83.62 — This is a major capability ... KnowledgeOS becomes capable of Temporal Explainability. Not 'Why does the system think this now?' but 'Why was this considered correct and authorized then?'
statement: Names the emergent capability 'Temporal Explainability': answering not 'why does the system think this now' but 'why was this considered correct and authorized then'.

anchor: 83.63 — Temporal snapshots ... Snapshot(t). But snapshots alone may be expensive and insufficient. A more complete architecture may combine Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots.
statement: Argues snapshotting alone (Snapshot(t)) is expensive/insufficient and proposes combining Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots as an implementation strategy for temporal reconstruction.

anchor: 83.64 — Experiment 29 ... Only current-state snapshots are stored. Historical transition path is lost. Expected: LimitedHistoricalReasoning. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: storing only current-state snapshots (losing the historical transition path) is expected to yield LimitedHistoricalReasoning; result PASS.

anchor: 83.65 — Time-travel queries ... StateAt(t), KnowledgeAt(t), PolicyAt(t), AuthorityAt(t), ArchitectureAt(t). These are distinct operations.
statement: Proposes a family of distinct 'time-travel' query operations: StateAt(t), KnowledgeAt(t), PolicyAt(t), AuthorityAt(t), ArchitectureAt(t).

anchor: 83.66 — Experiment 30 ... Query: ArchitectureAt(2025-06-01). Expected: Return the architecture valid at that time, not today's architecture. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: ArchitectureAt(2025-06-01) must return the architecture valid at that historical date, not today's; result PASS.

anchor: 83.67 — New invariants: I_TemporalTruth, I_EventTime, I_HistoricalIntegrity, I_TemporalAuthority, I_TemporalUncertainty, I_TemporalSupersession
statement: States six new named invariants: I_TemporalTruth (claims whose truth can change must have explicit temporal interpretation), I_EventTime (event/observation/processing times must remain distinguishable when materially relevant), I_HistoricalIntegrity (historical decisions must be interpreted using knowledge/models/policies/authorities valid at decision time), I_TemporalAuthority (authorization must be evaluated at time of action), I_TemporalUncertainty (unknown/interval timestamps must not be converted into false point precision), I_TemporalSupersession (superseded knowledge remains historically reconstructable).

anchor: 83.68 — Step 83 verdict: STEP 83 — PASS ... Knowledge(t) ... Governance(t) ... Decision(t)=f(Knowledge(t),Uncertainty(t),CausalModel(t),DecisionModel(t),Policy(t),Authority(t),Context(t))
statement: Records the Step 83 verdict as PASS and restates the KnowledgeOS core model with explicit time dependence: Knowledge(t), Governance(t), and Decision(t) = f(Knowledge(t), Uncertainty(t), CausalModel(t), DecisionModel(t), Policy(t), Authority(t), Context(t)).

type_signature.domain: Knowledge(t) x Uncertainty(t) x CausalModel(t) x DecisionModel(t) x Policy(t) x Authority(t) x Context(t)

anchor: The emerging KnowledgeOS mathematical object ... A temporally versioned, provenance-aware, uncertainty-aware, governed knowledge-and-decision system. ... What can we legitimately conclude, given what was observable, known, modeled, authorized, and valid at a particular time?
statement: Reframes the emerging KnowledgeOS object as 'a temporally versioned, provenance-aware, uncertainty-aware, governed knowledge-and-decision system' whose core question is what can legitimately be concluded given what was observable, known, modeled, authorized and valid at a particular time.

anchor: Step 84 — Next boundary: counterfactual reasoning ... What if we had not deployed? ... distinguish P(Y|X) from P(Y|do(X)) and from P(Y_x|X=x'). This takes us directly into causal inference, interventions, potential outcomes, counterfactual reasoning, causal graphs...

unknown_candidate.why_uncertain: References do(X)/potential-outcomes counterfactual machinery which may be the same object as the existing causal-reasoning-assurance-layer label, but this file introduces it as a forward preview rather than the full formalization, so identity is uncertain.

statement: Previews Step 84: engineering decisions often ask counterfactual questions ('what would have happened if we had done something else'), which requires KnowledgeOS to distinguish P(Y|X) from P(Y|do(X)) from P(Y_x|X=x'), entering causal inference, interventions, potential outcomes, counterfactual reasoning and causal graphs.

lineage_claims.quote: The next step will therefore test whether KnowledgeOS can correctly distinguish P(Y|X) from P(Y|do(X)) and from P(Y_x|X=x').

anchor: We now test whether our mathematical model remains correct when uncertainty passes through multiple layers ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision. Uncertainty must propagate through reasoning; it must never disappear merely because the representation changed.
statement: States the step's central principle: uncertainty must propagate through the reasoning pipeline (Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision) and must never disappear merely because representation changed.

anchor: 82.1 — Measurement uncertainty ... X=100 with σ_X=5. We should not represent the epistemic state simply as X=100. A better representation is X≈100±5 under an explicitly defined uncertainty model.
statement: Argues a measured quantity with known measurement uncertainty (X=100, σ_X=5) should be represented as X≈100±5 under an explicit uncertainty model, not as a bare point value.

anchor: 82.2 — Experiment 1: uncertainty deletion ... X=100±5. Y=X+10. System stores Y=110. Expected: UncertaintyLossDetected. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: a system that computes Y=X+10 from X=100±5 and stores only Y=110 (dropping the uncertainty) should trigger UncertaintyLossDetected; result PASS.

anchor: 82.3 — Simple deterministic transformation ... Y=X+c, then σ_Y=σ_X. 100±5 → 110±5.
statement: For a deterministic shift Y=X+c, uncertainty is unchanged: σ_Y=σ_X, e.g. 100±5 → 110±5.

anchor: 82.4 — Experiment 2 ... X=100±5, Y=X+10. Expected: Y=110±5. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2 confirms the additive-shift rule: X=100±5, Y=X+10 yields Y=110±5; result PASS.

anchor: 82.5 — Multiplication ... Y=aX where a is exact. σ_Y=|a|σ_X. X=100±5, a=2 → Y=200±10.
statement: For Y=aX with exact scalar a, σ_Y=|a|σ_X; e.g. X=100±5 scaled by a=2 gives Y=200±10.

anchor: 82.6 — Experiment 3 ... Expected: σ_Y=10. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3 confirms the multiplicative scaling rule numerically: σ_Y=10; result PASS.

anchor: 82.7 — Addition of independent uncertainties ... Z=X+Y. If X,Y independent: Var(Z)=Var(X)+Var(Y). σ_Z=sqrt(σ_X^2+σ_Y^2).
statement: For independent X,Y summed as Z=X+Y, variances add: Var(Z)=Var(X)+Var(Y), so σ_Z=sqrt(σ_X²+σ_Y²).

anchor: 82.8 — Experiment 4 ... X=100±3, Y=50±4. Z=150, σ_Z=sqrt(3²+4²)=5. Expected: Z=150±5. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4 confirms independent-variance addition numerically: X=100±3 plus Y=50±4 gives Z=150±5; result PASS.

anchor: 82.9 — Correlation changes everything ... Cov(X,Y)≠0. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independence cannot be assumed automatically. This connects directly to our previous evidence-independence work.
statement: Warns that when Cov(X,Y)≠0, Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y), so independence cannot be assumed automatically; the file explicitly links this to prior evidence-independence work.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects directly to our previous evidence-independence work.

anchor: 82.10 — Experiment 5 ... System assumes Cov(X,Y)=0. But both measurements originate from the same sensor. Expected: PotentialUnderestimatedUncertainty. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 5: assuming independence (Cov=0) for two measurements from the same sensor is expected to yield PotentialUnderestimatedUncertainty; result PASS.

anchor: 82.11 — Negative correlation ... If Cov(X,Y)<0, uncertainty can partially cancel. Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y). Correlation can either increase or decrease uncertainty depending on the transformation.
statement: Shows negative correlation can partially cancel uncertainty in a difference: Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y); correlation's effect on uncertainty is transformation-dependent, not uniformly increasing.

anchor: 82.12 — Experiment 6 ... Two measurement errors are strongly correlated. System assumes independence. Expected: IncorrectVariance. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: assuming independence for strongly correlated measurement errors is expected to produce IncorrectVariance; result PASS.

anchor: 82.13 — Nonlinear transformations ... Y=f(X). Var(Y)≈[f'(E[X])]²Var(X). This is the delta method.
statement: Introduces the delta method: for Y=f(X) with small uncertainty, Var(Y)≈[f'(E[X])]²Var(X).
Worked delta-method example: Y=X² with X=10±1 gives f'(X)=2X so σ_Y≈2(10)(1)=20, i.e. Y≈100±20.

anchor: 82.15 — Experiment 7 ... System calculates 10±1 → 100±1. Expected: FalsePrecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: a system computing 10±1 → 100±1 (ignoring the delta-method scaling, i.e. treating nonlinear propagation as if uncertainty passes through unchanged) is expected to be FalsePrecision; result PASS.

anchor: 82.16 — Nonlinear uncertainty can be asymmetric ... Y=e^X. A symmetric uncertainty in X produces asymmetric uncertainty in Y. Mean±σ is not universally sufficient.
statement: Argues that strongly nonlinear transforms (e.g. Y=e^X) turn symmetric input uncertainty into asymmetric output uncertainty, so mean±σ is not universally a sufficient representation.

anchor: 82.17 — Experiment 8 ... X=0±2. Y=e^X. System represents Y as 1±2. Expected: InvalidRepresentation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: representing Y=e^X (with X=0±2) as the symmetric interval 1±2 is expected to be InvalidRepresentation; result PASS.

anchor: 82.18 — Distribution-level representation ... For sufficiently complex uncertainty, KnowledgeOS may need P(X) rather than (X,σ). P(Y)=∫P(Y|X)P(X)dX. This is much richer.
statement: Proposes moving from a (mean,σ) representation to a full distribution P(X), with P(Y)=∫P(Y|X)P(X)dX for propagation, as a richer representation.

anchor: 82.19 — Experiment 9 ... Two variables have identical means and variances but their distributions differ significantly. Expected: MeanVarianceRepresentation may not preserve enough information. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: two variables with identical mean and variance but different distribution shapes show that mean/variance representation may not preserve enough information; result PASS.

anchor: 82.20 — Bayesian updating ... P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E). KnowledgeOS should distinguish Prior from Posterior.
statement: States Bayes' rule P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) and requires KnowledgeOS to distinguish Prior from Posterior explicitly.

anchor: 82.21 — Experiment 10 ... Prior P(H)=0.3. Evidence increases belief to P(H|E)=0.7. System overwrites the prior with 0.7 and loses the evidence relationship. Expected: ProvenanceLoss. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: overwriting a prior (0.3) with the posterior (0.7) and losing the evidence relationship is expected to yield ProvenanceLoss; result PASS.

anchor: 82.22 — Belief revision ... Belief_0 --Evidence--> Belief_1. Not Belief_1 with no historical lineage. This allows us to answer: Why did our belief change?
statement: States belief revision must be modeled as Belief_0 --Evidence--> Belief_1 (retaining lineage), not as an unexplained new Belief_1, so the system can answer 'why did our belief change'.

anchor: 82.23 — Experiment 11 ... P(H)=0.2 → evidence → 0.8 → contradictory evidence → 0.4. Expected: 0.2→0.8→0.4 remains reconstructable. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: a belief trajectory P(H): 0.2→0.8→0.4 across two evidence updates (the second contradictory) must remain fully reconstructable; result PASS.

anchor: 82.24 — Confidence is not probability ... A confidence score 0.9 does not automatically mean P(H)=0.9. Different uncertainty representations have different semantics. Confidence ≠ Probability.
statement: States as essential that a confidence score (e.g. 0.9) does not automatically equal a probability P(H)=0.9; different uncertainty representations carry different semantics — Confidence ≠ Probability.

anchor: 82.25 — Experiment 12 ... LLM says confidence = 0.95. System stores P(H)=0.95. Expected: SemanticError. Result: PASS. Unless the confidence measure has explicitly been calibrated to represent probability.
statement: Experiment 12: converting an LLM's self-reported confidence=0.95 directly into P(H)=0.95 is a SemanticError unless the confidence measure has been explicitly calibrated to represent probability; result PASS.

anchor: 82.26 — Calibration ... If a system predicts P(H)=0.8, then among many comparable cases, approximately 80% should be true if the probability is well calibrated. Different from merely asking the model 'how confident are you?'
statement: Defines calibration: a well-calibrated P(H)=0.8 prediction should be true in ~80% of comparable cases empirically, distinct from simply asking a model to self-report confidence.

anchor: 82.27 — Experiment 13 ... AI produces 0.9 confidence. Historical calibration shows only 0.65 of such predictions are correct. Expected: ConfidenceCalibrationProblem. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: an AI's 0.9-confidence predictions being correct only 65% of the time historically is expected to be flagged ConfidenceCalibrationProblem; result PASS.

anchor: 82.28 — Decision uncertainty ... P(D|E). Often the decision itself is deterministic given the model. D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B. Small changes in P(H) near 0.8 can flip the decision.
statement: Notes that although the decision rule D=A if P(H)>0.8 else B is itself deterministic given the model, small changes in P(H) near the 0.8 threshold can flip the decision.

anchor: 82.29 — Experiment 14 ... P(H)=0.79 → Decision B. New evidence P(H)=0.81 → Decision A. Expected: DecisionSensitivity=True. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: P(H) moving from 0.79 (Decision B) to 0.81 (Decision A) across a 0.8 threshold demonstrates DecisionSensitivity=True; result PASS.

anchor: 82.30 — Decision boundary ... θ=0.8. P(H)>θ⇒A. Near the boundary |P(H)-θ|≈0, small uncertainty can have large decision impact.
statement: Defines a decision boundary θ=0.8 and argues that near the boundary, small uncertainty in P(H) can have disproportionately large decision impact.

anchor: 82.31 — Experiment 15 ... P(H)=0.801, σ=0.05. System declares DecisionCertain. Expected: FalseCertainty. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: declaring DecisionCertain when P(H)=0.801 has σ=0.05 (uncertainty band straddling the θ=0.8 boundary) is FalseCertainty; result PASS.

anchor: 82.32 — Probability intervals ... P(H)∈[0.75,0.85]. The decision boundary lies inside the uncertainty interval. Correct status: DecisionUndetermined if the policy requires certainty relative to that boundary.
statement: Proposes representing P(H) as an interval [0.75,0.85]; when the decision boundary θ falls inside this interval, the correct status is DecisionUndetermined (given a policy requiring certainty relative to the boundary).

anchor: 82.33 — Experiment 16 ... P(H)∈[0.75,0.85], θ=0.8. Expected: DecisionStatus=Sensitive/Undetermined. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16 confirms: P(H)∈[0.75,0.85] straddling θ=0.8 yields DecisionStatus=Sensitive/Undetermined; result PASS.

anchor: 82.34 — Monte Carlo reasoning ... X~P(X). Generate X_1..X_N. D_i=f(X_i). P(D=A)≈(1/N)Σ1[D_i=A]. This can reveal how often a decision changes under plausible uncertainty.
statement: Proposes Monte Carlo simulation (sampling X_i~P(X), computing D_i=f(X_i), estimating P(D=A) by frequency) to reveal how often a decision changes under plausible uncertainty.

type_signature.domain: distribution P(X) x decision function f

anchor: 82.35 — Experiment 17 ... 10,000 plausible simulations produce A: 72%, B: 28%. Expected: KnowledgeOS should be able to represent P(D=A)≈0.72 rather than simply D=A. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations giving A:72%/B:28% should be represented as P(D=A)≈0.72, not collapsed to a bare D=A; result PASS.

anchor: 82.36 — Model uncertainty ... uncertain not only about parameters θ, but about the model itself M_1,M_2,M_3. P(D)=Σ_m P(D|M_m)P(M_m). This is model uncertainty.
statement: Defines model uncertainty as uncertainty over which model (M_1,M_2,M_3,...) is correct, formalized via model averaging P(D)=Σ_m P(D|M_m)P(M_m), distinct from parameter uncertainty.

anchor: 82.37 — Experiment 18 ... Model M_1: P(A)=0.9. Model M_2: P(A)=0.2. Both plausible. Expected: OverallUncertainty must reflect model uncertainty. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: two plausible models giving wildly different P(A) (0.9 vs 0.2) means OverallUncertainty must reflect this model-level disagreement; result PASS.

anchor: 82.38 — Parameter uncertainty versus model uncertainty ... ParameterUncertainty from ModelUncertainty. Otherwise the system can underestimate uncertainty substantially.
statement: Warns that conflating ParameterUncertainty with ModelUncertainty can cause the system to substantially underestimate total uncertainty.

anchor: 82.39 — Experiment 19 ... System reports Risk=2%. But this includes parameter uncertainty and ignores uncertainty over model structure. Expected: IncompleteRiskEstimate. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: a reported Risk=2% that accounts only for parameter uncertainty and ignores model-structure uncertainty is an IncompleteRiskEstimate; result PASS.

anchor: 82.40 — Epistemic versus aleatory uncertainty ... Aleatory: intrinsic variability X~P(X). Epistemic: lack of knowledge, UnknownParameter. These behave differently.
statement: Distinguishes aleatory uncertainty (intrinsic variability, X~P(X)) from epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge, e.g. an unknown parameter), noting they behave differently.

anchor: 82.41 — Experiment 20 ... System observes varying demand. It labels all uncertainty 'data noise'. But part of the uncertainty comes from missing information about the system. Expected: UncertaintyClassificationError. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: labeling all demand-variation uncertainty as 'data noise' (aleatory) when part is actually epistemic (missing system information) is an UncertaintyClassificationError; result PASS.

anchor: 82.42 — Why this matters ... If uncertainty is epistemic, MoreEvidence may reduce it. If uncertainty is intrinsic, MoreObservation may not eliminate the underlying variability.
statement: Explains the practical stakes of the aleatory/epistemic distinction: epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by more evidence, while aleatory/intrinsic uncertainty may not be eliminated by more observation.

anchor: 82.43 — Experiment 21 ... Demand is inherently stochastic. Collecting more data does not make tomorrow's demand deterministic. Expected: ResidualAleatoryUncertainty. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: more data collection on inherently stochastic demand cannot eliminate ResidualAleatoryUncertainty; result PASS.

anchor: 82.44 — Uncertainty budget ... D=f(X_1,...,X_n). Uncertainty(D)=U_1+U_2+... with interaction terms where required. The objective is not merely 'we are uncertain' but 'what is causing the uncertainty?'
statement: Introduces the notion of an uncertainty budget: decomposing Uncertainty(D) for D=f(X_1..X_n) into per-component contributions (plus interaction terms), shifting the question from 'are we uncertain' to 'what is causing the uncertainty'.

anchor: 82.45 — Experiment 22 ... Decision uncertainty is high. Analysis shows 80% comes from one unknown parameter. Expected: ObservationPriority should focus on that parameter. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: an uncertainty budget attributing 80% of decision uncertainty to one parameter implies ObservationPriority should focus there; result PASS.

anchor: 82.46 — Value of information returns ... VOI=ExpectedImprovement-CostOfInformation. This links Step 75 and Step 82. KnowledgeOS can prioritize evidence acquisition based on its expected decision impact.
statement: Restates Value of Information VOI = ExpectedImprovement - CostOfInformation, explicitly linking Step 75's VOI concept to Step 82's uncertainty-propagation framework for prioritizing evidence acquisition.

lineage_claims.quote: This links Step 75 and Step 82.

anchor: 82.47 — Experiment 23 ... Investigation A costs €1,000, expected value €10,000 decision change. Investigation B costs €1,000 but almost never changes the decision. Expected: A has higher information value. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: comparing two equal-cost investigations, A (high expected decision-change value) correctly has higher information value than B (rarely changes the decision); result PASS.

anchor: 82.48 — Uncertainty propagation through causal models ... X→Y. β=0.5±0.1. do(X=x) produces uncertainty in E[Y|do(X=x)]. The uncertainty in the causal effect must propagate into the decision.
statement: Argues that causal-effect estimates (e.g. β=0.5±0.1 for X→Y) carry uncertainty that must propagate through an intervention do(X=x) into the resulting decision.

anchor: 82.49 — Experiment 24 ... Estimated causal effect β=0.5±0.1. System uses β=0.5 as exact. Expected: CausalUncertaintyLoss. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 24: treating an estimated causal effect β=0.5±0.1 as exact (β=0.5) is expected to produce CausalUncertaintyLoss; result PASS.

anchor: 82.50 — Confounding uncertainty ... an unobserved confounder exists. Uncertainty is not merely σ_β. It may involve ModelStructure. CausalUncertainty can be structural, not merely numerical.
statement: Argues causal uncertainty can be structural (e.g. an unobserved confounder invalidating the causal model), not merely numerical (σ_β) — CausalUncertainty can be structural, not merely numerical.

anchor: 82.51 — Experiment 25 ... Causal estimate assumes NoUnmeasuredConfounding. But that assumption is unverified. Expected: AssumptionRisk must be exposed. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: a causal estimate resting on an unverified NoUnmeasuredConfounding assumption must have that AssumptionRisk exposed; result PASS.

anchor: 82.52 — Assumptions are first-class ... Assumption(A) with Status: Supported or Unverified or Contradicted.
statement: Proposes Assumption(A) as a first-class object carrying a Status in {Supported, Unverified, Contradicted}.

anchor: 82.53 — Experiment 26 ... Decision depends on assumption A. A becomes contradicted. Expected: DependentDecision must be reconsidered. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: a decision that depended on assumption A must be flagged for reconsideration when A becomes Contradicted; result PASS.

anchor: 82.54 — This is a major KnowledgeOS property ... A change in Assumption can propagate through Model→Prediction→Decision. Therefore assumptions need dependency lineage.
statement: States that because a change in an Assumption can propagate through Model→Prediction→Decision, assumptions require explicit dependency lineage tracking.

anchor: 82.55 — Uncertainty propagation graph ... O_1→K_1→M→P→D. If uncertainty enters at O_1, we should be able to determine which downstream decisions are affected. This is UncertaintyImpactPropagation.
statement: Proposes an uncertainty-propagation/impact graph O_1→K_1→M→P→D enabling determination of which downstream decisions are affected when uncertainty enters at a given observation — named UncertaintyImpactPropagation.

anchor: 82.56 — Experiment 27 ... Observation O_1 is later found unreliable. Expected system identifies K_1 dependent on O_1, then M dependent on K_1, then D dependent on M. Expected: AffectedDecisionSet is discoverable. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: when O_1 is found unreliable, the system must be able to discover the full downstream AffectedDecisionSet (K_1→M→D); result PASS.

anchor: 82.57 — This creates a new capability ... Impact(O_i) meaning: which knowledge, models, decisions, policies, or actions depend materially on this observation? This is much stronger than ordinary document search.
statement: Names a new capability Impact(O_i) — determining which knowledge, models, decisions, policies or actions materially depend on a given observation — described as much stronger than ordinary document search.

anchor: 82.58 — Experiment 28 ... A critical source is revoked. System identifies 47 downstream claims and 12 decisions affected. Expected: RevalidationWorkflow. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: revoking a critical source and identifying 47 downstream claims / 12 affected decisions should trigger a RevalidationWorkflow; result PASS.

anchor: 82.59 — Uncertainty should not silently accumulate ... If the system simply stores Confidence=0.9 at each stage, multiplying 0.9^4 would itself be unjustified. The semantics of the confidence measures must be known.
statement: Warns against naively multiplying stage-wise confidence scores (e.g. 0.9^4 across four pipeline stages) without knowing what each confidence measure actually means semantically.

anchor: 82.60 — Experiment 29 ... System calculates 0.9×0.9×0.9 without defining what each confidence means. Expected: UnsupportedProbabilityCalculation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: multiplying undefined confidence scores (0.9×0.9×0.9) is an UnsupportedProbabilityCalculation; result PASS.

anchor: 82.61 — False precision ... Input: 'roughly 80%' becoming Output: 0.813742. The mathematical formatting has become more precise than the underlying information.
statement: Illustrates false precision: a qualitative input ('roughly 80%') rendered as an overly precise numeric output (0.813742) misrepresents the underlying information's actual precision.

anchor: 82.62 — Experiment 30 ... Source uncertainty is qualitative: 'likely'. System outputs P=0.8734. No calibration exists. Expected: FalsePrecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: converting a qualitative source ('likely') into an uncalibrated precise number P=0.8734 is FalsePrecision; result PASS.

anchor: 82.63 — Precision versus accuracy ... Precision ≠ Accuracy. A system can produce 0.873421 and still be badly wrong.
statement: States Precision ≠ Accuracy: a highly precise-looking number (0.873421) can still be badly inaccurate.

anchor: 82.64 — Experiment 31 ... Model predicts 87.3421%. Historical calibration shows 52%. Expected: HighNumericalPrecision but LowPredictiveAccuracy. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 31: a model prediction of 87.3421% with historical calibration showing only 52% accuracy demonstrates HighNumericalPrecision but LowPredictiveAccuracy; result PASS.

anchor: 82.65 — The KnowledgeOS rule ... Representational precision must not exceed epistemically justified precision. This should become a formal design principle.
statement: States the design principle: representational precision must not exceed epistemically justified precision, proposed as a formal KnowledgeOS design principle.

anchor: 82.66 — Decision-level uncertainty state ... enrich True/False/Unknown model. A decision may have Determinate, Sensitive, Underdetermined, Robust depending on the uncertainty structure.
statement: Extends the earlier True/False/Unknown model with decision-level uncertainty states: Determinate, Sensitive, Underdetermined, Robust.

anchor: 82.67 — Experiment 32 ... Decision A wins under 95% of plausible states. Expected: RobustlyA rather than simply A. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 32: a decision that wins in 95% of plausible states should be labeled RobustlyA rather than an unqualified A; result PASS.

anchor: 82.68 — Decision robustness ... Decision A is robust if ∀u∈U: D(u)=A. This is much stronger than D(E[u])=A.
statement: Defines decision robustness formally: A is robust over uncertainty set U if D(u)=A for all u∈U — much stronger than merely D(E[u])=A (decision at the expected value).

anchor: 82.69 — Experiment 33 ... Expected-value analysis selects A. But for some plausible parameter values, D=B. Expected: A is not robust. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 33: expected-value analysis selecting A while some plausible parameter values give D=B shows A is not robust by the 82.68 definition; result PASS.

anchor: 82.70 — This connects directly to Step 76 ... Decision=f(Knowledge,DecisionModel,Policy). Now: Decision=f(Knowledge,Uncertainty,DecisionModel,Policy,Context). Knowledge itself contains uncertainty.
statement: Enriches Step 76's Decision=f(Knowledge,DecisionModel,Policy) formula to Decision=f(Knowledge,Uncertainty,DecisionModel,Policy,Context), noting Knowledge itself contains uncertainty.

type_signature.domain: Knowledge x Uncertainty x DecisionModel x Policy x Context

lineage_claims.quote: This connects directly to Step 76.

anchor: 82.71 — Full uncertainty-aware pipeline ... Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→Model→Prediction→Decision with uncertainty U_O→U_K→U_M→U_P→U_D. Every transformation must preserve the semantics of uncertainty.
statement: Restates the full pipeline with a parallel uncertainty-propagation chain U_O→U_K→U_M→U_P→U_D; the requirement is not monotonic increase but that every transformation preserves the semantics of uncertainty.

anchor: 82.72 — New invariants: I_UncertaintyPreservation, I_Dependence, I_ModelUncertainty, I_Calibration, I_EpistemicPrecision, I_DecisionSensitivity, I_UncertaintyImpact
statement: States seven new named invariants: I_UncertaintyPreservation (transformations must not silently discard material uncertainty), I_Dependence (dependencies between uncertain variables must be represented when material), I_ModelUncertainty (model-structure uncertainty must be distinguished from parameter uncertainty), I_Calibration (probabilistic claims should have defined semantics and empirical calibration where applicable), I_EpistemicPrecision (output precision must not misrepresent evidence quality), I_DecisionSensitivity (when uncertainty can change the selected action, sensitivity must remain visible), I_UncertaintyImpact (material upstream evidence changes must permit identification of affected downstream knowledge/decisions).

anchor: 82.73 — Step 82 verdict: STEP 82 — PASS ... KnowledgeOS cannot merely store confidence. It needs a mathematically meaningful uncertainty model and must preserve that uncertainty through transformations. Statistics+Bayesian inference+Causal reasoning+Decision theory+Governance+Software architecture.
statement: Records Step 82 verdict PASS with the conclusion that KnowledgeOS needs a mathematically meaningful uncertainty model preserved through transformations, connecting Statistics, Bayesian inference, Causal reasoning, Decision theory, Governance, and Software architecture.

anchor: Current model after Step 82 ... Reality→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→CausalModel→Prediction→DecisionModel→Decision→Authority→Action→Outcome→Observation, with three critical cross-cutting structures: Provenance, Uncertainty, Governance. WorldModel≠ValueModel≠PolicyModel≠ExecutionModel.
statement: Presents the cumulative KnowledgeOS pipeline as a closed loop Reality→Observation→Evidence→Knowledge→CausalModel→Prediction→DecisionModel→Decision→Authority→Action→Outcome→Observation, cross-cut by Provenance, Uncertainty and Governance, restating WorldModel≠ValueModel≠PolicyModel≠ExecutionModel.

anchor: Step 83 — Next mathematical boundary: temporal reasoning ... Knowledge_t, Architecture_t, Policy_t, DecisionModel_t, AgentAuthority_t, SystemState_t. We need Truth at Time and potentially Truth over Interval.
statement: Previews Step 83: since KnowledgeOS objects are all time-indexed (Knowledge_t, Architecture_t, Policy_t, DecisionModel_t, AgentAuthority_t, SystemState_t), ordinary Truth is insufficient — the next step needs 'Truth at Time' and 'Truth over Interval', covering temporal knowledge, event vs processing time, validity intervals, temporal provenance, historical reconstruction, temporal causality, late-arriving evidence, policy effective dates, architectural evolution, and time-dependent decisions.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 83 will therefore examine: temporal knowledge; event time vs processing time; validity intervals...

anchor: We now move from historical reasoning to causal reasoning about alternatives ... Step 84 asks: What would have happened if we had done something different?
statement: Frames Step 84 as moving from Step 83's historical question ('what was true at time t') to the counterfactual question 'what would have happened if we had done something different', called a fundamentally different mathematical question.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 83 established that KnowledgeOS can ask: What was true at time t?

anchor: 84.1 — Prediction is not counterfactual reasoning ... P(Y|X=x) ... P(Y_x'|X=x). These are not generally equal.
statement: Distinguishes ordinary prediction P(Y|X=x) from the counterfactual question P(Y_x'|X=x) ('what would Y have been if X had been x' instead'), noting they are not generally equal.

anchor: 84.2 — Experiment 1: correlation mistaken for intervention ... P(Y|X=1)=0.8. KnowledgeOS concludes setting X=1 will cause Y with probability 0.8. Expected: INVALID because P(Y|X) is observational, does not automatically equal P(Y|do(X)). Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: inferring a causal claim ('setting X=1 will cause Y with probability 0.8') directly from an observational conditional P(Y|X=1)=0.8 is INVALID because P(Y|X) does not automatically equal P(Y|do(X)); result PASS.

anchor: 84.3 — Intervention ... do(X=x) means set X to x, rather than merely observing that X=x. P(Y|do(X=x)) is a causal quantity.
statement: Defines the do-operator: do(X=x) means setting X to x rather than merely observing X=x; P(Y|do(X=x)) is a causal quantity.

anchor: 84.4 — Experiment 2 ... P(Y|X=1)=0.9 but X is strongly influenced by Z. Expected: KnowledgeOS must not automatically infer P(Y|do(X=1))=0.9. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: when X is strongly influenced by a third variable Z, an observational P(Y|X=1)=0.9 must not be automatically equated with the interventional P(Y|do(X=1))=0.9; result PASS.

anchor: 84.5 — Confounding ... Z→X and Z→Y. Then X and Y may be correlated even if X↛Y. This is the classic confounding problem.
statement: Defines confounding: if Z causes both X and Y, X and Y may be correlated even absent a direct causal link X→Y.

anchor: 84.6 — Experiment 3 ... Architecture teams using technology X have fewer incidents, but highly experienced teams are more likely to choose X. Expected: 'Technology X causes fewer incidents' is not established merely by observing the correlation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3 (engineering example of confounding): team experience Z affects both technology choice X and incident rate Y, so the claim 'technology X causes fewer incidents' is not established by correlation alone; result PASS.

anchor: 84.7 — Causal graph ... Z→X, Z→Y, and potentially X→Y. KnowledgeOS should preserve this distinction.
statement: Proposes representing causal structure as a graph (Z→X, Z→Y, potentially X→Y) that KnowledgeOS should preserve.

anchor: 84.8 — Experiment 4: intervention simulation ... do(X=1). The causal graph changes because the incoming causes of X are removed for the intervention (Z→X is cut). Expected: KnowledgeOS distinguishes Observed(X=1) from Intervened(X=1). Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: representing an intervention do(X=1) must cut incoming causal edges into X (graph surgery) and distinguish Observed(X=1) from Intervened(X=1); result PASS.

anchor: 84.9 — Structural causal model ... X=f_X(Z,U_X), Y=f_Y(X,Z,U_Y). Z observed causal variables; U_X,U_Y exogenous factors. do(X=x) replaces X=f_X(...) with X=x.
statement: Introduces a structural causal model with structural equations X=f_X(Z,U_X), Y=f_Y(X,Z,U_Y) (Z observed causal variables, U_X/U_Y exogenous noise); an intervention do(X=x) replaces the equation for X with the constant x.

anchor: 84.10 — Experiment 5 ... System predicts the result of an intervention while still allowing the original causal mechanism to determine X. Expected: IncorrectCounterfactual. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 5: failing to replace X's structural equation (i.e. still letting the original mechanism determine X) when simulating an intervention produces IncorrectCounterfactual; result PASS.

anchor: 84.11 — Potential outcomes ... Y_0 outcome if X=0, Y_1 outcome if X=1. Individual causal effect tau=Y_1-Y_0.
statement: Introduces the potential-outcomes framework: Y_0/Y_1 as outcomes under X=0/X=1, and individual causal effect tau=Y_1-Y_0.

anchor: 84.12 — Fundamental problem of causal inference ... For one historical case, we can normally observe only one potential outcome. Y_0 is counterfactual. We cannot directly observe both potential outcomes for the same historical instance.
statement: States the fundamental problem of causal inference: for any single historical instance only one potential outcome (e.g. Y_1 given X=1) is observed; the other (Y_0) is inherently counterfactual and unobservable for that same instance.

anchor: 84.13 — Experiment 6 ... A deployment used architecture A, observed Y_A. KnowledgeOS claims it knows exactly what would have happened under architecture B. Expected: NotIdentifiable unless sufficient causal assumptions/evidence exist. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: claiming exact knowledge of the counterfactual outcome under architecture B (having only observed outcome Y_A under A) is NotIdentifiable unless sufficient causal assumptions/evidence exist; result PASS.

anchor: 84.14 — This is a crucial limitation ... KnowledgeOS must distinguish ObservedOutcome from CounterfactualOutcome. The second is a model-based inference.
statement: States as a crucial limitation that ObservedOutcome must be distinguished from CounterfactualOutcome, the latter being an inherently model-based inference rather than an observation.

anchor: 84.15 — Counterfactual architecture decision ... A=microservices was chosen. What would have happened if we had chosen a modular monolith? KnowledgeOS can potentially estimate P(Y_monolith|evidence,model). But this requires assumptions.
statement: Worked engineering example: estimating P(Y_monolith|evidence,model) as the counterfactual for an actual microservices choice requires explicit causal assumptions.

anchor: 84.16 — Experiment 7 ... KnowledgeOS responds 'The modular monolith would definitely have reduced operational cost.' No causal evidence or model supports this. Expected: UnsupportedCounterfactual. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: an unqualified counterfactual claim ('would definitely have reduced cost') with no supporting causal evidence/model is UnsupportedCounterfactual; result PASS.

anchor: 84.17 — Counterfactual assumptions ... CF=(Intervention,Model,Evidence,Assumptions,OutcomeDistribution). Then the result becomes auditable.
statement: Defines a counterfactual as a structured tuple CF=(Intervention,Model,Evidence,Assumptions,OutcomeDistribution) so that its result becomes auditable.

type_signature.domain: Intervention x Model x Evidence x Assumptions

anchor: 84.18 — Experiment 8 ... Counterfactual do(X=B) is estimated using causal model M, evidence E, assumptions A. Expected: the system can identify M,E,A. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: confirms the system can identify the (M,E,A) components underlying a given counterfactual do(X=B); result PASS.

anchor: 84.19 — Structural versus predictive models ... predictive model Y=f(X). causal model Y=f(X,Z,U). The distinction matters because interventions modify the generating process.
statement: Distinguishes predictive models (Y=f(X)) from causal/structural models (Y=f(X,Z,U)); the distinction matters because interventions modify the generating process, which only the causal model captures correctly.

anchor: 84.20 — Experiment 9 ... ML model predicts Failure=f(Technology,TeamSize). KnowledgeOS uses it directly to answer 'what happens if we force Technology X?' Expected: CausalValidityNotEstablished. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: using a purely predictive ML model directly to answer an interventional question ('what happens if we force Technology X') is CausalValidityNotEstablished; result PASS.

anchor: 84.21 — Counterfactual uncertainty ... Instead of Y_B=70, we may obtain E[Y_B]=70 with 95% CI=[60,80]. Or an entire P(Y_B).
statement: Extends counterfactual outcomes to carry uncertainty: rather than a point Y_B=70, represent E[Y_B]=70 with a 95% CI=[60,80] or a full distribution P(Y_B).

anchor: 84.22 — Experiment 10 ... Counterfactual prediction 70±15. System stores 70. Expected: UncertaintyLoss. Result: PASS. This connects Step 84 directly to Step 82.
statement: Experiment 10: storing a counterfactual prediction of 70±15 as a bare 70 (dropping uncertainty) is UncertaintyLoss; result PASS; explicitly links Step 84 to Step 82's uncertainty-propagation invariants.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects Step 84 directly to Step 82.

anchor: 84.23 — Counterfactual comparison ... Delta=Y_B-Y_A. E[Delta] is the expected benefit of choosing B instead of A.
statement: Defines the counterfactual comparison Delta=Y_B-Y_A and its expectation E[Delta] as the expected benefit of choosing B over A.

anchor: 84.24 — Experiment 11 ... Cost_A=€100k. E[Cost_B]=€80k. Expected: E[Delta]=-€20k. But uncertainty 95% interval=[-€50k,+€10k]. Correct conclusion: B appears cheaper on average, but the result is uncertain. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: a counterfactual cost comparison (E[Delta]=-€20k, 95% CI=[-€50k,+€10k]) concludes B appears cheaper on average but the result remains uncertain; result PASS.

anchor: 84.25 — Counterfactual regret ... Regret(A)=Y_best-Y_A. But the best alternative outcome may itself be counterfactual. Therefore regret estimates carry uncertainty.
statement: Defines Regret(A)=Y_best-Y_A and notes that since Y_best is itself typically counterfactual, regret estimates inherently carry uncertainty.

anchor: 84.26 — Experiment 12 ... 'How much did we lose by not choosing B?' KnowledgeOS produces €2.3M as an exact number. Expected: FalseCounterfactualPrecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: producing an exact-number regret estimate (€2.3M) for a counterfactual loss is FalseCounterfactualPrecision; result PASS.

anchor: 84.27 — Counterfactuals are model-relative ... 'What would have happened?' is incomplete. More precise: 'What would have happened under model M, assumptions A, and intervention I?' Counterfactual(M,A,I).
statement: States as a fundamental philosophical/mathematical point that counterfactual questions are model-relative: the well-formed question is Counterfactual(M,A,I), not a bare 'what would have happened'.

anchor: 84.28 — Experiment 13 ... Two plausible causal models M_1 and M_2 produce different counterfactual outcomes. Expected: KnowledgeOS reports model sensitivity. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: when M_1 and M_2 produce different counterfactual outcomes for the same intervention, KnowledgeOS must report this model sensitivity; result PASS.

anchor: 84.29 — Model disagreement ... M_1: P(Y_B)=0.8, M_2: P(Y_B)=0.4. The correct output is not automatically 0.6. We need a justified model combination.
statement: Warns that when two causal models disagree (P(Y_B)=0.8 vs 0.4), simple averaging to 0.6 is not automatically correct — a justified model-combination method is needed.

anchor: 84.30 — Experiment 14 ... System averages model outputs (0.8+0.4)/2=0.6 without assigning model probabilities. Expected: UnsupportedAggregation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: naive averaging of disagreeing model outputs without justified model probabilities is UnsupportedAggregation; result PASS.

anchor: 84.31 — Causal assumptions become first-class knowledge ... A1: NoUnmeasuredConfounding. A2: StableTreatmentDefinition. A3: NoInterference. A4: CorrectTemporalOrdering. Each assumption has evidence status.
statement: Names four standard causal-inference assumptions as first-class knowledge objects with evidence status: A1 NoUnmeasuredConfounding, A2 StableTreatmentDefinition (SUTVA-related), A3 NoInterference, A4 CorrectTemporalOrdering.

anchor: 84.32 — Experiment 15 ... Counterfactual depends on A1. Later evidence contradicts A1. Expected: CounterfactualInvalidation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: when evidence later contradicts an assumption (A1) a dependent counterfactual relied on, the counterfactual must undergo CounterfactualInvalidation; result PASS.

anchor: 84.33 — Counterfactual dependency graph ... Evidence→CausalModel→Counterfactual→Decision. If evidence changes, Counterfactual may need recalculation.
statement: Proposes a dependency chain Evidence→CausalModel→Counterfactual→Decision, so that evidence changes propagate to require counterfactual recalculation.

anchor: 84.34 — Experiment 16 ... Evidence source is revoked, supporting a causal relationship used by CF_1,CF_2,CF_3. Expected: All affected counterfactuals become RevalidationRequired. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: revoking an evidence source underlying three counterfactuals (CF_1,CF_2,CF_3) must mark all three RevalidationRequired; result PASS.

anchor: 84.35 — Counterfactual decision support ... allows KnowledgeOS to answer 'What if we reject this change?' rather than merely 'What happens if we approve?'
statement: Argues counterfactual reasoning lets KnowledgeOS answer rejection-side questions ('what if we reject this change') not just approval-side predictions.

anchor: 84.36 — Experiment 17 ... Two possible decisions D_A and D_B. KnowledgeOS estimates P(Y|do(D_A)) and P(Y|do(D_B)). Expected: Compare distributions, not just point estimates. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: comparing two candidate decisions must compare full outcome distributions P(Y|do(D_A)) vs P(Y|do(D_B)), not just point estimates; result PASS.

anchor: 84.37 — Multi-step interventions ... do(A_1)→do(A_2)→do(A_3). S_{t+1}=F(S_t,A_1), S_{t+2}=F(S_{t+1},A_2). The counterfactual concerns a trajectory, not a single point.
statement: Extends counterfactual reasoning to sequences of interventions do(A_1)→do(A_2)→do(A_3) with state transitions S_{t+1}=F(S_t,A_1), noting the counterfactual concerns a whole trajectory, not a single point.

anchor: 84.38 — Experiment 18 ... Architecture migration requires A_1,A_2,A_3. KnowledgeOS evaluates only the first intervention. Expected: IncompleteCounterfactual. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: evaluating only the first step (A_1) of a three-step migration counterfactual (A_1,A_2,A_3) is IncompleteCounterfactual; result PASS.

anchor: 84.39 — Trajectory counterfactual ... P(S_{t:t+H}|do(A_{0:H})). This connects directly to Step 80's dynamic system model.
statement: Defines a trajectory counterfactual P(S_{t:t+H}|do(A_{0:H})) over a horizon H, explicitly linked to Step 80's dynamic system model.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects directly to Step 80's dynamic system model.

anchor: 84.40 — Experiment 19 ... Alternative architecture looks beneficial at t+1 but creates greater migration risk at t+6. Expected: LongHorizonCounterfactualAnalysis. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: an alternative that looks beneficial short-term (t+1) but riskier long-term (t+6) requires LongHorizonCounterfactualAnalysis; result PASS.

anchor: 84.41 — Interference between agents ... Y_i=f(X_i,X_j,...), standard individual-treatment assumptions can fail. Especially relevant to KnowledgeOS because we explicitly modeled interacting agents in Step 79.
statement: Notes that when one agent's outcome depends on other agents' actions (Y_i=f(X_i,X_j,...)), standard individual-treatment (SUTVA-style) assumptions fail — explicitly linked to Step 79's interacting-agent model.

lineage_claims.quote: This is especially relevant to KnowledgeOS because we explicitly modeled interacting agents in Step 79.

anchor: 84.42 — Experiment 20 ... Agent A changes a shared service. Agent B's outcome changes even though B's own action remains constant. Expected: InterferenceDetected. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: agent B's outcome changing due to agent A's action on a shared service (despite B's own action being constant) must be InterferenceDetected; result PASS.

anchor: 84.43 — Therefore individual counterfactuals may be insufficient ... Instead of Y_i(X_i), we may need Y_i(X_1,...,X_n). This is another reason KnowledgeOS needs system-level models.
statement: Concludes individual-level counterfactuals Y_i(X_i) may be insufficient under interference; a system-level model Y_i(X_1,...,X_n) covering all agents' actions may be needed.

anchor: 84.44 — Experiment 21 ... 'What would happen if agent A changed behavior?' But A interacts strongly with B and C. Expected: counterfactual model should account for B,C responses where material. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: a counterfactual about agent A's behavior must account for material responses from interacting agents B and C; result PASS.

anchor: 84.45 — Policy counterfactual ... What if policy P_2 had been active instead of P_1? do(Policy=P_2). Policy changes may alter agent decisions, authority, action space, system state. Policy counterfactuals can propagate through the entire system.
statement: Defines policy counterfactuals do(Policy=P_2) as potentially propagating through agent decisions, authority, action space, and system state — a system-wide effect, not a local one.

anchor: 84.46 — Experiment 22 ... Historical policy P_1 allowed A. Alternative P_2 would have prohibited A. System evaluates only the immediate policy decision and ignores downstream effects. Expected: IncompletePolicyCounterfactual. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: evaluating only the immediate effect of a policy counterfactual (P_1 vs P_2) while ignoring downstream system effects is IncompletePolicyCounterfactual; result PASS.

anchor: 84.47 — Architecture counterfactual ... do(Architecture=A_2) can change Dependencies, Operations, Security, Cost, TeamStructure. Architectural counterfactuals are multi-dimensional.
statement: Notes that an architecture counterfactual do(Architecture=A_2) can affect Dependencies, Operations, Security, Cost, and TeamStructure simultaneously — architectural counterfactuals are inherently multi-dimensional.

anchor: 84.48 — Experiment 23 ... Architecture B improves coupling but increases operational complexity. Expected: KnowledgeOS should expose both effects rather than reducing the comparison to one score without justification. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: architecture B improving coupling while worsening operational complexity must have both effects exposed, not collapsed into an unjustified single score; result PASS.

anchor: 84.49 — Multi-objective counterfactuals ... Y=(Cost,Risk,Performance,Maintainability). Architecture decisions are vector-valued. There may be no universally superior alternative.
statement: Formalizes architecture-decision outcomes as vector-valued Y=(Cost,Risk,Performance,Maintainability), noting there may be no universally superior alternative.

anchor: 84.50 — Experiment 24 ... Architecture A: Cost=80,Risk=40. Architecture B: Cost=60,Risk=60. Expected: Neither necessarily dominates the other. Result: PASS. This connects to our earlier multi-objective decision theory.
statement: Experiment 24: architectures A (Cost=80,Risk=40) and B (Cost=60,Risk=60) show neither dominates the other under multi-objective comparison; result PASS; links to earlier multi-objective decision theory.

anchor: 84.51 — Pareto frontier ... An alternative is Pareto-dominated if another alternative is at least as good in every relevant dimension and strictly better in one. KnowledgeOS can potentially eliminate dominated alternatives. But it should not invent preferences between non-dominated alternatives.
statement: Defines Pareto dominance and states KnowledgeOS may eliminate dominated alternatives but must not invent preferences between non-dominated (Pareto-optimal) alternatives.

anchor: 84.52 — Experiment 25 ... A and B are both Pareto-optimal. System selects A without an explicit value model. Expected: UnsupportedPreference. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: selecting A over B when both are Pareto-optimal, absent an explicit value model, is UnsupportedPreference; result PASS.

anchor: 84.53 — Counterfactual and ethics/governance ... Feasible ≠ Permitted. An intervention can be CausallyModelable but GovernanceForbidden.
statement: States Feasible ≠ Permitted: an intervention can be CausallyModelable while being GovernanceForbidden.

anchor: 84.54 — Experiment 26 ... 'What if we bypassed the required architecture review?' Technically modelable. But policy prohibits it. Expected: CounterfactualCanBeAnalyzed while ActionNotAuthorized. Result: PASS. This distinction is essential.
statement: Experiment 26: a counterfactual about bypassing a required architecture review can be analyzed (CounterfactualCanBeAnalyzed) while the actual action remains ActionNotAuthorized — called essential; result PASS.

anchor: 84.55 — Counterfactual versus recommendation ... P(Y|do(B))>P(Y|do(A)) does not automatically mean Recommend(B). Recommendation additionally depends on Policy, Authority, Values, Constraints.
statement: States that a superior estimated outcome (P(Y|do(B))>P(Y|do(A))) does not automatically justify Recommend(B); recommendation additionally depends on Policy, Authority, Values, and Constraints.

anchor: 84.56 — Experiment 27 ... B has better expected technical outcome. But violates a constitutional constraint. Expected: Recommendation(B)=False. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: option B, despite better expected technical outcome, must have Recommendation(B)=False when it violates a constitutional constraint; result PASS.

anchor: 84.57 — Counterfactual auditability ... Every important counterfactual should answer: intervention, model, evidence, assumptions, uncertainty, alternatives compared, governance constraints. This makes counterfactual reasoning auditable.
statement: Lists seven required disclosures for auditable counterfactual reasoning: intervention considered, model used, supporting evidence, assumptions made, remaining uncertainty, alternatives compared, and applicable governance constraints.

anchor: 84.58 — Experiment 28 ... System outputs 'Option B is better.' No model, evidence, assumptions, or uncertainty. Expected: CounterfactualAuditInsufficient. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: an unsupported output ('Option B is better') lacking model/evidence/assumptions/uncertainty is CounterfactualAuditInsufficient; result PASS.

anchor: 84.59 — Counterfactual provenance ... CF←Model←Evidence and CF←Assumptions. Then Decision←CF. This is consistent with our general provenance graph.
statement: States the counterfactual provenance chain CF←Model←Evidence, CF←Assumptions, Decision←CF, consistent with the project's general provenance graph.

anchor: 84.60 — New mathematical distinction ... Historical: what happened? Predictive: what is likely to happen? Counterfactual: what would have happened under an alternative intervention? These must never be collapsed.
statement: States the three-way distinction between Historical, Predictive, and Counterfactual questions, insisting they must never be collapsed into each other.

anchor: 84.61 — Experiment 29 ... KnowledgeOS uses a predictive model to answer a historical counterfactual question. Expected: SemanticModelMismatch. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: answering a historical-counterfactual question using a purely predictive model is a SemanticModelMismatch; result PASS.

anchor: 84.62 — The complete causal chain ... Evidence→CausalModel→Intervention→CounterfactualDistribution→Decision. With uncertainty U_E→U_M→U_{CF}→U_D. And governance Policy+Authority+Constraints must still govern the resulting action.
statement: Restates the complete causal-reasoning chain Evidence→CausalModel→Intervention→CounterfactualDistribution→Decision with a parallel uncertainty chain U_E→U_M→U_CF→U_D, noting governance (Policy+Authority+Constraints) still governs the resulting action.

anchor: 84.63 — New invariants: I_Intervention, I_CounterfactualProvenance, I_CounterfactualUncertainty, I_TemporalCausalSeparation, I_CounterfactualGovernance, I_Interference
