statement: Experiment 25: an unknown configuration version leaves runtime reconstruction incomplete even with a known application version; result PASS.

anchor: 106.54 — Runtime security ... UnauthorizedAccess, PrivilegeEscalation, ForbiddenConnection.
statement: Lists runtime security observability examples: UnauthorizedAccess, PrivilegeEscalation, ForbiddenConnection.

anchor: 106.55 — Experiment 26 ... Agent attempts unauthorized tool access. Runtime records Denied. Expected: security evidence can be linked to agent identity and policy. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: a denied unauthorized tool-access attempt must be linkable to agent identity and policy; result PASS.

anchor: 106.56 — Runtime privacy ... Observability ≠ UnlimitedDataExposure.
statement: States Observability ≠ UnlimitedDataExposure: observability must not compromise privacy.

anchor: 106.57 — Experiment 27 ... Runtime logs contain sensitive user information. Expected: KnowledgeOS architecture requires appropriate masking/access controls before that information becomes broadly available. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: sensitive runtime log information requires masking/access controls before broad availability; result PASS.

anchor: 106.58 — Runtime agent behavior ... we now return to Step 105. If Codex performs Action, runtime should be able to associate it with AgentIdentity.
statement: Explicitly returns to Step 105, requiring runtime association of agent actions with AgentIdentity.

lineage_claims.quote: We now return to Step 105.

anchor: 106.59 — Experiment 28 ... Runtime observes repository modification. Expected trace: Commit→AgentSession→Codex→Authorization. Result: PASS. If this chain cannot be established, agent assurance is incomplete.
statement: Experiment 28: a repository modification must trace Commit→AgentSession→Codex→Authorization, or agent assurance is incomplete; result PASS.

anchor: 106.60 — Runtime governance ... GovernanceRule→RuntimeControl→RuntimeEvidence. Rule: NoUnauthorizedDeployment. Runtime: DeploymentEvent. KnowledgeOS evaluates Compliant?
statement: Defines the runtime governance evaluation chain GovernanceRule→RuntimeControl→RuntimeEvidence, e.g. testing NoUnauthorizedDeployment against an observed DeploymentEvent.

anchor: 106.61 — Experiment 29 ... Deployment has no corresponding approval. Expected: GovernanceViolation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: a deployment with no corresponding approval is GovernanceViolation; result PASS.

anchor: 106.62 — Runtime architecture assurance ... RuntimeConformance(C,t) as C_runtime=(Architecture,Security,Governance,Configuration,Version,Dependency). Each dimension can have Pass/Fail/Unknown.
statement: Defines multidimensional RuntimeConformance(C,t)=(Architecture,Security,Governance,Configuration,Version,Dependency), each independently Pass/Fail/Unknown.

anchor: 106.63 — Experiment 30 ... Runtime is architecturally conformant. Security evidence is unavailable. Expected: Architecture=Pass but Security=Unknown. Not FullyAssured. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: architectural Pass alongside Security=Unknown must not be reported as FullyAssured; result PASS.

anchor: 106.64 — Runtime confidence ... the final assurance statement should be multi-dimensional, e.g. Architecture:Pass, Security:Pass, Governance:Unknown, Privacy:Pass, Observability:Partial. Much more useful than a single percentage.
statement: States the final assurance statement should be a multi-dimensional structured breakdown, not a single percentage score.

anchor: 106.65 — Runtime architecture graph ... Governance->Architecture->Code->Deployment->Runtime Graph->{Trace,Event,Metric}->Evidence->Knowledge->Governance. This is essentially the complete KnowledgeOS feedback architecture.
statement: Presents the complete KnowledgeOS feedback architecture diagram from Governance through Runtime Graph (Trace/Event/Metric) to Evidence/Knowledge back to Governance.

anchor: 106.66 — The architecture is becoming self-observing ... The system no longer merely stores Architecture. It observes RuntimeArchitecture. And compares Expected↔Actual.
statement: States the architecture is becoming self-observing: it observes RuntimeArchitecture and compares Expected↔Actual, not merely stores Architecture.

anchor: 106.67 — Architecture drift becomes a first-class object ... Drift=(ExpectedState,ObservedState,Timestamp,Evidence,Impact,Status). Possible status: New, Investigating, Accepted, Remediating, Resolved, Exception.
statement: Defines Drift=(ExpectedState,ObservedState,Timestamp,Evidence,Impact,Status) with a six-value status lifecycle (New/Investigating/Accepted/Remediating/Resolved/Exception).

anchor: 106.68 — Experiment 31 ... Drift is detected. Architecture team approves it as intentional. Expected: DriftStatus=Accepted/Exception. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 31: an intentional, approved drift is DriftStatus=Accepted/Exception; result PASS.

anchor: 106.69 — Drift should not disappear ... Even accepted drift should retain Reason, Authority, Validity. Otherwise it becomes undocumented architecture.
statement: States even accepted drift must retain Reason/Authority/Validity, or it becomes undocumented architecture.

anchor: 106.70 — Experiment 32 ... Architecture exception expires. Runtime still exhibits the deviation. Expected: ExceptionExpired→GovernanceFinding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 32: a continuing deviation after exception expiry produces ExceptionExpired→GovernanceFinding; result PASS.

anchor: 106.71 — This is a powerful property ... KnowledgeOS can detect TemporalGovernanceDrift. Not merely TechnicalDrift.
statement: States KnowledgeOS can detect TemporalGovernanceDrift (drift caused by expiry), distinct from mere TechnicalDrift.

anchor: 106.72 — Runtime and organizational reality ... Technical reality (what software/infrastructure does) versus Organizational reality (what people have decided and authorized). KnowledgeOS must compare both. TechnicalReality↔OrganizationalIntent.
statement: Distinguishes TechnicalReality from OrganizationalIntent as two realities KnowledgeOS must compare.

anchor: 106.73 — Experiment 33 ... Organization decides service X must be retired. Runtime continues operating service X. Expected: OrganizationalIntent ≠ TechnicalReality. Result: PASS. This becomes a governance/architecture finding.
statement: Experiment 33: a still-running service despite an organizational retirement decision demonstrates OrganizationalIntent ≠ TechnicalReality, becoming a governance/architecture finding; result PASS.

anchor: 106.74 — This closes the larger loop ... Intent→Governance→Architecture→Implementation→Deployment→Runtime and Runtime→Evidence→Knowledge→Governance→Intent'. This is the architecture we were trying to establish from the beginning.
statement: States the closed bidirectional loop Intent→Governance→Architecture→Implementation→Deployment→Runtime and Runtime→Evidence→Knowledge→Governance→Intent', called the architecture sought from the beginning.

anchor: 106.75 — Runtime conformance matrix ... Component topology, Versions, Configuration, Dependencies, Security boundaries, Agent actions, Governance controls, Observability, Architecture drift, Historical reconstruction -- Expected/Observed/Evidence/Status, all TBD.
statement: Presents a ten-dimension runtime conformance matrix (Expected/Observed/Evidence/Status), all cells marked TBD pending real-system assessment.

anchor: 106.76 — Runtime invariants: I_RuntimeIdentity, I_RuntimeProvenance, I_DesiredActual, I_Drift, I_DriftGovernance, I_RuntimeEvidence, I_HistoricalRuntime
statement: States seven new runtime invariants: I_RuntimeIdentity (every material runtime component must be identifiable against its logical component and deployed version), I_RuntimeProvenance (material runtime observations must retain sufficient provenance for when/where/how they were observed), I_DesiredActual (desired architecture and observed runtime state must remain distinguishable), I_Drift (material deviations between expected and observed architecture must be detectable), I_DriftGovernance (intentional deviations must have explicit authority/scope/validity), I_RuntimeEvidence (material runtime observations must be capable of becoming provenance-bearing evidence), I_HistoricalRuntime (material historical runtime states required for assurance/incident analysis must remain reconstructable).

anchor: 106.77 — Step 106 verdict: STEP 106 — RUNTIME MODEL: PASS at the architectural level. But the empirical implementation status remains RuntimeConformance=TBD. And that distinction is becoming increasingly important.
statement: Records Step 106 verdict as architectural-level PASS with empirical RuntimeConformance explicitly TBD.

anchor: 106.78 — Where we stand now ... After Steps 101-106: Inventory, Semantics, Governance, Agents, Runtime all Defined architecturally but Needs evidence for actual implementation. We have not yet proven that the current software implements the full architecture. But we now have a sufficiently precise m
statement: Summarizes all five conformance layers (Inventory/Semantics/Governance/Agents/Runtime) as architecturally Defined but empirically Needs evidence, concluding a sufficiently precise model now exists to perform the proof.

anchor: Step 107 — Architecture Drift Analysis ... A_I vs A_C vs A_R, classify every discrepancy into: 1. Intent is wrong, 2. Implementation is wrong (A_C≠A_I), 3. Deployment is wrong (A_D≠A_C), 4. Runtime is wrong (A_R≠A_D), 5. Difference is intentional (Authorized), 6. We simply do not know (Unknown). Ste
statement: Previews Step 107: classifying every A_I/A_C/A_R discrepancy into six categories (intent wrong, implementation wrong, deployment wrong, runtime wrong, intentional/authorized, or unknown), moving beyond treating every mismatch as a generic bug.

anchor: Step 106 established A_I→A_C→A_D→A_R. Step 107 asks: when these four differ, what exactly does the difference mean? Not every difference is a defect.
statement: Frames Step 107's question: what a discrepancy in A_I/A_C/A_D/A_R actually means, since not every difference is a defect.

anchor: 107.1 — The central principle ... We must never automatically conclude A_I≠A_R ⇒ ArchitectureWrong. Instead Difference→Classification→Decision.
statement: States the central principle: A_I≠A_R does not automatically mean ArchitectureWrong; instead Difference→Classification→Decision.

anchor: 107.2 — Six possible explanations ... D1 Architecture defect (A_I old→new), D2 Implementation defect (A_C≠A_I), D3 Deployment defect (A_D≠A_C), D4 Runtime defect (A_R≠A_D), D5 Authorized deviation (A_R≠A_I but AuthorizedDeviation=True), D6 Unknown (EvidenceInsufficient). This sixth state is essentia
statement: Defines six mutually exclusive discrepancy categories D1-D6 (architecture defect, implementation defect, deployment defect, runtime defect, authorized deviation, unknown/insufficient evidence), with D6 called essential.

anchor: 107.3 — Experiment 1: architecture obsolete ... A later approved architecture decision replaces B with C. Runtime: A→C. Expected: not a runtime violation. The architecture model is outdated. Result: D1 — Architecture evolution.
statement: Experiment 1: runtime A→C reflecting an already-approved architecture change (B replaced by C) is classified D1 — Architecture evolution, not a runtime violation.

anchor: 107.4 — Experiment 2: implementation defect ... Architecture says A↛Database. Source code contains A→Database. No exception exists. Result: D2 — Implementation defect.
statement: Experiment 2: source code containing a forbidden A→Database connection with no exception is classified D2 — Implementation defect.

anchor: 107.5 — Experiment 3: deployment defect ... Source contains Version=5.0. Production runs Version=4.9. Result: D3 — Deployment drift.
statement: Experiment 3: production running an older version (4.9) than source (5.0) is classified D3 — Deployment drift.

anchor: 107.6 — Experiment 4: runtime defect ... Correct version is deployed. Configuration is correct. Runtime nevertheless opens a forbidden connection. Result: D4 — Runtime violation.
statement: Experiment 4: a forbidden connection opened despite correct version/configuration is classified D4 — Runtime violation.

anchor: 107.7 — Experiment 5: authorized deviation ... Architecture requires DatabaseA. A temporary migration exception authorizes DatabaseB until 2026-12-31. Runtime uses B. Result: D5 — Authorized deviation.
statement: Experiment 5: runtime using DatabaseB under an authorized temporary exception (valid until 2026-12-31) is classified D5 — Authorized deviation.

anchor: 107.8 — Experiment 6: insufficient evidence ... Architecture says A→B. Repository evidence is incomplete. Runtime traces are unavailable. Result: D6 — Unknown. We must not invent the answer.
statement: Experiment 6: incomplete repository evidence and unavailable runtime traces yield D6 — Unknown, with the answer explicitly not invented.

anchor: 107.9 — Why this classification matters ... Mistake A: change documentation to match reality (A_I:=A_R), which can hide defects. Mistake B: declare runtime nonconformance without understanding intentional changes. Both are dangerous.
statement: Names two dangerous mistakes the classification model prevents: silently redefining A_I:=A_R (hiding defects) and declaring nonconformance without recognizing legitimate intentional changes.

anchor: 107.10 — Architecture drift object ... Drift=(Expected,Observed,Difference,Evidence,Classification,Impact,Authority,Validity,Resolution).
statement: Defines the full Drift object Drift=(Expected,Observed,Difference,Evidence,Classification,Impact,Authority,Validity,Resolution).

type_signature.codomain: Difference x Classification x Impact x Authority x Validity x Resolution

anchor: 107.11 — Expected versus observed ... ExpectedState and ObservedState. Delta=Observed-Expected.
statement: Defines Delta=Observed-Expected as the measurable difference between ExpectedState and ObservedState.

anchor: 107.12 — Experiment 7 ... Expected Replicas=4. Observed Replicas=3. Delta=-1. Expected: a measurable drift finding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: Replicas=4 expected vs 3 observed gives Delta=-1, a measurable drift finding; result PASS.

anchor: 107.13 — Semantic drift ... Architecture still calls something 'Repository.' But the implementation now represents 'Knowledge Source.' That can indicate a bounded-context or ubiquitous-language problem.
statement: Defines SemanticDrift: architecture terminology diverging from actual implemented meaning, indicating a possible bounded-context/ubiquitous-language problem.

anchor: 107.14 — Experiment 8 ... Code uses KnowledgeItem but its semantics have evolved into DecisionRecord. Expected: potential semantic drift. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: a KnowledgeItem class whose actual semantics have evolved into DecisionRecord is potential semantic drift; result PASS.

anchor: 107.15 — Governance drift ... GovernanceRule ≠ ImplementedControl. Rule: all production changes require approval. Implementation allows direct production deployment. Expected: GovernanceDrift.
statement: Defines GovernanceDrift: a stated rule (approval required) diverging from the actually implemented control (direct deployment allowed).

anchor: 107.16 — Agent drift ... KnowledgeOS says Claude→KnowledgeOS. But .claude/ contains an independent copy of authoritative architecture knowledge. Expected: AgentBoundaryDrift.
statement: Defines AgentBoundaryDrift: .claude/ accumulating an independent authoritative-knowledge copy diverging from the intended Claude→KnowledgeOS pointer relationship, extending Step 105's agent-boundary concerns.

anchor: 107.17 — Experiment 9 ... .codex/ begins accumulating its own authoritative architecture rules. Expected: potential divergence from KnowledgeOS. Result: PASS — drift detectable.
statement: Experiment 9: .codex/ accumulating its own authoritative rules is potential divergence, detectable as agent drift; result PASS.

anchor: 107.18 — Security drift ... Expected Agent↛ProductionDB. Observed Agent→ProductionDB. Expected: SecurityDrift. This may be higher severity than ordinary architecture drift.
statement: Defines SecurityDrift (an observed forbidden Agent→ProductionDB connection), noted as potentially higher severity than ordinary drift.

anchor: 107.19 — Configuration drift ... Expected PolicyMode=Enforced. Observed PolicyMode=Permissive. Expected: ConfigurationDrift.
statement: Defines ConfigurationDrift, e.g. PolicyMode observed as Permissive against an expected Enforced.

anchor: 107.20 — Dependency drift ... Expected A→B. Observed A→C. Expected: DependencyDrift. But again DependencyDrift ≠ Violation until classified.
statement: Defines DependencyDrift, reiterating it is not automatically a Violation until classified.

anchor: 107.21 — Version drift ... Expected ComponentVersion=3.7. Observed 3.6. Expected: VersionDrift.
statement: Defines VersionDrift for observed-vs-expected version mismatches.

anchor: 107.22 — Ownership drift ... Expected Owner=TeamA. Current organization says Owner=TeamB. Expected: GovernanceMetadataDrift. This may be less technically dangerous but highly relevant for accountability.
statement: Defines GovernanceMetadataDrift (ownership mismatch), noting it is less technically dangerous but highly relevant for accountability.

anchor: 107.23 — Drift severity ... Severity ∈ {Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational}.
statement: Defines a five-level drift severity scale: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational.

anchor: 107.24 — Experiment 10 ... Documentation formatting differs from the standard. Expected: potential Informational/Low.
statement: Experiment 10: a documentation-formatting discrepancy is potential Informational/Low severity.

anchor: 107.25 — Experiment 11 ... Agent can bypass production authorization. Expected: Critical/High. The exact severity requires organizational policy.
statement: Experiment 11: an agent capable of bypassing production authorization is Critical/High severity, with exact severity requiring organizational policy.

anchor: 107.26 — Impact ... Drift→AffectedComponents→AffectedCapabilities→BusinessImpact.
statement: Defines the impact-analysis chain Drift→AffectedComponents→AffectedCapabilities→BusinessImpact.

anchor: 107.27 — Experiment 12 ... Evidence storage changes. Dependency graph identifies governance, agent context, architecture verification as consumers. Expected: impact analysis identifies all three. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: an evidence-storage change's impact analysis correctly identifies all three affected consumers (governance, agent context, architecture verification); result PASS.

anchor: 107.28 — Drift propagation ... C_1→C_2→C_3. Impact(C_1)=TransitiveDependencies(C_1).
statement: Defines Impact(C_1)=TransitiveDependencies(C_1) for propagated drift impact through dependency chains.

anchor: 107.29 — Experiment 13 ... Schema change affects service A. A affects agent context. Agent context affects verification. Expected: impact analysis includes the complete chain. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a schema change's impact analysis must include the full transitive chain (service A→agent context→verification); result PASS.

anchor: 107.30 — Drift lifecycle ... Detected→Triaged→Classified→Assigned→Remediated→Verified→Closed.
statement: Defines the seven-stage drift lifecycle Detected→Triaged→Classified→Assigned→Remediated→Verified→Closed.

anchor: 107.31 — Experiment 14 ... Drift is detected and manually fixed. No verification occurs. Expected: NotClosed. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: a manually-fixed drift with no verification remains NotClosed; result PASS.

anchor: 107.32 — Remediation does not equal resolution ... Remediation ≠ Verification. A developer may say 'fixed.' KnowledgeOS should ask what evidence demonstrates that it is fixed?
statement: States Remediation ≠ Verification: an unverified developer claim of 'fixed' is not itself resolution evidence.

anchor: 107.33 — Experiment 15 ... Forbidden dependency removed. Static test passes. Runtime still uses the dependency. Expected: NotResolved. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: a static-test-passing but still-present-at-runtime forbidden dependency is NotResolved; result PASS.

anchor: 107.34 — Drift verification ... Resolution requires ExpectedState=ObservedState or AuthorizedDeviation.
statement: States drift resolution requires either ExpectedState=ObservedState or an AuthorizedDeviation.

anchor: 107.35 — Experiment 16 ... Expected A↛C. After remediation A↛C. Runtime evidence confirms. Expected: Resolved. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: runtime-confirmed remediation (A↛C restored) is Resolved; result PASS.

anchor: 107.36 — Architecture evolution ... sometimes the correct response is not remediation. It is architecture evolution: A_I→A_I'. This requires Decision+Authority+Rationale.
statement: States architecture evolution A_I→A_I' as an alternative to remediation, requiring Decision+Authority+Rationale.

anchor: 107.37 — Experiment 17 ... Runtime reveals that the original architecture unnecessarily constrains scalability. Architecture Board approves a new architecture. Expected: ArchitectureEvolution. Not ArchitectureViolation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: a board-approved architecture change in response to a discovered scalability constraint is ArchitectureEvolution, not ArchitectureViolation; result PASS.

anchor: 107.38 — The dangerous shortcut ... We must not do RuntimeDifference→UpdateArchitecture. Instead RuntimeDifference→Finding→Analysis→Decision. Only then ArchitectureUpdate.
statement: Forbids the shortcut RuntimeDifference→UpdateArchitecture, requiring RuntimeDifference→Finding→Analysis→Decision→ArchitectureUpdate instead.

anchor: 107.39 — This protects architectural integrity ... Otherwise KnowledgeOS could become a system that simply rationalizes whatever is already running. That would invert the purpose of governance.
statement: States the risk that unchecked runtime-to-architecture updates would invert governance's purpose into rationalizing whatever already runs.

anchor: 107.40 — Desired relationship ... Architecture→Governance→Engineering while also allowing Engineering→Evidence→ArchitectureEvolution. But the second path requires controlled decision-making.
statement: States the desired bidirectional relationship Architecture→Governance→Engineering and Engineering→Evidence→ArchitectureEvolution, the latter requiring controlled decision-making.

anchor: 107.41 — Drift and knowledge ... Drift→Evidence→Finding→Knowledge. That knowledge can reveal architectural weaknesses, undocumented dependencies, obsolete standards, process failures, runtime anomalies.
statement: Defines Drift→Evidence→Finding→Knowledge, revealing architectural weaknesses/undocumented dependencies/obsolete standards/process failures/runtime anomalies.

anchor: 107.42 — Experiment 18 ... Repeated drift occurs around the same architecture rule. Expected: KnowledgeOS identifies a recurring pattern. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: repeated drift around one rule must be identified as a recurring pattern; result PASS.

statement: States recurring drift on one rule should prompt examining whether the rule itself is unrealistic/poorly understood/poorly enforced, making governance empirical.

anchor: 107.44 — Experiment 19 ... Rule is violated 20 times. Every violation requires manual remediation. Expected: potential systemic governance problem. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: 20 repeated violations each requiring manual remediation is a potential systemic governance problem; result PASS.

anchor: 107.45 — Architecture debt ... Repeated drift can become ArchitectureDebt. But Debt ≠ Failure. It means known deviation requiring future attention.
statement: Defines ArchitectureDebt as recurring drift, explicitly Debt ≠ Failure, meaning known deviation requiring future attention.

anchor: 107.46 — Exception debt ... ExceptionCount can reveal that governance rules are too restrictive or the system is systematically bypassing them.
statement: States ExceptionCount as a signal for either overly restrictive rules or systematic bypass.

anchor: 107.47 — Experiment 20 ... A temporary exception is renewed 12 times. Expected: KnowledgeOS identifies ExceptionPattern. Result: PASS. This could trigger architectural review.
statement: Experiment 20: an exception renewed 12 times is identified as ExceptionPattern, potentially triggering architectural review; result PASS.

anchor: 107.48 — Drift and agents ... An agent can introduce changes very rapidly. ChangeVelocity↑ requires AssuranceAutomation↑.
statement: States rising agent-driven ChangeVelocity requires proportionally rising AssuranceAutomation.

anchor: 107.49 — Experiment 21 ... Codex generates 50 changes per day. Manual architecture review remains the only control. Expected: governance bottleneck. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: 50 daily Codex changes with only manual review is a governance bottleneck; result PASS.

anchor: 107.50 — This is why KnowledgeOS must be executable ... if every agent action requires a human to manually inspect everything, scalability collapses. LowRisk→AutomatedControls. HighRisk→HumanGovernance.
statement: States the necessity of risk-routed controls: LowRisk→AutomatedControls, HighRisk→HumanGovernance, to avoid scalability collapse.

anchor: 107.51 — Risk-based assurance ... RequiredAssurance=f(Risk,Impact,Authority,ChangeType).
statement: Defines RequiredAssurance=f(Risk,Impact,Authority,ChangeType).

type_signature.domain: Risk x Impact x Authority x ChangeType

anchor: 107.52 — Experiment 22 ... Formatting change: Risk=Low. Expected: automated validation sufficient. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: a low-risk formatting change needs only automated validation; result PASS.

anchor: 107.53 — Experiment 23 ... Production security boundary change: Risk=High. Expected: stronger approval and verification. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: a high-risk security-boundary change requires stronger approval/verification; result PASS.

anchor: 107.54 — Drift and architecture board ... Architecture Board should not receive every low-level event. KnowledgeOS should aggregate Events→Findings→Patterns→GovernanceIssues.
statement: Defines the aggregation chain Events→Findings→Patterns→GovernanceIssues, sparing the Architecture Board from raw event floods.

anchor: 107.55 — Experiment 24 ... 10,000 normal runtime events occur. Expected: board receives meaningful architectural findings, not 10,000 raw events. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 24: 10,000 events must be aggregated into meaningful findings for the board, not delivered raw; result PASS.

anchor: 107.56 — Evidence compression ... RawEvidence→RelevantFinding. AI can assist here. But AI Summary ≠ OriginalEvidence. The evidence must remain available.
statement: States AI Summary ≠ OriginalEvidence: AI-assisted compression must retain access to original evidence.

statement: Experiment 25: an AI's 'architecture appears healthy' summary of 500 events is not sufficient assurance evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 107.58 — Evidence lineage ... we preserve Summary→SourceEvidence. This allows audit and verification.
statement: Requires preserving Summary→SourceEvidence lineage for audit and verification.

anchor: 107.59 — Drift detection architecture ... Expected Architecture→Conformance Rules→{Source Analysis, Runtime Analysis}→Drift Findings→Classification→{Remediate,Exception,Evolve}→Verification→Evidence. This is becoming a concrete KnowledgeOS subsystem.
statement: Presents a complete drift-detection pipeline diagram as a concrete KnowledgeOS subsystem.

anchor: 107.60 — Architecture drift engine ... Architecture Conformance Engine: compare expected/observed, detect differences, classify differences, collect evidence, determine impact, route governance, track remediation, verify closure.
statement: Names the Architecture Conformance Engine with eight responsibilities: compare, detect, classify, collect evidence, determine impact, route governance, track remediation, verify closure.

anchor: 107.61 — It should not autonomously rewrite architecture ... The engine detects and analyzes. It should not silently modify ArchitectureTruth.
statement: States the Architecture Conformance Engine must never silently modify ArchitectureTruth; it only detects and analyzes.

anchor: 107.62 — Experiment 26 ... Engine detects a runtime dependency not in architecture. Expected: create finding. Not automatically add dependency to architecture. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: an undocumented dependency creates a Finding, never an automatic architecture update; result PASS.

anchor: 107.63 — This gives us a powerful separation ... Detection ≠ Decision. Recommendation ≠ Approval. Remediation ≠ Verification. These distinctions have now appeared repeatedly. That consistency is itself evidence that the architecture is internally coherent.
statement: Restates three recurring separations (Detection≠Decision, Recommendation≠Approval, Remediation≠Verification), noting their repeated appearance is itself evidence of internal architectural coherence.

anchor: 107.64 — Architecture drift versus architecture change ... Drift: Observed≠Expected. Resolution∈{Remediate, AuthorizeDeviation, ChangeArchitecture}. This is a very clean model.
statement: States the clean drift-resolution model: Drift=Observed≠Expected, with Resolution∈{Remediate, AuthorizeDeviation, ChangeArchitecture}.

anchor: 107.65 — Experiment 27 ... Observed behavior is better than expected architecture. Architecture is formally changed. Expected: old drift finding can reference ArchitectureChangeDecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: a formally-changed architecture (because observed behavior was better) leaves the old drift finding referencing the ArchitectureChangeDecision; result PASS.

anchor: 107.66 — Historical traceability ... retain OldArchitecture, DriftFinding, Decision, NewArchitecture. A_{I,t1}→Finding→Decision→A_{I,t2}.
statement: Defines the historical traceability chain A_{I,t1}→Finding→Decision→A_{I,t2}, retaining OldArchitecture/DriftFinding/Decision/NewArchitecture.

anchor: 107.67 — This is architecture evolution with evidence ... not 'we changed the diagram' but 'evidence showed X, the discrepancy was analyzed, the authorized decision was Y, and architecture version 2 superseded version 1.' That is exactly the kind of organizational memory KnowledgeOS is intended to p
statement: States architecture evolution must be evidence-backed organizational memory (evidence→analysis→decision→superseded version), not an undocumented diagram change.

anchor: 107.68 — Step 107 verdict: STEP 107 — ARCHITECTURE DRIFT MODEL: PASS. We now have a rigorous interpretation of discrepancies between A_I, A_C, A_D, A_R.
statement: Records Step 107 verdict PASS, providing a rigorous interpretation of A_I/A_C/A_D/A_R discrepancies.

anchor: 107.69 — More importantly: the architecture now has a correction mechanism ... Detect→Understand→Decide→Change→Verify. This means KnowledgeOS is not merely a static architecture repository. It supports controlled architectural evolution.
statement: States the architecture now has a correction mechanism Detect→Understand→Decide→Change→Verify, supporting controlled architectural evolution rather than static repository behavior.

anchor: 107.70 — Where we stand after Step 107 ... Semantic Integrity + Governance + Agent Control + Runtime Observation + Drift Detection + Controlled Evolution. This is a major milestone.
statement: Summarizes the cumulative capabilities after Step 107: Semantic Integrity + Governance + Agent Control + Runtime Observation + Drift Detection + Controlled Evolution.

anchor: Step 108 — Conformance Matrix ... Requirement × Architecture × Implementation × Verification × Runtime × Governance. Classify Implemented/PartiallyImplemented/SpecifiedButMissing/ImplementedIncorrectly/NotYetVerified. Step 108 is where we stop merely defining what the matrix should look like and beg
statement: Previews Step 108: constructing the Requirement×Architecture×Implementation×Verification×Runtime×Governance conformance matrix, marking the first step where actual KnowledgeOS artifacts populate the matrix rather than merely defining its shape, to empirically answer how much of the architecture already exists in the real software.

anchor: We now move from defining the architecture to measuring conformance. ConformanceMatrix=Requirement×Architecture×Implementation×Verification×Runtime×Governance.
statement: Defines the central artifact ConformanceMatrix=Requirement×Architecture×Implementation×Verification×Runtime×Governance, transitioning from architecture definition to conformance measurement.

anchor: The purpose is not to create another documentation exercise. The purpose is to establish an evidence-backed answer to: How much of the intended KnowledgeOS architecture actually exists in the software?
statement: States the purpose of the conformance matrix: an evidence-backed answer to how much of the intended architecture actually exists in the software, not a documentation exercise.

anchor: 108.1 — The fundamental rule ... Specified ≠ Implemented ≠ Verified ≠ Runtime Proven. A design document saying 'KnowledgeOS provides provenance' does not establish that provenance exists in the implementation.
statement: States the fundamental rule Specified≠Implemented≠Verified≠RuntimeProven, illustrated by a design-doc provenance claim not establishing implementation, an existing table not establishing correct population, and passing tests not establishing runtime conformance.

anchor: 108.2 — Conformance states ... C0 Not specified, C1 Specified, C2 Designed, C3 Implemented, C4 Verified, C5 Runtime proven, C6 Governed. These dimensions should not be collapsed into one number.
statement: Defines seven conformance states C0 (not specified) through C6 (governed), stating they should not be collapsed into a single number.

anchor: 108.3 — Why a single maturity score is dangerous ... Implementation=100% but RuntimeEvidence=0%. 'KnowledgeOS is 100% implemented' would be misleading. Instead we want a per-dimension status table.
statement: Warns that a single maturity score is dangerous (100% implementation with 0% runtime evidence would make '100% implemented' misleading), preferring a per-dimension status table (Specification/Design/Implementation Complete, Verification Partial, Runtime Unknown, Governance Complete).

anchor: 108.4 — The conformance tuple ... K=(S,D,I,V,R,G) where S=specification, D=design, I=implementation, V=verification, R=runtime evidence, G=governance.
statement: Defines the per-capability conformance tuple K=(S,D,I,V,R,G): specification, design, implementation, verification, runtime evidence, governance.

type_signature.codomain: S x D x I x V x R x G

statement: Worked example: a provenance requirement is traced through architecture/implementation/tests/runtime/governance stages, with Conformance=Strong claimable only once every stage has evidence.

anchor: 108.6 — Evidence hierarchy ... E1=Architecture statement, E2=Source implementation, E3=Automated test, E4=Deployment evidence, E5=Runtime observation, E6=Independent verification. The higher levels generally provide stronger empirical support.
statement: Defines an evidence-strength hierarchy E1 (architecture statement) through E6 (independent verification), with higher levels providing stronger empirical support for implementation claims.

statement: Experiment 1: an architecture-only claim ('Agents use KnowledgeOS') with no supporting code yields Specified=True, Implemented=Unknown; result PASS.

anchor: 108.8 — Experiment 2 ... Repository contains KnowledgeClient but no tests. Expected: Implemented=True, Verified=Unknown. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: an implemented KnowledgeClient with no tests yields Implemented=True, Verified=Unknown; result PASS.

anchor: 108.9 — Experiment 3 ... Tests exist but are never executed in CI. Expected: TestExists=True but VerificationStrength=Reduced. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: tests existing but never run in CI yield TestExists=True with VerificationStrength=Reduced; result PASS.

anchor: 108.10 — Evidence must be traceable ... Claim→Evidence. C: 'KnowledgeOS records decisions.' Evidence: SourceFile+Test+RuntimeRecord.
statement: States every conformance claim must trace to evidence (Claim→Evidence), illustrated by a decision-recording claim backed by SourceFile+Test+RuntimeRecord.

anchor: 108.11 — No evidence, no conformance claim ... NoEvidence ⇒ NoVerifiedClaim. The result should be Unknown rather than Pass.
statement: States the rule NoEvidence⇒NoVerifiedClaim: absent evidence, the result must default to Unknown rather than Pass.

invariants.name: I_NoEvidenceNoVerifiedClaim
invariants.statement: Absence of evidence yields Unknown, never Pass, for a conformance claim.

anchor: 108.12 — Conformance categories ... CONF, PART, SPEC, IMPL, DRIFT, VIOL, EXC, UNK, OBS. These are more useful than simple pass/fail.
statement: Defines nine practical conformance category codes (CONF/PART/SPEC/IMPL/DRIFT/VIOL/EXC/UNK/OBS), stated as more useful than binary pass/fail.

anchor: 108.13 — First conformance domain: Knowledge model ... Evidence, Claims, Inference, Decisions, Authority, Actions, Observations, Provenance, Temporal validity, Conflict handling — all cells UNK, deliberately using '?'. We do not fill these cells from architectural assumptions.
statement: Presents the Knowledge-model conformance domain table with ten capabilities, all cells deliberately marked '?'/UNK rather than filled from architectural assumption.

anchor: 108.14 — Second domain: Governance ... Rule registry, Authority, Rule lifecycle, Change classification, Governance routing, Exceptions, Approval evidence, Governance drift, Rule versioning — all UNK.
statement: Presents the Governance conformance domain table with nine capabilities, all cells UNK.

anchor: 108.15 — Third domain: Agent architecture ... Pointer-layer model, Shared knowledge, Agent identity, Tool authorization, Recommendation boundary, Action provenance, Memory separation, Knowledge promotion, columns Claude/Codex/KnowledgeOS/Verification — all UNK.
statement: Presents the Agent-architecture conformance domain table with eight capabilities across Claude/Codex/KnowledgeOS/Verification columns, all cells UNK.

anchor: 108.16 — Fourth domain: Runtime ... Topology, Versions, Configuration, Dependencies, Security boundaries, Agent activity, Governance controls, Drift detection — all UNK.
statement: Presents the Runtime conformance domain table with eight capabilities, all cells UNK.

anchor: 108.17 — Fifth domain: assurance ... We need to distinguish AIJudgment from DeterministicVerification. 'The architecture looks compliant' is not equivalent to ArchitectureCheck=PASS.
statement: Introduces the assurance domain, distinguishing AIJudgment from DeterministicVerification: an AI's compliance impression is not equivalent to a deterministic ArchitectureCheck=PASS.

anchor: 108.18 — Experiment 4 ... LLM says 'The repository follows the architecture.' No deterministic check exists. Expected: AIAssessment not VerifiedConformance. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: an LLM's unchecked 'follows the architecture' claim is AIAssessment, not VerifiedConformance; result PASS.

anchor: 108.19 — Deterministic assurance ... Rule→MachineCheck→Result. NoDirectDBAccess checked via dependency graph → PASS/FAIL.
statement: Prefers deterministic assurance Rule→MachineCheck→Result where possible, illustrated by a NoDirectDBAccess rule checked via dependency-graph analysis.

anchor: 108.20 — Experiment 5 ... Agent claims 'No service accesses the database directly.' Static dependency scanner finds one. Expected: DeterministicCheck=FAIL. Result: PASS. The machine check wins over the AI assertion.
statement: Experiment 5: a static scanner contradicting an agent's no-direct-DB-access claim yields DeterministicCheck=FAIL, with the machine check winning over the AI assertion; result PASS.

anchor: 108.21 — Assurance hierarchy ... DeterministicEvidence > ReproducibleVerification > RuntimeObservation > AIInterpretation > UnverifiedAssertion. This is not an absolute ranking for every purpose, but it is a strong default for conformance claims.
statement: Defines the assurance hierarchy DeterministicEvidence > ReproducibleVerification > RuntimeObservation > AIInterpretation > UnverifiedAssertion, explicitly a strong default rather than an absolute ranking.

anchor: 108.22 — Architecture rules as executable specifications ... A↛B should ideally be encoded as Check(A,B). ArchitectureRule→AutomatedTest.
statement: States architecture rules should be encoded as executable checks (ArchitectureRule→AutomatedTest), e.g. Check(A,B) for a forbidden dependency A↛B.

anchor: 108.23 — Experiment 6 ... Architecture rule exists. No automated check exists. Expected: Governance/ArchitectureAutomationGap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: an architecture rule with no automated check yields a Governance/ArchitectureAutomationGap finding; result PASS.

anchor: 108.24 — The conformance chain ... Rule→Check→Evidence→Finding and Finding→Decision→Remediation→Verification. This is the executable assurance loop.
statement: Defines the executable assurance loop: Rule→Check→Evidence→Finding→Decision→Remediation→Verification.

anchor: 108.25 — Requirement traceability ... Implementation→Requirement (backward) and Requirement→Verification (forward).
statement: States every important implementation capability should trace backward to a requirement and forward to verification.

anchor: 108.26 — Experiment 7 ... A major service exists. Nobody can identify which architectural requirement justified it. Expected: potential orphan implementation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: a major service with no identifiable justifying requirement is flagged as a potential orphan implementation; result PASS.

anchor: 108.27 — Orphan architecture ... Requirement R exists. No implementation satisfies it. Expected: ImplementationGap.
statement: Defines the reverse orphan case: a requirement with no satisfying implementation is an ImplementationGap.

anchor: 108.28 — Experiment 8 ... Requirement: 'All agent actions require auditability.' No implementation evidence exists. Expected: Gap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: an auditability requirement with no implementation evidence yields a Gap finding; result PASS.

anchor: 108.29 — Bidirectional traceability ... Requirement↔Implementation↔Verification is required for high-assurance capabilities.
statement: States bidirectional traceability Requirement↔Implementation↔Verification is required for high-assurance capabilities.

anchor: 108.30 — Architecture-to-code traceability ... ArchitectureDecision→CodeArea. Example: ADR-042→Knowledge Service.
statement: Defines architecture-decision-to-code traceability (ArchitectureDecision→CodeArea), illustrated by ADR-042→Knowledge Service.

anchor: 108.31 — Experiment 9 ... ADR says 'Use event-driven communication.' Repository has event infrastructure. But nobody can determine which parts implement ADR-042. Expected: Weak traceability. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: existing event infrastructure that cannot be tied to the specific ADR-042 that motivated it is Weak traceability; result PASS.

anchor: 108.32 — Code-to-architecture traceability ... CodeComponent→ArchitectureDecision. This helps explain why a component exists.
statement: Defines the reverse code-to-architecture traceability CodeComponent→ArchitectureDecision, explaining why a component exists.

anchor: 108.33 — Experiment 10 ... Component exists. No architectural context is discoverable. Expected: potential architecture debt. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: a component with no discoverable architectural context is potential architecture debt; result PASS.

anchor: 108.34 — Conformance is a graph ... G_C=(V,E) with nodes requirements/principles/rules/ADRs/components/code/tests/deployments/runtime observations/findings/decisions, and edges implements/verifies/supports/violates/supersedes/dependsOn.
statement: Reframes the conformance matrix as a graph G_C=(V,E) with eleven node types and six edge types (implements/verifies/supports/violates/supersedes/dependsOn).

anchor: 108.35 — Experiment 11 ... A component has no relationship to any architecture requirement. Expected: Graph identifies an orphan node. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: an unrelated component is identified by the graph as an orphan node; result PASS.

anchor: 108.36 — Architecture knowledge graph ... This gives KnowledgeOS another important role: ConformanceGraph rather than merely DocumentRepository.
statement: States KnowledgeOS's role as a ConformanceGraph rather than merely a DocumentRepository.

anchor: 108.37 — Conformance queries ... Which architecture rules are not implemented? Rules-ImplementedBy. Which implemented components have no architectural justification? Components-JustifiedBy. Which governance rules have no enforcement? Rules-EnforcedBy. Which runtime violations have no remediation? Fi
statement: Presents four illustrative conformance graph queries: unimplemented rules, unjustified components, unenforced governance rules, unremediated findings.

anchor: 108.38 — Experiment 12 ... Query: Show architecture rules with no verification. Expected: KnowledgeOS can produce the set. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: KnowledgeOS can produce the set of architecture rules lacking verification via graph query; result PASS.

anchor: 108.39 — This changes the role of documentation ... Documentation becomes KnowledgeGraphView rather than the sole source of truth. A document can explain a relationship. The graph preserves the relationship.
statement: States documentation becomes a KnowledgeGraphView rather than the sole source of truth; the graph, not the document, preserves the relationship.

anchor: 108.40 — Evidence freshness ... Conformance evidence itself becomes stale. A test passed yesterday. That does not necessarily establish today's runtime. EvidenceValidity(t).
statement: Defines EvidenceValidity(t): conformance evidence becomes stale, and a previously-passing test does not establish current runtime conformance.

anchor: 108.41 — Experiment 13 ... Architecture test passed six months ago. System changed significantly since then. Expected: Evidence freshness must be considered. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a six-month-old passing test on a significantly changed system requires evidence-freshness consideration; result PASS.

anchor: 108.42 — Continuous conformance ... Conformance=f(t). Not Conformance=Constant.
statement: States conformance must be modeled as Conformance=f(t), not a constant.

anchor: 108.43 — Experiment 14 ... Deployment changes a critical component. Expected: relevant conformance checks become stale or are rerun. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: deployment of a critical-component change should stale-mark or rerun relevant conformance checks; result PASS.

anchor: 108.44 — Conformance triggers ... CodeChange, ArchitectureChange, PolicyChange, Deployment, RuntimeDrift, SecurityEvent.
statement: Lists six conformance-recheck triggers: CodeChange, ArchitectureChange, PolicyChange, Deployment, RuntimeDrift, SecurityEvent.

anchor: 108.45 — Experiment 15 ... Architecture rule changes. Expected: affected verification checks are identified. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: a changed architecture rule should have its affected verification checks identified; result PASS.

anchor: 108.46 — KnowledgeOS as assurance infrastructure ... Architecture Assurance Plane. It connects Intent→Implementation→Verification→Runtime. This is stronger than a normal documentation platform.
statement: Names the Architecture Assurance Plane capability connecting Intent→Implementation→Verification→Runtime, stronger than an ordinary documentation platform.

anchor: 108.47 — Assurance finding ... A failed conformance check becomes a Finding, containing Rule, Expected, Observed, Evidence, Severity, Owner, Status.
statement: Defines the Finding object (Rule,Expected,Observed,Evidence,Severity,Owner,Status) produced by a failed conformance check.

type_signature.codomain: Rule x Expected x Observed x Evidence x Severity x Owner x Status

anchor: 108.48 — Experiment 16 ... Architecture check fails. No owner assigned. Expected: UnmanagedFinding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: an owner-less failed check is classified UnmanagedFinding; result PASS.

anchor: 108.49 — Finding governance ... A finding becomes a governance object when material. Finding→GovernanceWorkflow.
statement: States a material finding becomes a governance object, routed via Finding→GovernanceWorkflow.

anchor: 108.50 — Experiment 17 ... Critical security architecture violation occurs. Expected: automatic escalation according to policy. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: a critical security-architecture violation triggers automatic policy-driven escalation; result PASS.

anchor: 108.51 — Closure evidence ... Finding closure requires evidence: Finding→Remediation→VerificationEvidence.
statement: States finding closure requires Finding→Remediation→VerificationEvidence, not remediation claims alone.

anchor: 108.52 — Experiment 18 ... Developer marks finding 'resolved.' No verification exists. Expected: Status≠Closed. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: a developer's unverified 'resolved' claim leaves Status≠Closed; result PASS.

anchor: 108.53 — Conformance debt ... Unresolved findings accumulate as ConformanceDebt. This should not simply become 'Number of tickets.' It should account for Severity, Age, Impact, Risk.
statement: Defines ConformanceDebt from accumulated unresolved findings, warning it must be weighted by Severity/Age/Impact/Risk, never reduced to a ticket count.

anchor: 108.54 — Experiment 19 ... One critical violation is more important than 100 low-risk documentation deviations. Expected: risk-weighted assessment. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: one critical violation must outweigh 100 low-risk deviations under a risk-weighted assessment; result PASS.

anchor: 108.55 — The conformance score ... A numeric score may eventually be useful, but only after the evidence matrix exists. Score=WeightedEvidence. Never Score=NumberOfImplementedClasses.
statement: States a numeric conformance score is only meaningful after the evidence matrix exists, and must be Score=WeightedEvidence, never a raw class count.

anchor: 108.56 — Experiment 20 ... System has 100 classes named 'Knowledge.' Expected: this does not establish semantic conformance. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: 100 classes literally named 'Knowledge' do not establish semantic conformance; result PASS.

anchor: 108.57 — Implementation archaeology ... Step A find architectural claim, Step B find implementation candidates, Step C find tests, Step D find runtime evidence, Step E find governance ownership, Step F classify.
statement: Defines a six-step implementation-archaeology methodology: find claim, find implementation candidates, find tests, find runtime evidence, find governance ownership, classify.

anchor: 108.58 — Evidence collection discipline ... We should not search only for files named knowledge/architecture/governance, because architecture may be encoded indirectly in database schemas, migrations, APIs, services, policies, tests, CI, hooks, configuration, scripts.
statement: Warns against filename-only evidence search, since architecture may be encoded indirectly in schemas, migrations, APIs, services, policies, tests, CI, hooks, configuration, or scripts.

anchor: 108.59 — Experiment 21 ... Architecture capability 'Agent action logging.' Implementation may exist as session-changes-logger rather than AgentAuditService. Expected: semantic search rather than filename search. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: an 'agent action logging' capability implemented as session-changes-logger (not AgentAuditService) requires semantic rather than filename search; result PASS.

anchor: 108.60 — This is why evidence reconstruction matters ... The architecture must be reconstructed from Artifacts+Behavior+Relationships. Not from class names alone.
statement: States architecture must be reconstructed from Artifacts+Behavior+Relationships, not from class names alone.

anchor: 108.61 — Current conformance matrix baseline ... D={Knowledge,Governance,Agents,Runtime,Assurance,Traceability}. Each domain contains concrete capabilities.
statement: Defines the baseline conformance domain set D={Knowledge,Governance,Agents,Runtime,Assurance,Traceability}.

anchor: 108.62 — Master matrix ... capabilities across Knowledge/Governance/Agents/Runtime/Assurance/Traceability domains, columns Intended/Implementation/Verification/Runtime/Governance, all cells '?'. The question marks are intentional.
statement: Presents the master capability matrix across all six domains with all Implementation/Verification/Runtime/Governance cells deliberately left as '?'.

anchor: 108.63 — The next phase begins here ... Until Step 108 we have mostly answered: What must KnowledgeOS be? Now we can ask: What is KnowledgeOS actually? This is a methodological transition from ArchitectureConstruction to ArchitectureVerification.
statement: States the methodological transition from ArchitectureConstruction (what must KnowledgeOS be) to ArchitectureVerification (what is KnowledgeOS actually).

anchor: 108.64 — Step 108 verdict: STEP 108 — CONFORMANCE MODEL: PASS. The conformance framework is now sufficiently defined to perform empirical reconstruction. The implementation status of individual capabilities remains TBD until evidence is mapped.
statement: Records Step 108 verdict PASS, scoped to the conformance framework's sufficiency for empirical reconstruction; individual capability status remains TBD.

anchor: 108.65 — The next step: Step 109 — Evidence-Based Repository Reconstruction. This is where we should stop inventing additional conceptual layers and begin the actual archaeological examination of KnowledgeOS/EKS. Architecture Claim→Artifact→Code→Test→Runtime Evidence. Output: KnowledgeOS Actual Comp
statement: Previews Step 109: the transition from conceptual layering to actual archaeological examination of KnowledgeOS/EKS, following Architecture Claim→Artifact→Code→Test→Runtime Evidence, starting with system boundaries and major components, producing a ten-category KnowledgeOS Actual Component Inventory.

anchor: We now change mode. The previous steps established the target architecture. Step 109 begins the reconstruction of the actual KnowledgeOS/EKS system. The governing principle is: No architectural assertion without evidence.
statement: States the governing principle for Step 109's methodological shift from target-architecture definition to actual-system reconstruction: no architectural assertion without evidence.

anchor: We will therefore distinguish rigorously between Observed, Inferred, Specified, Claimed, and Not yet evidenced.
statement: Introduces a five-way epistemic status distinction: Observed, Inferred, Specified, Claimed, Not-yet-evidenced.

anchor: 109.1 — The reconstruction question ... What software, artifacts, processes and runtime mechanisms actually constitute KnowledgeOS today? K_actual=Artifacts+Code+Configuration+Workflows+RuntimeBehavior. We then compare K_actual↔K_intended.
statement: Reframes the guiding question as K_actual=Artifacts+Code+Configuration+Workflows+RuntimeBehavior, compared against K_intended.

anchor: 109.2 — Evidence sources ... repository structure; configuration; source code; schemas/migrations; APIs; tests; CI/CD; agent harnesses; generated artifacts; runtime/operational evidence. No single category is sufficient.
statement: Lists ten evidence sources in increasing behavioral strength, stating no single category is sufficient alone.

anchor: 109.3 — Evidence classification ... E0 Name only, E1 Structural evidence, E2 Implementation evidence, E3 Verification evidence, E4 Runtime evidence, E5 Governance evidence. The strongest conformance claim normally requires several levels.
statement: Defines a six-level evidence classification E0 (name only) through E5 (governance evidence).

anchor: 109.4 — Experiment 1 ... We discover knowledge/ directory. Can we conclude 'KnowledgeOS has a knowledge domain'? No. Expected: E0/E1. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: discovering a bare knowledge/ directory yields only E0/E1 evidence, not a knowledge-domain conclusion; result PASS.

anchor: 109.5 — Experiment 2 ... Inside the directory we find KnowledgeRepository, KnowledgeService, KnowledgeController. Expected: implementation evidence for a knowledge-related capability, but not yet proof it is the authoritative KnowledgeOS knowledge layer. Result: E2
statement: Experiment 2: finding named knowledge-related classes gives E2 implementation evidence without proving authoritative status.

anchor: 109.6 — Experiment 3 ... Tests demonstrate KnowledgeServiceTest and CI executes them. Expected: E3. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: CI-executed tests yield E3 verification evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 109.7 — Experiment 4 ... Production records demonstrate actual knowledge operations. Expected: E4. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: production records demonstrating actual operations yield E4 runtime evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 109.8 — Experiment 5 ... Architecture governance explicitly identifies the component as authoritative. Expected: E5. Only now do we have a strong chain: Structure→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Governance.
statement: Experiment 5: explicit governance identification yields E5, completing the strong evidence chain Structure→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Governance.

anchor: 109.9 — Actual component inventory ... ComponentInventory_actual. Each component gets Component ID, Name, Location, Type, Responsibility, Dependencies, Knowledge role, Governance role, Agent role, Runtime role, Evidence, Confidence, Status.
statement: Defines the ActualComponentInventory schema with 13 attributes per component (ID, Name, Location, Type, Responsibility, Dependencies, Knowledge/Governance/Agent/Runtime roles, Evidence, Confidence, Status).

anchor: 109.10 — Component classification ... Knowledge, Ingestion, Semantic processing, Governance, Agent integration, Assurance, Storage, Runtime infrastructure, Interface, Operational tooling.
statement: Defines ten semantic component categories: Knowledge, Ingestion, Semantic processing, Governance, Agent integration, Assurance, Storage, Runtime infrastructure, Interface, Operational tooling.

anchor: 109.11 — Important rule ... A component can have more than one role. AgentGateway may be AgentIntegration+SecurityBoundary+API. We should not force artificial classification.
statement: States components can hold multiple roles simultaneously (e.g. AgentGateway = AgentIntegration+SecurityBoundary+API), forbidding forced single-category classification.

anchor: 109.12 — Repository topology ... What is the actual repository topology? We must derive the actual tree from evidence rather than assume this structure exists.
statement: States repository topology must be derived from evidence, not assumed.

anchor: 109.13 — Experiment 6 ... Documentation describes knowledge/governance/agents. Repository actually contains app/packages/scripts. Expected: the repository structure wins for the implementation topology. Result: PASS. Documentation remains evidence of intended architecture.
statement: Experiment 6: when documented and actual repository structures diverge, actual structure wins for implementation topology while documentation remains evidence of intent; result PASS.

anchor: 109.14 — Repository boundaries ... Is KnowledgeOS one repository? multiple repositories? a platform plus consumers? This cannot be assumed.
statement: States repository boundaries (single repo, multiple repos, platform-plus-consumers, etc.) cannot be assumed and must be established.

anchor: 109.15 — Experiment 7 ... Claude harness is in one repository. KnowledgeOS backend is in another. Expected: they may still constitute one logical ecosystem, but we must distinguish RepositoryBoundary from SystemBoundary. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: separately-repository'd Claude harness and KnowledgeOS backend may still form one logical ecosystem, distinguishing RepositoryBoundary from SystemBoundary; result PASS.

anchor: 109.16 — System boundary ... KnowledgeOS_SystemBoundary containing all components demonstrably part of the ecosystem: EKS+KnowledgeOS+AgentHarnesses+Governance+Assurance. But each inclusion must be evidenced.
statement: Defines KnowledgeOS_SystemBoundary as the evidenced union of demonstrably-related components (potentially EKS+KnowledgeOS+AgentHarnesses+Governance+Assurance), each inclusion requiring evidence.

anchor: 109.17 — Experiment 8 ... A generic CI tool is used by KnowledgeOS. Does that make the CI tool a KnowledgeOS component? No. Expected: External dependency unless the architecture explicitly treats it as internal. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: a generic CI tool used by KnowledgeOS remains an external dependency unless explicitly treated as internal; result PASS.

anchor: 109.18 — Dependency versus component ... Uses(X,Y) does not imply Y∈KnowledgeOS. We need to distinguish InternalComponent from ExternalDependency.
statement: States Uses(X,Y) does not imply membership Y∈KnowledgeOS, distinguishing InternalComponent from ExternalDependency.

anchor: 109.19 — Component ownership ... Owner(Component). If ownership cannot be established: Owner=Unknown. We do not infer ownership merely from the directory.
statement: States component ownership defaults to Unknown unless evidenced, never inferred merely from directory location.

anchor: 109.20 — Experiment 9 ... Repository directory governance/ does not prove Owner=ArchitectureBoard. Expected: ownership remains unknown until evidenced. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: a governance/ directory does not by itself prove ownership by the Architecture Board; ownership remains Unknown until evidenced; result PASS.

anchor: 109.21 — Interfaces ... ComponentA→API→ComponentB. Possible interface types: REST, GraphQL, CLI, message bus, database, filesystem, Git, event, webhook, agent protocol.
statement: Lists ten possible interface types for actual interface reconstruction: REST, GraphQL, CLI, message bus, database, filesystem, Git, event, webhook, agent protocol.

anchor: 109.22 — Experiment 10 ... Source contains KnowledgeClient but no evidence of network communication. Expected: do not assume it is a remote service; it may be an in-process abstraction. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: a KnowledgeClient with no network evidence should not be assumed to be a remote service call, possibly an in-process abstraction instead; result PASS.

anchor: 109.23 — Interface evidence ... InterfaceDeclared, InterfaceUsed, InterfaceObserved.
statement: Distinguishes InterfaceDeclared, InterfaceUsed, and InterfaceObserved as three separate levels of interface evidence.

anchor: 109.24 — Data stores ... Store=(Type,Purpose,Owner,DataClass,Authority,Retention). Examples: relational database, vector index, Git repository, filesystem, object storage, cache. But these are categories, not assumptions about the actual implementation.
statement: Defines the Store=(Type,Purpose,Owner,DataClass,Authority,Retention) tuple for reconstructing actual data stores.

type_signature.codomain: Type x Purpose x Owner x DataClass x Authority x Retention

anchor: 109.25 — Experiment 11 ... A vector database exists. Expected: it does not automatically constitute the KnowledgeOS semantic knowledge store; it may simply support retrieval. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: an existing vector database does not automatically constitute the semantic knowledge store; it may merely support retrieval; result PASS.

anchor: 109.26 — This distinction is critical ... VectorStore≠KnowledgeModel. A vector store answers what content is semantically similar. KnowledgeOS must additionally answer what does this information mean, what supports it, who owns it, and what authority does it have?
statement: States VectorStore≠KnowledgeModel: semantic similarity retrieval is distinct from meaning, support, ownership, and authority questions a knowledge model must answer.

anchor: 109.27 — Database schema archaeology ... The schema often provides stronger evidence than documentation. tables; fields; foreign keys; indexes; constraints; migrations; enum/state models. These reveal what the system actually believes exists.
statement: States database schema often provides stronger evidence than documentation, revealing what the system actually believes exists via tables/fields/foreign keys/indexes/constraints/migrations/state models.

anchor: 109.28 — Experiment 12 ... Documentation claims decisions have provenance. Schema has decisions(id,content) but no provenance relationship. Expected: potential implementation gap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: a documented provenance claim contradicted by a schema lacking any provenance relationship is a potential implementation gap; result PASS.

anchor: 109.29 — API archaeology ... Endpoint→UseCase→DomainModel→Persistence. This can expose whether semantics actually exist.
statement: Defines API archaeology as tracing Endpoint→UseCase→DomainModel→Persistence to expose whether claimed semantics actually exist.

anchor: 109.30 — Experiment 13 ... API POST /knowledge accepts only content. Expected: this does not demonstrate support for provenance, authority, temporal validity, semantic type. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a POST /knowledge endpoint accepting only 'content' does not demonstrate provenance/authority/temporal-validity/semantic-type support; result PASS.

anchor: 109.31 — State machines ... Draft→Approved→Published. If the implementation contains explicit transitions, we have evidence that lifecycle semantics are real.
statement: States explicit state-machine transitions in implementation (e.g. Draft→Approved→Published) are strong evidence that lifecycle semantics are real.

anchor: 109.32 — Experiment 14 ... Documentation describes approval. Implementation allows status='approved' from any state. Expected: approval semantics may not be enforced. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: an implementation allowing status='approved' from any state despite documented approval semantics suggests unenforced approval logic; result PASS.

anchor: 109.33 — Business rules ... validators; policies; authorization checks; domain services; database constraints; CI gates; runtime middleware. The same rule may be enforced at several layers.
statement: Lists seven layers where business rules may be enforced (validators, policies, authorization checks, domain services, DB constraints, CI gates, runtime middleware), noting the same rule may span several.

anchor: 109.34 — Experiment 15 ... Architecture requires Decision.authority≠null. Database permits authority=NULL. Expected: potential enforcement gap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: a database permitting authority=NULL despite an architecture rule requiring Decision.authority≠null is a potential enforcement gap; result PASS.

anchor: 109.35 — Tests as executable architecture ... Unit, Integration, Contract, Architecture, Security, EndToEnd, Runtime.
statement: States tests reveal what behavior developers believe must remain true, classified into Unit/Integration/Contract/Architecture/Security/EndToEnd/Runtime categories.

anchor: 109.36 — Experiment 16 ... Architecture rule exists. An architecture test enforces it. Expected: strong implementation evidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: an architecture rule enforced by an architecture test is strong implementation evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 109.37 — CI as governance evidence ... TestExists is weaker than TestExecuted.
statement: States TestExists is weaker evidence than TestExecuted, since CI execution is required for governance-strength evidence.

anchor: 109.38 — Experiment 17 ... Architecture test exists but CI excludes its directory. Expected: VerificationGap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: an architecture test excluded from CI execution is a VerificationGap; result PASS.

anchor: 109.39 — Agent harness reconstruction ... AGENTS.md, .claude/, .codex/ and associated scripts/configuration. The objective is not to judge whether they are 'good.' It is to establish: What responsibility does each artifact actually have?
statement: States agent-harness reconstruction (AGENTS.md, .claude/, .codex/) aims to establish actual responsibility, not to judge quality.

anchor: 109.40 — Experiment 18 ... .claude/ contains settings, hooks, commands, memory. Expected: each must be classified individually. A directory named memory does not automatically mean authoritative KnowledgeOS memory. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: each .claude/ subdirectory (settings/hooks/commands/memory) must be classified individually; a 'memory' directory name does not itself imply authoritative KnowledgeOS memory; result PASS.

anchor: 109.41 — Pointer-layer test ... We specifically inspect whether .claude/ and .codex/ point toward shared knowledge or duplicate it. Desired: AgentHarness→KnowledgeOS.
statement: Defines the pointer-layer test: inspecting whether .claude/ and .codex/ point toward shared knowledge (AgentHarness→KnowledgeOS, desired) or duplicate it.

anchor: 109.42 — Experiment 19 ... Both harnesses reference the same architecture source. Expected: strong evidence for the pointer-layer architecture. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: both agent harnesses referencing the same architecture source is strong evidence for the pointer-layer architecture; result PASS.

anchor: 109.43 — Experiment 20 ... Claude contains an architecture document that differs from the authoritative repository architecture. Expected: AgentKnowledgeDrift. Result: DRIFT. This becomes a concrete finding rather than a theoretical concern.
statement: Experiment 20: Claude's local architecture document diverging from the authoritative repository architecture is classified AgentKnowledgeDrift with result DRIFT, becoming a concrete finding rather than a theoretical concern.

anchor: 109.44 — Scripts are architecture ... database safety; session logging; verification; synchronization; governance enforcement. A small script can implement a major architectural rule.
statement: States scripts must not be ignored during reconstruction, since a small script can implement a major architectural rule (database safety, session logging, verification, synchronization, governance enforcement).

anchor: 109.45 — Experiment 21 ... A shell script blocks destructive database commands. Expected: this is an actual enforcement mechanism, even if no formal service exists. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: a shell script blocking destructive database commands is counted as an actual enforcement mechanism even absent a formal service; result PASS.

anchor: 109.46 — Hooks ... AgentEvent→Control. SessionStart→ContextLoading. FileChange→Audit.
statement: Defines hooks as AgentEvent→Control mechanisms, illustrated by SessionStart→ContextLoading and FileChange→Audit.

anchor: 109.47 — Experiment 22 ... Session-change logger captures modifications made during agent sessions. Expected: evidence for AgentActionProvenance. But we still need completeness, reliability, storage, retention, runtime execution. Result: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 22: a session-change logger provides evidence for AgentActionProvenance but with open completeness/reliability/storage/retention/runtime-execution questions; result PARTIAL.

anchor: 109.48 — Configuration archaeology ... service URLs; databases; feature flags; authorization; environment boundaries; runtime dependencies. But configuration can also contain secrets. We must inspect safely and avoid exposing credentials.
statement: States configuration archaeology reveals integration points but warns of the need to inspect safely and avoid exposing credentials.

anchor: 109.49 — Experiment 23 ... Configuration references KNOWLEDGEOS_URL. Expected: evidence of an integration point. Not proof of successful runtime communication. Result: E2
statement: Experiment 23: a KNOWLEDGEOS_URL configuration reference is E2 evidence of an integration point, not proof of successful runtime communication.

anchor: 109.50 — Runtime integration ... Configuration→SuccessfulCall→RuntimeObservation. Then E4.
statement: Defines the promotion path Configuration→SuccessfulCall→RuntimeObservation reaching E4 evidence strength.

anchor: 109.51 — Actual versus intended architecture diagram ... Intended→Architecture→{Implementation,Governance}→{Deployment,Authority}→Runtime→Evidence→Conformance.
statement: Presents the actual-vs-intended architecture pipeline: Intended→Architecture→{Implementation,Governance}→{Deployment,Authority}→Runtime→Evidence→Conformance.

anchor: 109.52 — Actual architecture record ... ComponentActual=(ObservedRole,Dependencies,Interfaces,Data,Controls,Tests,Runtime,Owner). Then compare ComponentActual↔ComponentIntended.
statement: Defines the ComponentActual=(ObservedRole,Dependencies,Interfaces,Data,Controls,Tests,Runtime,Owner) tuple for direct comparison against ComponentIntended.

type_signature.codomain: ObservedRole x Dependencies x Interfaces x Data x Controls x Tests x Runtime x Owner

anchor: 109.53 — Experiment 24 ... Architecture describes KnowledgeService. Actual code contains three services with overlapping responsibilities. Expected: potential BoundaryDrift. Result: OBS. We do not yet call it a violation until semantics are established.
statement: Experiment 24: three overlapping actual services against one architected KnowledgeService is potential BoundaryDrift, classified OBS (not yet a violation) pending semantic analysis.

anchor: 109.54 — Semantic boundary reconstruction ... What does each component actually own? Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Invariant. This is essentially DDD-style archaeological reconstruction.
statement: Defines semantic boundary reconstruction as tracing Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Invariant, described as DDD-style archaeological reconstruction.

anchor: 109.55 — Experiment 25 ... Two services both mutate the same decision state. Expected: potential aggregate/boundary violation. But classification requires understanding their respective responsibilities. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 25: two services mutating the same decision state is a potential aggregate/boundary violation, classified OBS pending responsibility analysis.

anchor: 109.56 — Dependency graph ... G_actual=(V,E) where V=ActualComponents and E=ActualDependencies. Then compare G_actual against G_intended.
statement: Defines the actual dependency graph G_actual=(V,E) with V=ActualComponents, E=ActualDependencies, for comparison against G_intended.

anchor: 109.57 — Dependency evidence ... Each edge should have provenance: source import; API call; configuration; deployment; runtime trace. An inferred dependency is weaker than an observed runtime dependency.
statement: States each dependency-graph edge requires provenance (source import/API call/configuration/deployment/runtime trace), with inferred dependencies weaker than observed runtime dependencies.

anchor: 109.58 — Experiment 26 ... Source import exists A→B. Runtime never loads B in the relevant path. Expected: both facts can coexist. We record StaticDependency=True, RuntimeDependency=NotObserved. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: a source-level import A→B can coexist with an unobserved runtime dependency, recorded as StaticDependency=True/RuntimeDependency=NotObserved; result PASS.

anchor: 109.59 — Actual data flow ... Input→Processing→Storage→Output. This reveals whether the semantic model is reflected in actual data flow.
statement: Defines actual data flow reconstruction Input→Processing→Storage→Output to test whether the semantic model is reflected in practice.

anchor: 109.60 — Experiment 27 ... Claim enters the system. It is stored. But there is no relationship to evidence. Expected: knowledge semantics are incomplete despite the existence of a knowledge API. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: a stored claim lacking any evidence relationship shows incomplete knowledge semantics despite an existing knowledge API; result PASS.

anchor: 109.61 — Actual control flow ... Request→Authorization→BusinessRule→Action→Audit. If authorization occurs after the action, we have a serious control defect.
statement: Defines actual control-flow reconstruction Request→Authorization→BusinessRule→Action→Audit, warning that post-action authorization is a serious control defect.

anchor: 109.62 — Experiment 28 ... Agent invokes Action. Authorization occurs afterward. Expected: VIOLATION for a protected action.
statement: Experiment 28: an agent action followed by (rather than preceded by) authorization is classified VIOLATION for a protected action.

anchor: 109.63 — Evidence chain reconstruction ... Claim→Artifact→Code→Test→Runtime. If one link is missing: Chain=Incomplete.
statement: Defines the evidence-chain reconstruction Claim→Artifact→Code→Test→Runtime, with Chain=Incomplete when any link is missing.

anchor: 109.64 — Experiment 29 ... We have Code+Test. No runtime evidence. Expected: ImplementedAndVerified but RuntimeProven=Unknown. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: code+test evidence without runtime evidence yields ImplementedAndVerified but RuntimeProven=Unknown; result PASS.

anchor: 109.65 — Architecture confidence ... Confidence=f(EvidenceDepth,EvidenceIndependence,EvidenceFreshness). Not Confidence=f(LLMConfidence).
statement: Defines architecture confidence as Confidence=f(EvidenceDepth,EvidenceIndependence,EvidenceFreshness), explicitly not a function of LLM confidence.

anchor: 109.66 — Independent evidence ... SourceCode+ArchitectureTest+RuntimeTrace is stronger than Documentation+Documentation.
statement: States independent multi-source evidence (source+test+runtime trace) is stronger than duplicated single-source evidence (documentation+documentation).

anchor: 109.67 — Experiment 30 ... Architecture document and README both claim 'All agent actions are audited.' No implementation evidence. Expected: still Specified/Claimed, not Verified. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: two documentation sources both making an unimplemented claim remain Specified/Claimed, never Verified; result PASS.

anchor: 109.68 — Reconstruction output ... Step 109 should ultimately produce five concrete artifacts: ActualComponentInventory, ActualDependencyGraph, ActualDataFlow, ActualControlFlow, EvidenceLedger.
statement: Specifies five concrete Step 109 output artifacts: ActualComponentInventory, ActualDependencyGraph, ActualDataFlow, ActualControlFlow, EvidenceLedger.

anchor: 109.69 — Evidence Ledger ... ID, Claim, Evidence, Type, Strength, Status. This prevents us from making a strong claim based on one weak artifact.
statement: Defines the Evidence Ledger schema (ID/Claim/Evidence/Type/Strength/Status) with a worked example, preventing strong claims from single weak artifacts.

anchor: 109.70 — Negative evidence ... No provenance relation found in schema. This is not necessarily proof that provenance does not exist. It is NegativeSearchEvidence. NotFound≠DoesNotExist. Unless the search boundary is demonstrably exhaustive.
