statement: States NotFound≠DoesNotExist: absence of found evidence is NegativeSearchEvidence, not proof of non-existence, unless the search is demonstrably exhaustive.

invariants.name: I_NotFoundNeqDoesNotExist
invariants.statement: Absence of found evidence (NegativeSearchEvidence) is not proof of non-existence unless the search boundary is demonstrably exhaustive.

anchor: 109.71 — Experiment 31 ... No Decision class found. But decisions may be represented as workflow records or ADR objects. Expected: do not conclude DecisionCapability=False. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 31: absence of a literal Decision class does not license concluding DecisionCapability=False, since decisions may be represented as workflow records or ADR objects; result PASS.

anchor: 109.72 — Semantic search strategy ... search for concepts and behavior, not only names. For Decision: approve, reject, authorize, rationale, resolution, accepted, superseded. For Evidence: source, observation, provenance, finding, artifact, verification result.
statement: Prescribes a semantic-search strategy for reconstruction, searching for concepts and behavior (e.g. approve/reject/authorize/rationale/resolution for Decision; source/observation/provenance/finding for Evidence) rather than literal class names.

anchor: 109.73 — This is where prior KnowledgeOS sessions become valuable ... hypotheses H_1,...,H_n. Each hypothesis must now be tested against actual artifacts. Search(H)→Evidence. Possible results: Confirmed, PartiallyConfirmed, Contradicted, NotEstablished.
statement: States prior architectural hypotheses H_1..H_n must be tested against actual artifacts via Search(H)→Evidence, yielding Confirmed/PartiallyConfirmed/Contradicted/NotEstablished.

anchor: 109.74 — Experiment 32 ... Prior architectural discussion says 'There is a registry.' Repository has registry/ but it contains only agent configuration. Expected: the original interpretation is not automatically confirmed. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 32: a registry/ directory containing only agent configuration does not automatically confirm a prior 'there is a registry' claim; result PASS.

anchor: 109.75 — This protects against architectural mythology ... 'We already have this' can mean designed, partially implemented, prototyped, once implemented, intended, or manually performed. KnowledgeOS reconstruction must distinguish these.
statement: Warns against 'architectural mythology' -- the loose claim 'we already have this' spanning designed/partially-implemented/prototyped/once-implemented/intended/manually-performed states that reconstruction must distinguish.

anchor: 109.76 — Implementation status vocabulary ... Status∈{Designed, Prototype, Partial, Implemented, Verified, Operational, Governed, Deprecated}. These are materially different states.
statement: Defines an eight-value implementation status vocabulary: Designed, Prototype, Partial, Implemented, Verified, Operational, Governed, Deprecated.

anchor: 109.77 — Experiment 33 ... A feature exists in a prototype branch but not production. Expected: Prototype. Not Operational. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 33: a prototype-branch-only feature is classified Prototype, not Operational; result PASS.

anchor: 109.78 — Deprecated mechanisms ... If an old component still exists but is no longer used: Deprecated should be distinguished from Active.
statement: Distinguishes Deprecated (unused legacy component) from Active for old architecture mechanisms.

anchor: 109.79 — Experiment 34 ... Old memory synchronization script remains in repository. Current architecture no longer uses it. Expected: potential LegacyArtifact, not CurrentArchitectureComponent. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 34: an unused old memory synchronization script is a potential LegacyArtifact, not a CurrentArchitectureComponent; result PASS.

anchor: 109.80 — Reconstruction quality criterion ... Step 109 succeeds when we can answer 'What actually exists?' with evidence for Components, Interfaces, Data, Rules, Agents, Tests, Runtime, Governance.
statement: States the reconstruction quality criterion: success requires evidence across eight dimensions (Components, Interfaces, Data, Rules, Agents, Tests, Runtime, Governance).

anchor: 109.81 — Step 109 verdict: STEP 109 — RECONSTRUCTION METHOD: PASS. But unlike Steps 103–108, this step marks the transition to empirical work. Therefore the correct implementation verdict is KnowledgeOS_actual=NotYetFullyMapped rather than pretending that the target architecture is already implement
statement: Records Step 109 verdict PASS scoped to the reconstruction methodology itself, with the honest implementation verdict KnowledgeOS_actual=NotYetFullyMapped, explicitly avoiding the pretense that the target architecture is already implemented.

anchor: 109.82 — The next step is the actual inventory: Step 110 — KnowledgeOS System Boundary Reconstruction. What belongs to KnowledgeOS? Classify actual artifacts into Core, Supporting, External, Agent-specific, Legacy, Unknown. Decisive test: can we draw the system boundary from evidence rather than fro
statement: Previews Step 110: classifying actual artifacts into Core/Supporting/External/Agent-specific/Legacy/Unknown to build the first actual KnowledgeOS context map, with the decisive test being whether the boundary can be drawn from evidence rather than prior assumption.

anchor: We now need to establish the actual boundary of KnowledgeOS before analyzing individual components. This distinction is essential because otherwise the architecture will gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.
statement: States the need to establish the actual KnowledgeOS boundary before component analysis, warning that without it the architecture would gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.

anchor: 110.1 — The system boundary rule ... K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}. Not K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}. An external Git server may be essential to KnowledgeOS without becoming part of KnowledgeOS itself.
statement: Defines K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}, explicitly rejecting the weaker K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}.

anchor: 110.2 — Six boundary classifications ... CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN. This is intentionally conservative.
statement: Defines six intentionally conservative boundary classifications: CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN.

anchor: 110.3 — CORE ... A component is CORE when removing it would remove an essential KnowledgeOS capability. Examples: KnowledgeModel, KnowledgePersistence, GovernanceEngine, EvidenceModel, if these actually exist in the implementation. But we must verify their existence.
statement: Defines CORE as a component whose removal would remove an essential capability, listing candidate examples pending verification of actual existence.

anchor: 110.4 — SUPPORTING ... Database, MessageBroker, ObjectStorage, CI/CD, Observability. Used by KnowledgeOS does not mean semantically part of KnowledgeOS.
statement: Defines SUPPORTING infrastructure (Database/MessageBroker/ObjectStorage/CI-CD/Observability), stating usage does not entail semantic membership.

anchor: 110.5 — AGENT ... .claude/, .codex/, AGENTS.md, agent hooks, agent commands, agent-specific settings. Their purpose is AgentBehavior. They become part of the broader ecosystem but should not automatically be classified as the KnowledgeOS semantic core.
statement: Defines AGENT classification for .claude/.codex/AGENTS.md and agent hooks/commands/settings, ecosystem members not automatically semantic core.

anchor: 110.6 — EXTERNAL ... GitHub, GitLab, Jira, CI, CloudProvider. Its data may become KnowledgeOS evidence, but the external system retains its own system boundary.
statement: Defines EXTERNAL systems (GitHub/GitLab/Jira/CI/CloudProvider) that retain their own boundary even as their data becomes KnowledgeOS evidence.

anchor: 110.7 — LEGACY ... old-memory-sync, old-registry, deprecated-indexer, legacy-agent-script. A repository containing an artifact does not mean the artifact belongs to the current architecture.
statement: Defines LEGACY artifacts as especially dangerous for creating false architectural impressions, since repository presence does not entail current-architecture membership.

anchor: 110.8 — UNKNOWN ... This is a legitimate result. It means we have not yet established enough evidence to classify the artifact. It does not mean External.
statement: Defines UNKNOWN as a legitimate classification meaning insufficient evidence, explicitly distinct from External.

anchor: 110.9 — Experiment 1 ... scripts/session-changes-logger. Is it Core, Supporting, Agent, External or Legacy? If invoked by agent hooks: likely AGENT/SUPPORTING. But classification awaits evidence. Result: UNKNOWN until usage is established
statement: Experiment 1: session-changes-logger's classification (likely AGENT/SUPPORTING if hook-invoked) is UNKNOWN until usage evidence is established.

anchor: 110.10 — Experiment 2 ... .claude/settings.json controls Claude execution. Expected: AGENT. It is not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS. Result: AGENT
statement: Experiment 2: .claude/settings.json is classified AGENT, not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS.

anchor: 110.11 — Experiment 3 ... A PostgreSQL database stores KnowledgeOS records. Expected: SUPPORTING unless the architecture explicitly defines the database as part of the deployable KnowledgeOS product boundary. Result: SUPPORTING
statement: Experiment 3: a PostgreSQL database storing KnowledgeOS records is SUPPORTING unless explicitly defined as part of the deployable product boundary.

anchor: 110.12 — Logical boundary versus deployment boundary ... A system may logically contain KnowledgeService while deployment uses PostgreSQL as an external managed service. LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary.
statement: States LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary: a logical component may be deployed via an externally managed service.

anchor: 110.13 — Product boundary versus ecosystem boundary ... Product boundary K_product, Ecosystem boundary K_ecosystem, External environment K_environment. K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment.
statement: Defines a three-tier boundary containment K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment (Product/Ecosystem/External-environment boundaries).

anchor: 110.14 — Example ... KnowledgeOS Ecosystem diagram: Core (Knowledge/Governance/Assurance), Claude/Codex/CI-CD agents, then GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra outer systems interacting without becoming core.
statement: Presents a worked ecosystem diagram: KnowledgeOS Core surrounded by Claude/Codex/CI-CD, interacting with outer GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra systems without becoming core.

anchor: 110.15 — Agent harness boundary ... This resolves an earlier architectural question. Claude and Codex are EcosystemParticipants. Their harnesses are AgentOperatingLayers. KnowledgeOS remains SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance according to the actual implementation.
statement: Resolves the recurring agent-harness classification question: Claude/Codex are EcosystemParticipants with AgentOperatingLayers, while KnowledgeOS itself is SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance.

anchor: 110.16 — Experiment 4 ... Codex reads KnowledgeOS architecture. Does that make Codex part of KnowledgeOS? Not necessarily. Expected: Codex=EcosystemParticipant. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: Codex reading KnowledgeOS architecture does not make it part of KnowledgeOS; it is classified EcosystemParticipant; result PASS.

anchor: 110.17 — But the relationship must be explicit ... Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS. And potentially Codex-produces->Evidence. This is more informative than simply placing Codex inside the same directory.
statement: States the Codex-KnowledgeOS relationship should be modeled explicitly (consumes/produces), more informative than mere directory co-location.

anchor: 110.18 — External knowledge sources ... Git, Jira, Confluence, documents, runtime systems. These should be modeled as KnowledgeSources. Not automatically as KnowledgeOS components.
statement: Defines external ingestion sources (Git/Jira/Confluence/documents/runtime systems) as KnowledgeSources, not automatically KnowledgeOS components.

anchor: 110.19 — Experiment 5 ... Jira contains a change ticket. KnowledgeOS imports it as evidence. Expected: Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 5: an imported Jira ticket is classified Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource; result PASS.

anchor: 110.20 — Source authority ... External systems may remain authoritative for certain facts. Jira→ChangeRequestAuthority. KnowledgeOS may preserve a representation: KnowledgeOS→Reference/Projection. This distinction prevents duplicate authority.
statement: States external systems may retain authority over certain facts while KnowledgeOS holds only a Reference/Projection, preventing duplicate authority.

anchor: 110.21 — Experiment 6 ... Jira is authoritative for ticket status. KnowledgeOS stores ticket_status. Expected: KnowledgeOS should not silently become a competing authority unless explicitly designed to do so. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: KnowledgeOS storing a Jira-authoritative ticket_status field must not silently become a competing authority; result PASS.

anchor: 110.22 — Projection versus ownership ... Projection≠Ownership. KnowledgeOS may contain Projection(X) without owning Truth(X). This is particularly important for evidence.
statement: States Projection≠Ownership: holding Projection(X) does not entail owning Truth(X), important for evidence handling.

anchor: 110.23 — Evidence source graph ... Source→Observation→KnowledgeOS. Git→Commit→Observation→KnowledgeOS Evidence.
statement: Defines the evidence source graph Source→Observation→KnowledgeOS, illustrated by Git→Commit→Observation→KnowledgeOS Evidence.

anchor: 110.24 — Experiment 7 ... Git commit is imported. Expected: KnowledgeOS records source, commit identity, timestamp, repository, relationship to observed change. Result: PASS if implemented. The architectural requirement is clear; implementation remains to be evidenced.
statement: Experiment 7: importing a Git commit should record source/commit identity/timestamp/repository/relationship to change; result conditionally PASS pending implementation evidence.

anchor: 110.25 — Boundary discovery through dependency direction ... DependencyDirection. If A→B we ask: which system owns the contract? The caller is not necessarily the owner.
statement: States boundary discovery via dependency direction: for A→B, contract ownership must be determined separately, since the caller is not necessarily the owner.

anchor: 110.26 — Experiment 8 ... KnowledgeOS calls GitHub API. Expected: GitHub=External. KnowledgeOS is the consumer. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: KnowledgeOS calling the GitHub API leaves GitHub=External with KnowledgeOS as consumer; result PASS.

anchor: 110.27 — Reverse integration ... If GitHub webhook calls KnowledgeOS: GitHub remains external. The direction of invocation does not determine system ownership.
statement: States the direction of invocation does not determine system ownership: a GitHub-initiated webhook still leaves GitHub external.

anchor: 110.28 — Experiment 9 ... GitHub sends an event to KnowledgeOS. Expected: GitHub=EXTERNAL, KnowledgeOS=CORE. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: an inbound GitHub event still leaves GitHub=EXTERNAL, KnowledgeOS=CORE; result PASS.

anchor: 110.29 — Infrastructure boundary ... Podman, Kubernetes, Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka may be essential to operation. But InfrastructureDependency≠KnowledgeModel.
statement: States InfrastructureDependency≠KnowledgeModel: operational essentiality of infrastructure tools does not make them semantic components.

anchor: 110.30 — Experiment 10 ... KnowledgeOS cannot run without PostgreSQL. Expected: PostgreSQL is operationally essential but not automatically a KnowledgeOS semantic component. Result: SUPPORTING
statement: Experiment 10: PostgreSQL, though operationally essential, is classified SUPPORTING rather than a semantic component.

anchor: 110.31 — Runtime boundary ... A runtime process may be part of KnowledgeOS even if its source resides elsewhere. Conversely, source code may exist in the repository but never participate in the current runtime. RuntimeMembership must be separately established.
statement: States RuntimeMembership must be separately established from source-code presence, since runtime and repository membership can diverge in either direction.

anchor: 110.32 — Experiment 11 ... A repository contains legacy-indexer/. It is not deployed. Expected: LEGACY or UNKNOWN. Not CORE RuntimeComponent. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: an undeployed legacy-indexer/ is classified LEGACY or UNKNOWN, never CORE RuntimeComponent; result PASS.

anchor: 110.33 — The 'dead code' problem ... experimental code, abandoned prototypes, old migrations, historical scripts, unused libraries. RepositoryMembership≠SystemMembership. This is one of the most important findings of the reconstruction methodology.
statement: States RepositoryMembership≠SystemMembership as one of the reconstruction methodology's most important findings, given repositories' accumulation of experimental/abandoned/unused code.

anchor: 110.34 — Experiment 12 ... A module has 5,000 lines of sophisticated knowledge code. No build references it. Expected: it cannot be counted as operational KnowledgeOS functionality. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: a substantial but build-unreferenced module cannot be counted as operational functionality; result PASS.

anchor: 110.35 — Build graph ... BuildGraph. Is the module compiled? Is it packaged? Is it included in deployment? Is it referenced? Is it tested? This gives stronger evidence of actual membership.
statement: Defines the BuildGraph inspection (compiled/packaged/included/referenced/tested) as stronger evidence of actual system membership.

anchor: 110.36 — Experiment 13 ... Module is compiled but never deployed. Expected: IMPLEMENTED but NOT OPERATIONAL. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a compiled-but-never-deployed module is IMPLEMENTED but NOT OPERATIONAL; result PASS.

anchor: 110.37 — Deployment graph ... DeploymentGraph. Repository→BuildArtifact→Container→Deployment→Runtime. Only components with an established path should be treated as operational.
statement: Defines the DeploymentGraph Repository→BuildArtifact→Container→Deployment→Runtime as the required path for operational status.

anchor: 110.38 — Experiment 14 ... Source component exists. No build artifact contains it. Expected: NonOperational. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: a source component absent from any build artifact is NonOperational; result PASS.

anchor: 110.39 — Runtime graph ... RuntimeGraph. A component is operationally part of the system if we can establish Artifact→Deployment→RuntimeInstance.
statement: Defines the RuntimeGraph criterion Artifact→Deployment→RuntimeInstance for establishing operational membership.

anchor: 110.40 — Experiment 15 ... Deployment manifest contains service X. Runtime never starts it. Expected: DeploymentDefined but RuntimeNotObserved. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: a manifest-defined but never-started service is DeploymentDefined/RuntimeNotObserved; result PASS.

anchor: 110.41 — Boundary confidence ... Confidence∈{High,Medium,Low}. CoreComponent+BuildEvidence+RuntimeEvidence⇒High.
statement: Defines a three-level boundary-classification confidence scale (High/Medium/Low), with the composition rule CoreComponent+BuildEvidence+RuntimeEvidence⇒High.

anchor: 110.42 — Boundary evidence record ... BoundaryEvidence=(Classification,Reason,Evidence,Confidence,Date). This prevents later arguments based on memory.
statement: Defines the BoundaryEvidence=(Classification,Reason,Evidence,Confidence,Date) record schema, preventing later memory-based disputes over classification.

type_signature.codomain: Classification x Reason x Evidence x Confidence x Date

anchor: 110.43 — Experiment 16 ... Someone later asks why .claude/ is classified as agent-specific. Expected: KnowledgeOS can point to configuration semantics, invocation, hooks, agent-specific behavior. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: a later classification challenge (.claude/ as agent-specific) must be answerable by pointing to configuration semantics/invocation/hooks/behavior; result PASS.

anchor: 110.44 — Context map ... DDD-style context map: KnowledgeOS (Knowledge/Governance/Evidence/Assurance) surrounded by Claude/Codex/CI-CD, then External Sources (Git/Tickets/Documents/Runtime). This is the logical ecosystem map, not yet the final physical topology.
statement: Presents a DDD-style logical ecosystem context map (KnowledgeOS core, Claude/Codex/CI-CD, external Git/Tickets/Documents/Runtime), explicitly not yet the final physical topology.

anchor: 110.45 — Upstream/downstream relationships ... For each external interaction we should determine Upstream and Downstream. Git→KnowledgeOS may mean Git is upstream for source evidence.
statement: States per-interaction upstream/downstream determination is required, illustrated by Git as upstream source-evidence provider.

anchor: 110.46 — Experiment 17 ... KnowledgeOS publishes a governance result into Jira. KnowledgeOS→Jira. Jira is downstream for that interaction. The same external system can therefore be Upstream for one relationship and Downstream for another.
statement: Experiment 17: Jira, upstream as an evidence source, becomes downstream when KnowledgeOS publishes a governance result into it, showing the same system can hold both roles across relationships.

anchor: 110.47 — Relationship semantics ... We should avoid generic 'integrates with.' Instead classify relationships: Consumes, Produces, Reads, Writes, Publishes, Subscribes, Verifies, Authorizes, Projects. This makes the context map executable.
statement: Defines a nine-verb relationship-semantics vocabulary (Consumes/Produces/Reads/Writes/Publishes/Subscribes/Verifies/Authorizes/Projects) replacing generic 'integrates with' phrasing, making the context map executable.

anchor: 110.48 — Experiment 18 ... Codex reads architecture knowledge and writes code. Expected: Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS and Codex-produces->EngineeringChange. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: Codex's activity is modeled as Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS and Codex-produces->EngineeringChange; result PASS.

anchor: 110.49 — System boundary invariants ... I_Boundary: a component must not be classified as Core solely because it is stored in the same repository. I_AuthorityBoundary: data projection does not automatically transfer authority. I_RuntimeMembership: source existence does not establish runtime membersh
statement: Names five system-boundary invariants: I_Boundary, I_AuthorityBoundary, I_RuntimeMembership, I_AgentBoundary, I_External.

invariants.name: I_Boundary
invariants.statement: A component must not be classified as Core solely because it is stored in the same repository.

invariants.name: I_AuthorityBoundary
invariants.statement: Data projection does not automatically transfer authority.

invariants.name: I_RuntimeMembership
invariants.statement: Source existence does not establish runtime membership.

invariants.name: I_AgentBoundary
invariants.statement: Agent-specific operating artifacts must remain distinguishable from authoritative KnowledgeOS knowledge.

invariants.name: I_External
invariants.statement: External systems remain externally owned unless explicit system-boundary evidence establishes otherwise.

anchor: 110.50 — The first actual system map ... Organizational Governance/Intent → KNOWLEDGEOS (Knowledge/Evidence/Governance/Assurance/Semantic Relationships) → Claude Agent/Codex Agent/Engineering Systems → External Knowledge Sources → Git/Jira/Runtime. The exact components inside each box remain an empi
statement: Presents the first actual system map diagram from Organizational Governance/Intent through KnowledgeOS core, agent/engineering layers, to external knowledge sources, with exact box contents flagged as still empirical.

anchor: 110.51 — What Step 110 has established ... We have established the boundary method, not yet the final component list. The important result is that we now know how to decide whether an artifact belongs to Core versus Ecosystem versus External.
statement: States Step 110 establishes the boundary-classification method, not the final component list, having established how to decide Core vs Ecosystem vs External membership.

anchor: 110.52 — Step 110 verdict: STEP 110 — SYSTEM BOUNDARY MODEL: PASS. The conceptual boundary is coherent. The empirical boundary remains KnowledgeOS_ActualBoundary=TBD until the repository and operational evidence are mapped.
statement: Records Step 110 verdict PASS for conceptual boundary coherence, with the honest empirical verdict KnowledgeOS_ActualBoundary=TBD pending repository/operational evidence mapping.

anchor: 110.53 — The next step: Step 111 — Actual Component Inventory. Component→Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Interface→Dependency→Evidence→Runtime. Is there actually one coherent KnowledgeOS core, or has the current implementation evolved into several partially overlapping subsystems? That question will be
statement: Previews Step 111: reconstructing the real internal architecture via Component→Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Interface→Dependency→Evidence→Runtime, centered on whether KnowledgeOS is one coherent core or several partially overlapping subsystems.

anchor: We now move from system boundary to the inside of the system. Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence. A component is therefore not defined merely by its directory or class name.
statement: Defines Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence, stating a component is not defined merely by its directory or class name.

anchor: 111.1 — Component reconstruction principle ... C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner). Only after these are established can we decide whether two components are separate, overlapping, duplicates, parts of one bounded context
statement: Defines the full component reconstruction tuple C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner), a precondition for classifying inter-component relationships.

type_signature.codomain: Identity x Purpose x Responsibilities x Data x Commands x Queries x Dependencies x Interfaces x Invariants x Tests x Runtime x Owner

anchor: 111.2 — First question: what is a component? ... Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext. They are not equivalent.
statement: Distinguishes seven frequently-confused units of analysis: Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext.

anchor: 111.3 — Experiment 1 ... Repository contains KnowledgeService.java. Can we conclude KnowledgeService=KnowledgeBoundedContext? No. It may simply be an application service. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: a KnowledgeService.java class does not by itself establish a KnowledgeBoundedContext; it may be merely an application service; result PASS.

anchor: 111.4 — Component levels ... System→BoundedContext→{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, plus Supporting Systems. This prevents accidental conflation of implementation structure and domain structure.
statement: Defines a multi-level reconstruction tree (System->BoundedContext->{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, Supporting Systems) preventing conflation of implementation and domain structure.

anchor: 111.5 — Component identity ... ComponentID should not depend solely on ClassName. Because names change.
statement: States component identity must be stable and independent of class naming, since names change.

anchor: 111.6 — Experiment 2 ... Class KnowledgeService becomes EngineeringKnowledgeService. Expected: potentially the same logical component. Result: PASS. This is why logical identity and implementation naming must be separated.
statement: Experiment 2: a renamed class (KnowledgeService to EngineeringKnowledgeService) may remain the same logical component; result PASS, motivating separation of logical identity from naming.

anchor: 111.7 — Responsibility reconstruction ... What responsibility does this component actually own? Not what does its README claim? We inspect Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies.
statement: States responsibility must be reconstructed from actual Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies, not from README claims.

anchor: 111.8 — Experiment 3 ... Component named KnowledgeManager actually reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data. Expected: observed responsibility closer to KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing than KnowledgeAuthority. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: a KnowledgeManager's actual behavior (reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data) reveals its real responsibility as KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing rather than KnowledgeAuthority; result PASS.

anchor: 111.9 — Responsibility is more important than naming ... ObservedBehavior > ComponentName for determining actual responsibility.
statement: States the central rule ObservedBehavior>ComponentName for determining actual component responsibility.

invariants.name: I_ObservedBehaviorOverName
invariants.statement: ObservedBehavior outranks ComponentName when determining a component's actual responsibility.

anchor: 111.10 — Data ownership ... Which data does the component own? We distinguish Reads(Data) from Owns(Data). A service can read data without owning it.
statement: Distinguishes Reads(Data) from Owns(Data): a service reading data does not thereby own it.

anchor: 111.11 — Experiment 4 ... Component A reads Decision. Component B creates and changes Decision. Expected: B is the stronger candidate for ownership. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: the component that creates and changes Decision (B) is the stronger ownership candidate over one that merely reads it (A); result PASS.

anchor: 111.12 — Data ownership graph ... Component-owns->Data and separately Component-reads->Data. This becomes crucial for determining bounded-context boundaries.
statement: Defines the data-ownership graph with separate owns and reads edge types, crucial for bounded-context boundary determination.

anchor: 111.13 — Experiment 5 ... Two services directly modify the same decision table. Expected: potential shared-data coupling. Result: OBS. This does not yet prove architectural failure, but it is an important finding.
statement: Experiment 5: two services directly mutating the same decision table is potential shared-data coupling, classified OBS (an important finding, not yet a proven failure).

anchor: 111.14 — Aggregate ownership ... Aggregate→Invariant→Owner. Decision may own invariants such as Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.
statement: Defines the aggregate-ownership model Aggregate→Invariant→Owner, illustrated by Decision owning Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.

anchor: 111.15 — Experiment 6 ... Two unrelated services can independently set decision.status=APPROVED without passing through a common invariant boundary. Expected: potential aggregate-boundary violation. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 6: two independent services both able to set decision.status=APPROVED without a shared invariant boundary is a potential aggregate-boundary violation, classified OBS.

anchor: 111.16 — Command ownership ... Command→OwningComponent. CreateEvidence, ApproveDecision, RegisterAgent, RecordObservation.
statement: Defines command ownership Command→OwningComponent, with example commands CreateEvidence/ApproveDecision/RegisterAgent/RecordObservation.

anchor: 111.17 — Experiment 7 ... Both Service A and Service B implement ApproveDecision. Expected: potential duplicate business responsibility. Result: OBS. This is exactly the kind of issue the actual inventory should expose.
statement: Experiment 7: two services both implementing ApproveDecision is potential duplicate business responsibility, classified OBS, exemplifying the inventory's diagnostic purpose.

anchor: 111.18 — Query ownership ... Query→OwningSource. But multiple read models may legitimately expose the same information. DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership.
statement: States DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership: multiple read models exposing the same information may be legitimate rather than duplicated ownership.

anchor: 111.19 — Experiment 8 ... Two APIs expose GET /decisions. One is a UI projection. The other is the authoritative domain API. Expected: not automatically a duplicate domain capability. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: a UI-projection GET /decisions endpoint alongside an authoritative domain API endpoint is not automatically duplicate domain capability; result PASS.

anchor: 111.20 — Interface reconstruction ... Interfaces(C)=Inbound+Outbound. Inbound: API, command, event, CLI, scheduled invocation. Outbound: database, API, event, filesystem, agent, external service.
statement: Defines Interfaces(C)=Inbound+Outbound with five inbound categories (API/command/event/CLI/scheduled invocation) and six outbound categories (database/API/event/filesystem/agent/external service).

anchor: 111.21 — Experiment 9 ... Component exposes POST /knowledge and consumes GitHub API. Expected: its interface map includes both. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: a component exposing POST /knowledge while consuming the GitHub API has both interfaces recorded in its interface map; result PASS.

anchor: 111.22 — Synchronous versus asynchronous ... KnowledgeService→Git may be synchronous. Observation→EventBus→KnowledgeProcessor may be asynchronous. This matters architecturally.
statement: Classifies component communication as Sync vs Async, illustrated by a synchronous KnowledgeService->Git call and an asynchronous Observation->EventBus->KnowledgeProcessor path.

anchor: 111.23 — Experiment 10 ... Documentation says event-driven architecture. Actual code performs synchronous REST calls everywhere. Expected: potential architecture/implementation drift. Result: DRIFT
statement: Experiment 10: documented event-driven architecture contradicted by universal synchronous REST calls is classified DRIFT.

anchor: 111.24 — Dependency classification ... DomainDependency, ApplicationDependency, InfrastructureDependency, ExternalDependency.
statement: Defines a four-way dependency classification: DomainDependency, ApplicationDependency, InfrastructureDependency, ExternalDependency.

anchor: 111.25 — Experiment 11 ... Domain object imports a PostgreSQL driver. Expected: potential architectural layering violation. Result: OBS/DRIFT depending on the actual architecture rule.
statement: Experiment 11: a domain object importing a PostgreSQL driver is a potential layering violation, classified OBS/DRIFT depending on the actual architecture rule.

anchor: 111.26 — Layer reconstruction ... Presentation→Application→Domain→Infrastructure. The intended dependency direction must be established from the actual architecture rules.
statement: Defines layer reconstruction Presentation→Application→Domain→Infrastructure, noting the intended dependency direction must come from actual architecture rules, not assumption.

anchor: 111.27 — Experiment 12 ... Infrastructure calls domain logic. Expected: could be valid depending on dependency inversion. DependencyDirection must be interpreted semantically, not by simplistic layer rules. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: infrastructure calling domain logic may be valid under dependency inversion, requiring DependencyDirection to be interpreted semantically rather than by simplistic layer rules; result PASS.

anchor: 111.28 — Domain versus technical services ... DomainConcept or merely TechnicalCapability. KnowledgeIndexer is likely technical. Decision may represent domain semantics.
statement: Distinguishes DomainConcept from TechnicalCapability, illustrated by KnowledgeIndexer (likely technical) versus Decision (likely domain semantics).

anchor: 111.29 — Experiment 13 ... Component called KnowledgeProcessor does only EmbeddingGeneration. Expected: technical infrastructure, not necessarily domain logic. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a KnowledgeProcessor performing only EmbeddingGeneration is technical infrastructure, not domain logic; result PASS.

anchor: 111.30 — Domain language reconstruction ... UbiquitousLanguage. Terms actually used in classes, APIs, schemas, tests, workflows, documentation. Then compare them.
statement: Prescribes extracting UbiquitousLanguage from classes/APIs/schemas/tests/workflows/documentation and comparing across artifact types.

anchor: 111.31 — Experiment 14 ... Architecture uses Evidence. Code uses Document. Database uses Artifact. UI uses Knowledge Item. Expected: potential semantic inconsistency. Result: OBS. This could become a major finding.
statement: Experiment 14: four different terms (Evidence/Document/Artifact/Knowledge Item) used across architecture/code/database/UI for what may be one concept is a potential semantic inconsistency, classified OBS as a possible major finding.

anchor: 111.32 — Semantic collisions ... SameTerm→DifferentMeaning. 'Knowledge' may mean document, embedding, claim, fact, decision, observation. This is dangerous.
statement: Defines semantic collisions (SameTerm->DifferentMeaning), warning that 'Knowledge' meaning document/embedding/claim/fact/decision/observation across modules is dangerous.

anchor: 111.33 — Experiment 15 ... Two modules both use Knowledge but have incompatible semantics. Expected: potential bounded-context language collision. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 15: two modules using 'Knowledge' with incompatible semantics is a potential bounded-context language collision, classified OBS.

anchor: 111.34 — Semantic duplication ... DifferentTerms→SameMeaning. Evidence, Artifact, SourceRecord. This can indicate accidental duplication.
statement: Defines semantic duplication (DifferentTerms->SameMeaning), illustrated by Evidence/Artifact/SourceRecord potentially indicating accidental duplication.

anchor: 111.35 — Component cohesion ... Cohesion(C) based on the relationship between commands, data, invariants, dependencies.
statement: Defines Cohesion(C) based on the relationship among a component's commands, data, invariants, and dependencies.

anchor: 111.36 — Experiment 16 ... KnowledgeManager imports Git, manages users, performs embeddings, approves architecture, sends emails, writes audit records. Expected: very low semantic cohesion. Result: DRIFT/DECOMPOSITION CANDIDATE
statement: Experiment 16: a KnowledgeManager spanning six unrelated responsibilities (Git import, user management, embeddings, architecture approval, email, audit) shows very low cohesion, classified DRIFT/DECOMPOSITION CANDIDATE.

anchor: 111.37 — Component coupling ... Coupling(A,B) should be assessed. Strong coupling is not automatically bad. But unexplained coupling is valuable evidence.
statement: Defines Coupling(A,B) assessment, noting strong coupling is not automatically bad but unexplained coupling is valuable evidence.

anchor: 111.38 — Experiment 17 ... Governance component directly accesses six unrelated domain tables. Expected: potential excessive coupling. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 17: a governance component directly accessing six unrelated domain tables is potential excessive coupling, classified OBS.

anchor: 111.39 — Boundary candidate ... When we find HighCohesion+HighCoupling around a coherent concept, that may indicate a bounded-context candidate.
statement: States HighCohesion+HighCoupling clustered around a coherent concept may indicate a bounded-context candidate.

anchor: 111.40 — Experiment 18 ... Evidence-related data, commands, rules, APIs, tests are strongly clustered. Expected: strong evidence for EvidenceContext. Result: BOUNDARY CANDIDATE
statement: Experiment 18: strongly clustered evidence-related data/commands/rules/APIs/tests are strong evidence for an EvidenceContext, classified BOUNDARY CANDIDATE.

anchor: 111.41 — This connects to previous architecture work ... Evidence, Voting, Appointment/Mandate, Contestation, Adjudication. For KnowledgeOS reconstruction, we must not assume those boundaries apply automatically. We test whether the implementation supports them.
statement: States prior bounded-context candidates (Evidence/Voting/Appointment-Mandate/Contestation/Adjudication) must not be assumed to apply automatically to KnowledgeOS reconstruction; each requires independent implementation testing.

anchor: 111.42 — Experiment 19 ... Architecture says EvidenceContext. Implementation has evidence logic distributed across 8 unrelated modules. Expected: potential implementation mismatch. Result: DRIFT
statement: Experiment 19: an architecturally-named EvidenceContext implemented across 8 unrelated modules is a potential implementation mismatch, classified DRIFT.

anchor: 111.43 — Component inventory versus bounded contexts ... ComponentInventory≠BoundedContextMap. The inventory comes first. Then Components→ResponsibilityClusters→BoundedContextCandidates.
statement: States ComponentInventory≠BoundedContextMap, with the inventory strictly preceding Components->ResponsibilityClusters->BoundedContextCandidates.

anchor: 111.44 — Runtime identity ... LogicalComponent→DeploymentUnit→RuntimeInstance. This allows us to connect source architecture to production.
statement: Defines runtime identity LogicalComponent→DeploymentUnit→RuntimeInstance, connecting source architecture to production.

anchor: 111.45 — Experiment 20 ... One logical component is deployed as 3 containers. Expected: one logical component, three runtime instances. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: one logical component deployed as three containers is recorded as one logical component with three runtime instances; result PASS.

anchor: 111.46 — Component lifecycle ... Active, Experimental, Deprecated, Retired.
statement: Defines a four-value component lifecycle status: Active, Experimental, Deprecated, Retired.

anchor: 111.47 — Experiment 21 ... Component has source code but deployment is disabled. Expected: potential Deprecated/Inactive. Not ActiveRuntimeComponent. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: a component with disabled deployment is potentially Deprecated/Inactive, not an ActiveRuntimeComponent; result PASS.

anchor: 111.48 — Component ownership ... Owner(C). Possible owners: team, product, architecture domain, platform, external provider.
statement: Defines Owner(C) with five possible owner categories: team, product, architecture domain, platform, external provider.

anchor: 111.49 — Experiment 22 ... No owner can be established. Expected: Owner=Unknown. This is itself an architectural governance finding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: an unestablishable owner yields Owner=Unknown, itself an architectural governance finding; result PASS.

anchor: 111.50 — Component criticality ... Criticality(C)∈{Critical,High,Medium,Low}. Based on impact, not code size.
statement: Defines Criticality(C)∈{Critical,High,Medium,Low} based on impact rather than code size.

anchor: 111.51 — Experiment 23 ... A 50-line authorization service controls production changes. Expected: potentially Critical. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: a small 50-line authorization service controlling production changes is potentially Critical despite its size; result PASS.

anchor: 111.52 — Test coverage ... Verification(C) should identify unit tests, integration tests, architecture tests, security tests, runtime tests.
statement: Defines per-component Verification(C) identifying unit/integration/architecture/security/runtime tests.

anchor: 111.53 — Experiment 24 ... Critical governance component has no automated tests. Expected: AssuranceGap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 24: a critical governance component with no automated tests is an AssuranceGap; result PASS.

anchor: 111.54 — Component evidence card ... COMPONENT: X with Logical role, Observed responsibility, Owns, Reads, Writes, Inbound, Outbound, Dependencies, Rules, Tests, Runtime, Owner, Architecture mapping, Evidence, Confidence, Conformance. This becomes the atomic unit of reconstruction.
statement: Specifies the 16-field Component Evidence Card schema as the atomic unit of reconstruction.

anchor: 111.55 — Component relationship graph ... G_C=(Components,Relationships). Calls, Reads, Writes, Publishes, Subscribes, Implements, Verifies, Owns.
statement: Defines the component relationship graph G_C=(Components,Relationships) with eight relationship types.

anchor: 111.56 — Experiment 25 ... Two components share a database. Graph records A-writes->DB, B-writes->DB. Expected: potential ownership conflict becomes visible. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: two components both writing to a shared database surfaces a potential ownership conflict via the relationship graph; result PASS.

anchor: 111.57 — Architecture smell detection ... Hub component, Circular dependency, Shared database coupling, Orphan, Duplicate capability. These are signals, not automatic violations.
statement: Defines five architecture-smell patterns detectable from the component graph (Hub, Circular dependency, Shared database coupling, Orphan, Duplicate capability), explicitly framed as signals rather than automatic violations.

anchor: 111.58 — Experiment 26 ... Graph reveals A→B→C→A. Expected: CircularDependencyCandidate. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: a graph cycle A→B→C→A is flagged CircularDependencyCandidate; result PASS.

anchor: 111.59 — Agent component relationships ... Claude→KnowledgeOS, Codex→KnowledgeOS, Agent→Repository, Agent→Verification, Agent→Evidence.
statement: Defines agent-component relationship mapping: Claude/Codex to KnowledgeOS, Agent to Repository/Verification/Evidence.

anchor: 111.60 — Experiment 27 ... Claude modifies repository directly but bypasses KnowledgeOS governance. Expected: potential agent governance boundary violation. Result: OBS/DRIFT. The exact classification depends on the intended workflow.
statement: Experiment 27: Claude modifying the repository while bypassing KnowledgeOS governance is a potential agent governance boundary violation, classified OBS/DRIFT depending on intended workflow.

anchor: 111.61 — Shared infrastructure ... If Claude and Codex share VerificationEngine, that is useful evidence of a common assurance layer.
statement: States a shared VerificationEngine between Claude and Codex is useful evidence of a common assurance layer.

anchor: 111.62 — Experiment 28 ... Claude has one verification mechanism. Codex has another incompatible verification mechanism. Expected: potential assurance fragmentation. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 28: incompatible per-agent verification mechanisms (Claude vs Codex) is potential assurance fragmentation, classified OBS.

anchor: 111.63 — The ideal agent relationship ... KnowledgeOS with Common Rules, Common Evidence, Common Governance shared by Claude and Codex. Not Claude→private architecture, Codex→private architecture.
statement: Presents the ideal shared-infrastructure diagram (KnowledgeOS with Common Rules/Evidence/Governance shared by Claude and Codex), contrasted with the undesired private-per-agent-architecture pattern.

anchor: 111.64 — Component inventory status model ... Status∈{Confirmed,Candidate,Legacy,External,Duplicate,Overlapping,Unknown}. This avoids premature architecture decisions.
statement: Defines a seven-value component inventory status model (Confirmed/Candidate/Legacy/External/Duplicate/Overlapping/Unknown), avoiding premature architecture decisions.

anchor: 111.65 — Experiment 29 ... Two components appear to implement the same capability. Expected: DuplicateCandidate. Not immediately DeleteOne. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: two apparently-duplicate components are classified DuplicateCandidate, not immediately marked for deletion; result PASS.

anchor: 111.66 — Reconstruction confidence ... Confidence(C)=f(Structure,Source,Tests,Deployment,Runtime). High: Source+Tests+Runtime. Medium: Source+Tests. Low: DocumentationOnly.
statement: Defines Confidence(C)=f(Structure,Source,Tests,Deployment,Runtime) with High/Medium/Low compositions (Source+Tests+Runtime / Source+Tests / DocumentationOnly).

type_signature.domain: Structure x Source x Tests x Deployment x Runtime

anchor: 111.67 — Actual component map ... KnowledgeOS→Knowledge/Governance/Assurance→C1..C9. But the labels C1...C9 must come from actual repository evidence.
statement: Presents an illustrative actual component map (KnowledgeOS->Knowledge/Governance/Assurance->nine components C1-C9) with labels required to come from actual repository evidence, not invention.

anchor: 111.68 — The important discovery criterion ... The most important output is not the number of components. It is whether the component graph exhibits CoherentBoundaries. We want to discover whether Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Ownership aligns.
statement: States the central discovery criterion CoherentBoundaries: whether Responsibility->Data->Behavior->Ownership align, more important than component count.

anchor: 111.69 — The key diagnostic ... Outcome A Coherent (Components≈ArchitecturalBoundaries). Outcome B Fragmented (OneConcept→ManyOverlappingComponents). Outcome C Monolithic (ManyConcepts→OneLargeComponent). These lead to very different architectural conclusions.
statement: Defines three mutually exclusive architectural outcomes -- Coherent, Fragmented, Monolithic -- each stated to lead to materially different architectural conclusions.

anchor: 111.70 — Experiment 30 ... Evidence, governance, agent control and runtime assurance all live in one massive service with shared tables. Expected: potential MonolithicKnowledgeOSCore. This is not automatically wrong. But it is materially different from a distributed bounded-context architecture. Res
statement: Experiment 30: evidence/governance/agent-control/runtime-assurance sharing one monolithic service and tables is a potential MonolithicKnowledgeOSCore, classified OBS and explicitly not automatically wrong but materially different from a distributed architecture.

anchor: 111.71 — Conversely ... If Evidence exists in four unrelated implementations, while Governance exists in three different mechanisms, then ArchitectureFragmentation.
statement: Defines the converse ArchitectureFragmentation outcome, illustrated by Evidence spanning four unrelated implementations and Governance spanning three different mechanisms.

anchor: 111.72 — What we should not do yet ... We should not redesign anything. We should not conclude 'This service must be split.' We should first establish ObservedArchitecture. Then TargetArchitecture. Then Gap. Only afterward Remediation.
statement: States a strict anti-premature-redesign discipline: ObservedArchitecture->TargetArchitecture->Gap->Remediation in that order, never jumping to a redesign conclusion.

anchor: 111.73 — Step 111 verdict ... The actual component inventory methodology is now defined: Repository→Component→Responsibility→Data→Interface→Dependency→Verification→Runtime. The next empirical artifact is KnowledgeOS Actual Component Inventory with evidence attached to every significant claim.
statement: Records the Step 111 methodology pipeline Repository->Component->Responsibility->Data->Interface->Dependency->Verification->Runtime, naming the KnowledgeOS Actual Component Inventory as the next empirical artifact.

anchor: 111.74 — The next step: Step 112 — Semantic Ownership Reconstruction. Who actually owns the meaning of the data and decisions? We will reconstruct Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→BoundedContext and test whether the current KnowledgeOS implementation has a genuine semantic core, or whether 'knowledge' i
statement: Previews Step 112: reconstructing Data->Meaning->Invariant->Owner->BoundedContext to test whether KnowledgeOS has a genuine semantic core or is an aggregation of technically related but semantically different mechanisms, called one of the most important findings of the entire reconstruction.

anchor: We now move from component architecture to semantic architecture. What meaning does each component actually own? The central chain is Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→BoundedContext.
statement: Defines the central semantic-ownership chain Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→BoundedContext, shifting from component to semantic architecture.

anchor: 112.1 — Data is not knowledge ... Data≠Knowledge. A row in a database is data. Knowledge requires semantic interpretation. 'ADR-042 was approved on 2026-08-12.' can represent Decision with subject, authority, timestamp, rationale, status, provenance.
statement: States Data≠Knowledge: raw data (rows, documents, embeddings, logs) requires semantic interpretation to become knowledge, illustrated by an ADR-approval string requiring subject/authority/timestamp/rationale/status/provenance to constitute a Decision.

anchor: 112.2 — Experiment 1 ... Database contains status=APPROVED. Can we conclude that an authorized decision exists? Not necessarily. We need WhoApproved, UnderWhichAuthority, When, WhatWasApproved, WhatEvidenceSupportsIt. Result: PASS. A field value is not sufficient semantic evidence.
statement: Experiment 1: a bare status=APPROVED field value does not establish an authorized decision without who/under-what-authority/when/what/evidence; result PASS, a field value is not sufficient semantic evidence.

anchor: 112.3 — Semantic object ... Concept=(Identity,Meaning,State,Invariants,Relationships,Authority,Provenance). This becomes the basis for identifying genuine domain objects.
statement: Defines the semantic object tuple Concept=(Identity,Meaning,State,Invariants,Relationships,Authority,Provenance) as the basis for identifying genuine domain objects.

type_signature.codomain: Identity x Meaning x State x Invariants x Relationships x Authority x Provenance

anchor: 112.4 — Candidate concepts ... evidence, observations, claims, decisions, rules, architecture, agents, changes, findings, verification. But ConceptMention≠ConceptImplementation.
statement: Lists ten candidate semantic concepts and states ConceptMention≠ConceptImplementation.

anchor: 112.5 — Experiment 2 ... The word Evidence appears in EvidenceCollector, EvidenceStore, EvidenceReport, EvidenceAPI. Expected: this establishes terminology, not yet a coherent Evidence domain. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: four classes naming 'Evidence' establish terminology only, not proof of a coherent Evidence domain; result PASS.

anchor: 112.6 — Semantic definition ... What does this thing mean? Evidence=information that supports or constrains a claim. But the actual implementation may define it differently. The repository's actual semantics must therefore be reconstructed.
statement: States each candidate concept's meaning must be reconstructed from actual implementation semantics rather than an assumed definition.

anchor: 112.7 — Experiment 3 ... Module A treats an 'evidence' object as a source document. Module B treats 'evidence' as a runtime observation. Expected: potential semantic collision. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 3: Module A treating evidence as a source document versus Module B treating it as a runtime observation is a potential semantic collision, classified OBS.

anchor: 112.8 — Meaning boundary ... If two contexts use the same word differently: Evidence_A≠Evidence_B. That may be perfectly legitimate if the contexts are distinct. The problem arises when the system treats them as the same concept without an explicit translation.
statement: States Evidence_A≠Evidence_B across distinct contexts may be legitimate; the problem arises only when treated as the same concept without explicit translation.

anchor: 112.9 — Bounded Context hypothesis ... A bounded context exists when a coherent semantic model owns Concepts+Rules+Invariants+Language. Therefore BoundedContext≠Directory.
statement: Defines a bounded context as existing where a coherent semantic model owns Concepts+Rules+Invariants+Language, stating BoundedContext≠Directory.

anchor: 112.10 — Experiment 4 ... A directory is named evidence/ but contains only file parsing, OCR, embeddings. Expected: this may be an ingestion/indexing component, not necessarily an Evidence bounded context. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: an 'evidence/' directory containing only file parsing/OCR/embeddings may be ingestion infrastructure, not an Evidence bounded context; result PASS.

anchor: 112.11 — Semantic ownership ... Who owns the meaning? Not merely who stores the record? EvidenceRepository may store evidence. But EvidenceDomain should define what evidence means and what makes it valid.
statement: Reframes semantic ownership as 'who owns the meaning' distinct from 'who stores the record,' illustrated by EvidenceRepository (storage) vs EvidenceDomain (meaning/validity definition).

anchor: 112.12 — Experiment 5 ... Three services write evidence records. Only one defines evidence validation rules. Expected: the validating service is the stronger semantic owner candidate. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 5: among three evidence-writing services, the one defining validation rules is the stronger semantic-owner candidate; result PASS.

anchor: 112.13 — Invariants identify ownership ... Invariant→Owner. Claim⇒EvidenceRequired. The component enforcing that rule is a strong candidate for owning the relevant semantic boundary.
statement: States Invariant->Owner as one of the strongest ownership-identification techniques, illustrated by Claim⇒EvidenceRequired.

anchor: 112.14 — Experiment 6 ... Two components manipulate a Decision. Only one enforces Approved⇒AuthorityPresent. Expected: that component likely owns the decision invariant. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: among two Decision-manipulating components, the one enforcing Approved⇒AuthorityPresent likely owns the decision invariant; result PASS.

anchor: 112.15 — State transitions ... Candidate→Reviewed→Verified→Authoritative. Who is allowed to perform each transition? That reveals the governance boundary.
statement: States that authorized state-transition performers (Candidate->Reviewed->Verified->Authoritative) reveal the governance boundary.

anchor: 112.16 — Experiment 7 ... Any component can transition Candidate→Authoritative. Expected: potential semantic/governance defect. Result: OBS/VIOLATION depending on the actual intended rule.
statement: Experiment 7: any component being able to directly transition Candidate to Authoritative is a potential semantic/governance defect, classified OBS/VIOLATION depending on intended rule.

anchor: 112.17 — Identity ... DecisionID must remain stable even if wording changes, representation changes, document location changes.
statement: States decision identity (DecisionID) must remain stable across wording/representation/location changes.

anchor: 112.18 — Experiment 8 ... Decision is identified only by filename ADR-042.md. File is renamed. Expected: if the system treats the filename as identity, semantic identity is fragile. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 8: filename-based decision identity is fragile if the filename can be renamed; classified OBS.

anchor: 112.19 — Provenance ... KnowledgeObject→Provenance. Possible provenance: document, repository, commit, runtime event, human, agent, external system.
statement: Defines KnowledgeObject->Provenance with seven possible provenance types (document/repository/commit/runtime event/human/agent/external system).

anchor: 112.20 — Experiment 9 ... A claim exists with no source or provenance. Expected: potential weak knowledge object. Result: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 9: a claim with no source or provenance is a potential weak knowledge object; result PARTIAL.

anchor: 112.21 — Authority ... We distinguish True from Authoritative. A statement can be believed to be true without being the organization's official decision.
statement: Distinguishes True from Authoritative: belief in truth is distinct from official organizational decision status.

anchor: 112.22 — Experiment 10 ... AI generates 'The architecture should use Kafka.' Expected: Recommendation, not ArchitectureDecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: an AI-generated architecture suggestion is a Recommendation, not an ArchitectureDecision; result PASS.

anchor: 112.23 — Authority transition ... Suggestion→Review→Decision→AuthoritativeState. This is more precise than treating all generated content as knowledge.
statement: Defines the four-stage authority-transition model Suggestion→Review→Decision→AuthoritativeState.

anchor: 112.24 — Temporal semantics ... Knowledge(t). We need to distinguish Current from Historical and Superseded.
statement: Defines temporal semantics Knowledge(t), distinguishing Current, Historical, and Superseded states.

anchor: 112.25 — Experiment 11 ... Architecture rule v1.0 was valid in 2025. v1.2 replaced it in 2026. Expected: both remain historically meaningful. Only v1.2 is current. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: superseded architecture rule v1.0 remains historically meaningful alongside current v1.2; result PASS.

anchor: 112.26 — Semantic versioning ... Version should not be confused with SourceCodeVersion. Knowledge may evolve independently of software releases.
statement: States Knowledge-version≠SourceCodeVersion: knowledge can evolve independently of software releases.

anchor: 112.27 — Experiment 12 ... Architecture decision changes without application deployment. Expected: knowledge version changes while software version remains unchanged. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 12: an architecture-decision change without any deployment shows knowledge version changing independently of software version; result PASS.

anchor: 112.28 — Conflict semantics ... Claim_A and Claim_B where Claim_A≠Claim_B. The answer should not automatically be 'the newest claim wins.'
statement: Warns against automatically resolving conflicting claims (Claim_A≠Claim_B) via newest-wins.

anchor: 112.29 — Experiment 13 ... Two architecture documents disagree. Expected: KnowledgeOS records Conflict and identifies sources, dates, authorities, scope. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: two disagreeing architecture documents should be recorded as Conflict with sources/dates/authorities/scope; result PASS.

anchor: 112.30 — Conflict is knowledge ... Conflict→Finding→Resolution. Silently overwriting one side destroys organizational history.
statement: States conflict itself is useful knowledge (Conflict->Finding->Resolution), warning that silently overwriting one side destroys organizational history.

anchor: 112.31 — Semantic relationship types ... supports, contradicts, supersedes, derivedFrom, implements, verifies, authorizes, violates. These relationships are more important than simple foreign keys.
statement: Defines an eight-verb semantic relationship vocabulary (supports/contradicts/supersedes/derivedFrom/implements/verifies/authorizes/violates), stated as more important than plain foreign keys.

anchor: 112.32 — Experiment 14 ... Record A points to Record B. No semantic relationship type exists. Expected: weak knowledge graph. Result: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 14: an untyped pointer between records produces a weak knowledge graph; result PARTIAL.

anchor: 112.33 — The semantic graph ... G_K=(V_K,E_K) where V_K=KnowledgeObjects and E_K=SemanticRelationships.
statement: Defines the semantic graph G_K=(V_K,E_K) with V_K=KnowledgeObjects, E_K=SemanticRelationships.

anchor: 112.34 — Example ... Architecture Rule -implementedBy-> Component -verifiedBy-> Test -produces-> Evidence -observedAt-> Runtime. This is fundamentally different from a document repository.
statement: Presents a worked semantic-graph chain Architecture Rule->Component->Test->Evidence->Runtime, explicitly distinguished from a document repository.

anchor: 112.35 — Semantic ownership and DDD ... The strongest bounded-context candidate is the area where Meaning+Rules+Lifecycle+Ownership form a coherent cluster.
statement: States the strongest bounded-context candidate is where Meaning+Rules+Lifecycle+Ownership form a coherent cluster.

anchor: 112.36 — Experiment 15 ... Evidence-related concepts include Evidence, Source, Observation, Verification. If they share identity, lifecycle, invariants, language, then EvidenceContextCandidate. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: Evidence/Source/Observation/Verification sharing identity/lifecycle/invariants/language form an EvidenceContextCandidate; result PASS.

anchor: 112.37 — Context boundary through translation ... Governance refers to Finding. Runtime refers to Alert. A translation relationship may be RuntimeAlert→GovernanceFinding. That is healthier than pretending Alert=Finding.
statement: States context-boundary-through-translation: modeling RuntimeAlert->GovernanceFinding as an explicit mapping is healthier than pretending Alert=Finding.

anchor: 112.38 — Experiment 16 ... Runtime alert automatically becomes governance finding. Expected: only valid if semantic mapping rules are explicit. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: automatic runtime-alert-to-governance-finding conversion is only valid with explicit semantic mapping rules; result PASS.

anchor: 112.39 — Anti-corruption layer ... Where external concepts differ, an explicit translation mechanism is useful. ExternalModel→Translation→KnowledgeOSModel. This protects the internal semantic model.
statement: Defines the anti-corruption layer pattern ExternalModel->Translation->KnowledgeOSModel, protecting the internal semantic model from external concept differences.

anchor: 112.40 — Experiment 17 ... Jira's Issue is mapped to KnowledgeOS ChangeRequest. Expected: JiraIssue≠ChangeRequest. Instead Mapping(JiraIssue,ChangeRequest). Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: Jira's Issue and KnowledgeOS's ChangeRequest are related by an explicit Mapping, not identity (JiraIssue≠ChangeRequest); result PASS.

anchor: 112.41 — Semantic ownership matrix ... Concept x Meaning/Invariants/Data owner/Semantic owner/External source for Evidence, Observation, Claim, Decision, Rule, Finding, Verification, Agent Action -- all cells '?'. The question marks must be populated from actual evidence.
statement: Presents a semantic ownership matrix template across eight concepts and five attributes, all cells deliberately '?' pending actual evidence.

anchor: 112.42 — Semantic orphan ... Meaning exists but Owner=Unknown. 'Knowledge item' is used throughout the system, but nobody can explain what it means, what its lifecycle is, who owns it.
statement: Defines the semantic orphan pattern (Meaning present, Owner=Unknown), illustrated by 'Knowledge item' with no explainable meaning/lifecycle/owner.

anchor: 112.43 — Experiment 18 ... KnowledgeItem appears in five modules. No invariant or owner can be identified. Expected: SemanticOrphan. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 18: KnowledgeItem appearing in five modules with no identifiable invariant or owner is classified SemanticOrphan, OBS.

anchor: 112.44 — Semantic duplicate ... Concept_A and Concept_B have identical meaning and lifecycle. Expected: SemanticDuplicationCandidate.
statement: Defines the semantic duplicate pattern: two concepts with identical meaning and lifecycle are a SemanticDuplicationCandidate.

anchor: 112.45 — Experiment 19 ... KnowledgeRecord and KnowledgeItem have identical fields, identical lifecycle, identical API behavior. Expected: potential duplicate concepts. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 19: KnowledgeRecord and KnowledgeItem sharing identical fields/lifecycle/API behavior is a potential duplicate concept, classified OBS.

anchor: 112.46 — Semantic fragmentation ... The most serious pattern may be OneConcept→ManyOwners. Decision→ServiceA, Decision→ServiceB, Decision→AgentMemory. This creates ambiguity about truth.
statement: Defines semantic fragmentation (OneConcept->ManyOwners) as potentially the most serious pattern, illustrated by Decision owned independently by ServiceA/ServiceB/AgentMemory, creating ambiguity about truth.

anchor: 112.47 — Experiment 20 ... Three independent representations claim to be the current architecture decision. Expected: SemanticFragmentation. Result: DRIFT
statement: Experiment 20: three independent representations each claiming to be the current architecture decision is SemanticFragmentation, classified DRIFT.

anchor: 112.48 — One source of authority ... The solution is not necessarily one database. The requirement is one authoritative semantic owner. Physical projections may exist elsewhere.
statement: States semantic fragmentation is resolved not necessarily by physical database consolidation but by the requirement of exactly one authoritative semantic owner, with legitimate physical projections elsewhere.

anchor: 112.49 — Projection architecture ... Authoritative Decision → API View, Search Index, Agent Context. The projections are not competing authorities.
statement: Presents the projection architecture (one Authoritative Decision projected into API View/Search Index/Agent Context), none of which are competing authorities.

anchor: 112.50 — Experiment 21 ... Agent context contains a cached architecture decision. Expected: cache is valid only if Source→Version→Freshness can be established. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: a cached architecture decision in agent context is valid only if Source->Version->Freshness can be established; result PASS.

anchor: 112.51 — Semantic consistency ... Projection≈AuthoritativeModel. We need mechanisms to detect stale projections.
statement: States Projection≈AuthoritativeModel requires mechanisms to detect stale projections.

anchor: 112.52 — Experiment 22 ... KnowledgeOS changes decision version from 4 to 5. Agent cache still contains version 4. Expected: ProjectionStale. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: an agent cache retaining version 4 after the authoritative decision moves to version 5 is ProjectionStale; result PASS.

anchor: 112.53 — This connects back to agents ... The earlier pointer-layer principle now becomes semantic: Agent→AuthoritativeKnowledge. Agent memory may be Projection but not Authority.
statement: Reconnects the pointer-layer principle to semantics: Agent->AuthoritativeKnowledge, with agent memory as Projection but never Authority.

anchor: 112.54 — Semantic ownership and governance ... Authority itself must have an owner. Rule→Authority→AuthorityHolder.
statement: Extends ownership analysis to governance authority itself, requiring Rule->Authority->AuthorityHolder.

anchor: 112.55 — Experiment 23 ... Rule exists. No organization/person/body can be identified as its authority. Expected: GovernanceGap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: a rule with no identifiable authority holder is a GovernanceGap; result PASS.

anchor: 112.56 — Semantic lifecycle ... Claim: Proposed→Supported→Accepted→Superseded. Decision: Draft→Approved→Effective→Superseded. Finding: Open→Investigating→Remediating→Verified→Closed. These should not be conflated.
statement: Defines distinct per-concept semantic lifecycles for Claim, Decision, and Finding, stating they should not be conflated.

anchor: 112.57 — Experiment 24 ... All knowledge objects use status=ACTIVE|INACTIVE. Expected: potential semantic weakness because different concepts have different lifecycles. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 24: a uniform ACTIVE|INACTIVE status across all knowledge objects is a potential semantic weakness given differing per-concept lifecycles; result OBS.

anchor: 112.58 — Semantic state machines ... StateMachine(Concept). A mature KnowledgeOS should understand that DecisionStatus is not FindingStatus.
statement: States a mature KnowledgeOS must treat StateMachine(Concept) as concept-specific, e.g. DecisionStatus is not FindingStatus.

anchor: 112.59 — Semantic invariants ... InvariantSet(C). ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists. VerifiedEvidence⇒VerificationEventExists. SupersededRule⇒ReplacementExists where required by policy.
statement: Defines per-concept InvariantSet(C) with three example invariants: ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists, VerifiedEvidence⇒VerificationEventExists, SupersededRule⇒ReplacementExists.

anchor: 112.60 — Experiment 25 ... Database permits VerifiedEvidence without VerificationEvent. Expected: potential invariant enforcement gap. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: a database permitting VerifiedEvidence without a corresponding VerificationEvent is a potential invariant enforcement gap; result PASS.

anchor: 112.61 — Where invariants live ... domain code, application service, database constraint, policy engine, workflow, CI, runtime, human process.
statement: Requires identifying where each semantic invariant is actually enforced, across eight possible enforcement layers.

anchor: 112.62 — Experiment 26 ... Invariant exists only in a README. Expected: DocumentedRule. Not EnforcedInvariant. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: a README-only invariant is DocumentedRule, not EnforcedInvariant; result PASS.

anchor: 112.63 — Semantic assurance ... SemanticTruth→Invariant→Enforcement→Evidence. This is how semantic architecture becomes executable.
statement: Defines the executable-semantic-architecture chain SemanticTruth->Invariant->Enforcement->Evidence.

anchor: 112.64 — KnowledgeOS semantic core ... the smallest coherent set of concepts and invariants that defines what 'knowledge' means in the system. Potentially Evidence+Claim+Decision+Authority+Provenance+TemporalValidity but this is a hypothesis until the implementation confirms it.
statement: Defines the KnowledgeOS Semantic Core as the smallest coherent concept-and-invariant set defining 'knowledge,' hypothesized as Evidence+Claim+Decision+Authority+Provenance+TemporalValidity pending implementation confirmation.

anchor: 112.65 — Experiment 27 ... We remove the search/indexing subsystem. Knowledge semantics still exist. Expected: search is supporting infrastructure, not necessarily the semantic core. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: removing the search/indexing subsystem leaves knowledge semantics intact, indicating it is supporting infrastructure, not the semantic core; result PASS.

anchor: 112.66 — Experiment 28 ... We remove the semantic identity/provenance model. All knowledge becomes untraceable. Expected: potential destruction of the semantic core. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: removing the semantic identity/provenance model makes all knowledge untraceable, a potential destruction of the semantic core; result PASS.

anchor: 112.67 — Semantic core test ... If this component disappeared, would KnowledgeOS lose the meaning of its knowledge, or merely a technical capability? If meaning: CoreCandidate. If technical capability: SupportingCandidate.
statement: Defines the reusable semantic-core test: component-removal impact on meaning (CoreCandidate) versus mere technical capability (SupportingCandidate).

anchor: 112.68 — Step 112 verdict: STEP 112 — SEMANTIC OWNERSHIP MODEL: PASS. The semantic ownership model is Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→Context, giving the method to determine whether actual KnowledgeOS components form coherent semantic boundaries. The actual ownership map remains TBD until the repositor
statement: Records Step 112 verdict PASS for the semantic-ownership-model methodology, with the honest actual-ownership-map verdict TBD pending repository evidence mapping.

anchor: 112.69 — The next step: Step 113 — KnowledgeOS Semantic Core Reconstruction. What is the irreducible semantic core of KnowledgeOS? Evidence→Claim→Decision→Authority→Action→Observation with Provenance and TemporalValidity cross-cutting. The critical test will be whether these are real domain concepts
statement: Previews Step 113: testing whether Evidence->Claim->Decision->Authority->Action->Observation (with cross-cutting Provenance and TemporalValidity) are real, software-enforced domain concepts or merely projected concepts, determining whether KnowledgeOS is a genuine Knowledge Operating System or an AI engineering platform with knowledge-oriented tooling.

anchor: We now reach the central architectural question. What is the irreducible semantic core of KnowledgeOS? A platform can contain many 'knowledge' features without actually having a coherent knowledge model.
statement: States the central question: what is the irreducible semantic core of KnowledgeOS, distinguishing many 'knowledge' features from a genuinely coherent knowledge model.

anchor: 113.1 — The semantic-core hypothesis ... Evidence→Claim→Decision→Authority→Action→Observation with Provenance and TemporalValidity cross-cutting the graph. But this is still a hypothesis. Step 113 must determine whether the implementation actually supports it.
statement: Restates the semantic-core hypothesis Evidence->Claim->Decision->Authority->Action->Observation with cross-cutting Provenance/TemporalValidity, explicitly still a hypothesis pending implementation confirmation.

anchor: 113.2 — The falsification principle ... Does it exist? stable identity? defined meaning? lifecycle/state? invariants? relationships? identifiable ownership? persisted/represented? implemented behavior? verified? If most answers are 'no', the concept should not be treated as part of the actual semant
statement: Defines a ten-question falsification principle for admitting a candidate concept into the actual semantic core, rejecting concepts that fail most questions.

anchor: 113.3 — Candidate 1: Evidence ... Evidence=(Identity,Source,Content/Observation,Timestamp,Provenance,Context) possibly with VerificationStatus.
statement: Defines the minimal Evidence tuple (Identity,Source,Content/Observation,Timestamp,Provenance,Context[,VerificationStatus]).

anchor: 113.4 — Experiment 1 ... We find a file architecture.md. Can we call the file itself Evidence? Not automatically. It is an artifact. It becomes evidence when the system establishes its evidentiary role. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 1: a file is an artifact, not automatically Evidence, becoming evidence only once the system establishes its evidentiary role; result PASS.

anchor: 113.5 — Artifact versus evidence ... Artifact→Evidence is a semantic transformation. Git commit→Observed change→Evidence. The same artifact may provide different evidence depending on context.
statement: States Artifact->Evidence is a semantic transformation, not identity, illustrated by Git commit->Observed change->Evidence.

anchor: 113.6 — Experiment 2 ... A Git commit contains 'Changed authorization logic.' A verification process interprets it as evidence. Expected: Artifact≠Evidence but Artifact→Evidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: a Git commit message interpreted by a verification process confirms Artifact≠Evidence but Artifact->Evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 113.7 — Evidence ownership ... Does KnowledgeOS own evidence semantics, or merely collect evidence? Model A: EvidenceAuthority. Model B: EvidenceAggregator. Model C: EvidenceProcessingPlatform. The implementation must tell us which one is real.
statement: Presents three competing evidence-ownership architectures (EvidenceAuthority/EvidenceAggregator/EvidenceProcessingPlatform) to be resolved by implementation evidence.
