statement: Experiment 25: an agent's unevidenced relationship claim must remain an inference, not become a fact; result PASS.

anchor: 115.54 — Explicit inference ... Inference-basedOn->Evidence. This allows AI-generated conclusions to remain distinguishable from authoritative facts.
statement: Defines Inference-basedOn->Evidence, keeping AI-generated conclusions distinguishable from authoritative facts.

anchor: 115.55 — Three graph layers ... Layer 1 Fact graph=ObservedReality. Layer 2 Knowledge graph=Interpreted/validated knowledge. Layer 3 Reasoning graph=AI/Human inferences. These must not be silently merged.
statement: Defines a three-layer graph model (Fact/Knowledge/Reasoning) that must not be silently merged.

anchor: 115.56 — Experiment 26 ... Agent infers ComponentA→ArchitectureRuleB. No explicit architecture relationship exists. Expected: store as Inference. Not Fact. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 26: an agent's unevidenced component-to-rule inference must be stored as Inference, not Fact; result PASS.

anchor: 115.57 — Graph authority ... Inference≠Authority. An agent may discover a likely relationship. Only an authorized process should make it authoritative where governance requires that.
statement: States the Inference≠Authority invariant: only an authorized process may make an agent-discovered relationship authoritative where governance requires it.

invariants.name: I_InferenceNeqAuthority
invariants.statement: An agent-discovered relationship (Inference) becomes authoritative only through an authorized process, never automatically.

anchor: 115.58 — Graph mutation ... ReadGraph, ProposeGraphChange, AuthorizeGraphChange. This becomes another governance boundary.
statement: Distinguishes ReadGraph, ProposeGraphChange, and AuthorizeGraphChange as a governance boundary.

anchor: 115.59 — Experiment 27 ... Agent discovers a new architecture relationship. Expected: agent can propose CandidateEdge. It should not silently create AuthoritativeEdge. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: an agent discovering a new relationship may propose a CandidateEdge but must not silently create an AuthoritativeEdge; result PASS.

anchor: 115.60 — Graph evolution ... G_t→G_{t+1}. Changes need provenance. GraphChange→Actor+Reason+Evidence+Authority.
statement: Defines graph evolution G_t->G_{t+1} requiring GraphChange->Actor+Reason+Evidence+Authority provenance.

anchor: 115.61 — Experiment 28 ... An edge is deleted. No record explains why. Expected: potential knowledge-integrity problem. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: an unexplained edge deletion is a potential knowledge-integrity problem; result PASS.

anchor: 115.62 — The complete trace ... Authority-authorizes->Decision-basedOn->Claim-supportedBy->Evidence, with Observation-produces->Action-authorizedBy->Decision. This produces a closed assurance loop.
statement: Presents the complete strongest target path forming a closed assurance loop.

anchor: 115.63 — Closed-loop KnowledgeOS ... Knowledge→Decision→Action→Observation→Evidence→UpdatedKnowledge. This is the strongest formulation yet of the Operating System metaphor.
statement: States the closed-loop KnowledgeOS cycle Knowledge->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence->UpdatedKnowledge, the strongest formulation yet of the Operating System metaphor.

anchor: 115.64 — But again: target versus actual ... Case A ActualGraph≈TargetGraph. Case B ActualGraph⊂TargetGraph. Case C ActualGraph≈DerivedFromArtifacts. Case D ActualGraph=G_1∪G_2∪G_3. The last case would indicate fragmentation.
statement: Defines four possible target-vs-actual outcome cases (explicit/partial/mostly-implicit/fragmented-coexisting-models), the last indicating fragmentation.

anchor: 115.65 — Graph fragmentation test ... Evidence_1 in subsystem A, Evidence_2 in subsystem B. If there is no common identity or translation: Evidence_1≢Evidence_2. This is semantic fragmentation.
statement: Defines the graph fragmentation test: no common identity or translation between subsystem-local instances yields Evidence_1≢Evidence_2, semantic fragmentation.

anchor: 115.66 — Experiment 29 ... Claude memory contains architecture evidence. KnowledgeOS contains separate architecture evidence. Neither references the other. Expected: KnowledgeDuplication. Result: DRIFT CANDIDATE. This directly tests the pointer-layer architecture from earlier steps.
statement: Experiment 29: Claude memory and KnowledgeOS each holding separate unreferenced architecture evidence is KnowledgeDuplication, classified DRIFT CANDIDATE, directly testing the pointer-layer architecture.

anchor: 115.67 — Graph identity ... semantic objects need stable identity. KnowledgeObjectID. Projection_1→ObjectID. Projection_2→ObjectID.
statement: Defines stable KnowledgeObjectID-based identity to prevent semantic fragmentation, with multiple Projections referencing one ObjectID.

anchor: 115.68 — Experiment 30 ... Same decision appears in three systems. All three have different IDs. No cross-reference exists. Expected: potential identity fragmentation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: the same decision under three uncross-referenced IDs across three systems is potential identity fragmentation; result PASS.

anchor: 115.69 — Step 115 verdict ... G_actual=(V,E) with V=Evidence,Observation,Claim,Decision,Authority,Action,Finding,Rule,Verification,... and semantic edges supports,authorizes,produces,verifies,implements,supersedes,contradicts,derivedFrom. The critical end-to-end path is Authority→Decision→Action→Obs
statement: Records the complete semantic graph model (node/edge vocabulary) and the critical end-to-end path Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence->Knowledge.

anchor: 115.70 — Final status ... STEP 115 — SEMANTIC GRAPH MODEL: PASS. But the actual graph has not yet been proven. We have now reached the point where continuing to invent conceptual entities would provide diminishing value. The next phase must become evidence execution.
statement: Records Step 115 verdict PASS for the semantic graph model, explicitly noting the actual graph has not yet been proven and further conceptual elaboration would have diminishing value.

anchor: Step 116 — Actual KnowledgeOS Graph Extraction preview ... take the actual repository/system artifacts and construct G_actual from evidence. Compare G_actual against G_target. The decisive output will be a semantic gap matrix: TargetEdge→ActualEdge→Evidence→Gap. That is the point where we can stop a
statement: Previews Step 116: constructing G_actual from repository/system artifacts, comparing against G_target to produce the semantic gap matrix TargetEdge->ActualEdge->Evidence->Gap, shifting from could-be to how-much-already-exists.

anchor: Step 117 established the forward trace Intent→Decision→Authority→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Evidence→Knowledge. Now we test the reverse direction. When reality deviates from what was intended, can KnowledgeOS turn that deviation into governed engineering action and eventually verified knowl
statement: Frames Step 118 as testing the reverse of Step 117's forward trace, defining the target reverse loop Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification.

anchor: 118.1 — Why the reverse direction matters ... A system that only records what happened is essentially an audit system. A system that can detect Expected≠Actual and initiate a governed response has Feedback. Audit≠Control. Traceability≠ClosedLoopGovernance.
statement: States Audit≠Control and Traceability≠ClosedLoopGovernance: recording history is distinct from detecting deviation and initiating governed feedback.

anchor: 118.2 — The expected-state model ... S_expected and S_observed. Delta=S_observed-S_expected. If Delta=0 we have conformance. If Delta≠0 we have a candidate discrepancy.
statement: Defines the expected-state model S_expected/S_observed with Delta=S_observed-S_expected, Delta=0 conformant, Delta≠0 a candidate discrepancy.

anchor: 118.3 — Experiment 1 ... Architecture says Nexus must run using the approved containerized architecture. Runtime observation matches. Then S_expected=S_observed. Result: CONFORMANT
statement: Experiment 1: matching architecture-specified and observed container deployment yields S_expected=S_observed, classified CONFORMANT, no escalation required.

anchor: 118.4 — Experiment 2 ... Architecture says approved container deployment. Runtime shows legacy VM deployment still active. Then S_expected≠S_observed. Result: DISCREPANCY. This is the starting point of the reverse loop.
statement: Experiment 2: a legacy VM still active against an approved-container architecture is S_expected≠S_observed, classified DISCREPANCY, the starting point of the reverse loop.

anchor: 118.5 — Observation is not yet a finding ... Observation: LegacyDeploymentActive. We do not yet automatically have Finding: ArchitectureViolation. A rule must interpret the observation.
statement: States Observation≠Finding: an observation requires rule interpretation before becoming a finding.

anchor: 118.6 — Rule evaluation ... Rule+Observation→Evaluation. Rule: LegacyDeploymentForbidden. Observation: LegacyDeploymentActive. Then Evaluation=Violation.
statement: Defines Rule+Observation->Evaluation, illustrated by LegacyDeploymentForbidden+LegacyDeploymentActive->Violation.

anchor: 118.7 — Experiment 3 ... Monitoring detects a VM that is not described in the current architecture. Expected: Observation. Only if a relevant architecture rule applies do we create Finding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: an undescribed VM is merely an Observation until a relevant rule applies to create a Finding; result PASS.

anchor: 118.8 — Finding creation ... Finding=(Rule,Expected,Observed,Evidence,Impact,Scope,Timestamp). This allows the finding to be independently understood.
statement: Defines the Finding=(Rule,Expected,Observed,Evidence,Impact,Scope,Timestamp) tuple for independently understandable findings.

type_signature.codomain: Rule x Expected x Observed x Evidence x Impact x Scope x Timestamp

anchor: 118.9 — Experiment 4 ... Finding says only 'Architecture violation detected.' No rule or observation is attached. Expected: weak finding semantics. Result: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 4: a finding with no attached rule/observation has weak finding semantics; result PARTIAL.

anchor: 118.10 — Strong finding ... Rule: R-17, Expected: rootless container deployment, Observed: privileged VM process, Evidence: runtime observation O-41, Detected: 2026-08-28. Now Finding→Evidence is explicit.
statement: Presents a strong worked finding record with explicit Rule/Expected/Observed/Evidence/Detected fields, making Finding->Evidence explicit.

anchor: 118.11 — Finding ownership ... Who owns the response? Team, DomainArchitect, Security, Operations, ArchitectureBoard.
statement: Frames finding ownership as a governance question with five candidate owner categories.

anchor: 118.12 — Experiment 5 ... Finding exists. No responsible owner exists. Expected: GovernanceGap. Result: PASS. A detection system without accountable ownership cannot reliably close the loop.
statement: Experiment 5: an unowned finding is a GovernanceGap, since accountable ownership is required to reliably close the loop; result PASS.

anchor: 118.13 — Finding severity ... Severity from Priority. Severity=High describes impact. Priority=High describes response urgency. These should not be silently conflated.
statement: Distinguishes Severity (impact) from Priority (response urgency), stating they must not be conflated.

anchor: 118.14 — Experiment 6 ... A low-impact architecture deviation blocks a production deployment. Expected: potential Severity=Low but Priority=High. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: a low-impact but deployment-blocking deviation is potential Severity=Low/Priority=High; result PASS.

anchor: 118.15 — Finding → Governance ... Finding→GovernanceProcess. change management, architecture review, exception process, remediation workflow, incident process. The system must determine which path applies.
statement: Defines Finding->GovernanceProcess routing across five possible governance processes.

anchor: 118.16 — Experiment 7 ... Security finding occurs. It is routed into an architecture review process. Expected: potential governance mismatch if security policy requires a different path. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 7: a security finding routed to architecture review instead of a required security path is a potential governance mismatch, classified OBS.

anchor: 118.17 — Governance classification ... Finding→Classification→GovernancePath. ArchitectureDeviation→ArchitectureGovernance. SecurityViolation→SecurityGovernance. OperationalFailure→Operations.
statement: Defines Finding->Classification->GovernancePath with three example classification-to-path mappings.

anchor: 118.18 — Experiment 8 ... A finding can be classified automatically based on rule metadata. Expected: Classification→GovernancePath. Result: PASS provided the classification is deterministic and auditable.
statement: Experiment 8: automatic finding classification is acceptable (PASS) only if deterministic and auditable.

anchor: 118.19 — Governance escalation ... Not every finding needs board-level intervention. FindingSeverity+FindingType+Scope→EscalationLevel.
statement: Defines EscalationLevel as a function of FindingSeverity+FindingType+Scope.

anchor: 118.20 — Experiment 9 ... Minor documentation drift is detected. Expected: it should not automatically require Architecture Board approval. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: minor documentation drift should not automatically escalate to board-level approval; result PASS.

anchor: 118.21 — Exception handling ... Sometimes the observed state is intentionally different. Deviation may be Violation or ApprovedException. This distinction is essential.
statement: States the essential Violation-vs-ApprovedException distinction for deliberately different observed states.

anchor: 118.22 — Experiment 10 ... Architecture rule says Technology X is prohibited. Security exception formally permits Technology X until 2026-12-31. Runtime uses Technology X. Expected: not necessarily a violation, ExceptionValid=True. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: a formally time-boxed security exception permitting an otherwise-prohibited technology is ExceptionValid=True, not a violation; result PASS.

anchor: 118.23 — Exception authority ... An exception itself requires Authority. Exception→Authority. Exception→ValidityPeriod.
statement: States exceptions require Exception->Authority and Exception->ValidityPeriod.

anchor: 118.24 — Experiment 11 ... Exception exists but no expiration date exists. Expected: potential uncontrolled exception. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 11: an exception with no expiration date is a potential uncontrolled exception, classified OBS.

anchor: 118.25 — Exception expiration ... At t>ValidUntil the exception becomes inactive. Then Observation+Rule→Violation.
statement: Defines exception expiration semantics: past ValidUntil, Observation+Rule->Violation is regenerated.

anchor: 118.26 — Experiment 12 ... Exception expires. Runtime still uses the prohibited technology. Expected: new finding should be generated. Result: PASS. This demonstrates why temporal validity is part of the semantic core.
statement: Experiment 12: an expired exception with continued prohibited-technology use should generate a new finding, demonstrating temporal validity's role in the semantic core; result PASS.

anchor: 118.27 — Finding → Decision ... Finding→Decision. remediate, accept risk, grant exception, redesign, decommission.
statement: Lists five possible Finding->Decision resolutions: remediate, accept risk, grant exception, redesign, decommission.

anchor: 118.28 — Experiment 13 ... Architecture deviation is confirmed. Architecture authority decides: Remediate within 30 days. Expected: Finding→Decision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a confirmed deviation resolved by an authorized remediation decision demonstrates Finding->Decision; result PASS.

anchor: 118.29 — Decision type ... The resulting decision must retain its semantic type. RemediationDecision is not the same as ArchitectureDecision. Even though both are decisions.
statement: States RemediationDecision≠ArchitectureDecision, both decisions but semantically distinct types.

anchor: 118.30 — Experiment 14 ... A system stores all decisions as generic text. Expected: semantic precision is weak. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 14: storing all decisions as generic text loses semantic-type precision, classified OBS.

anchor: 118.31 — Decision → Remediation ... Decision→RemediationAction. The remediation must be traceable back to the decision.
statement: States Decision->RemediationAction must be traceable back to the originating decision.

anchor: 118.32 — Experiment 15 ... Approved remediation says replace VM deployment. Engineering creates a pull request replacing the deployment configuration. Expected: Decision→Implementation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: an approved remediation traced to a matching implementation pull request demonstrates Decision->Implementation; result PASS.

anchor: 118.33 — Remediation authorization ... The agent or engineer must operate within the decision's scope. For AI: DelegatedAuthority. For humans: Role/Authority.
statement: States remediation execution must operate within the authorizing decision's scope, via DelegatedAuthority for AI or Role/Authority for humans.

anchor: 118.34 — Experiment 16 ... Decision authorizes configuration change. Agent changes database schema. Expected: potential scope violation. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 16: an agent executing a database-schema change under a configuration-change decision is a potential scope violation, classified OBS.

anchor: 118.35 — Verification after remediation ... Remediation→Verification. The verification should test the original violated condition.
statement: States Remediation->Verification must test the originally violated condition, not merely the remediation action's surface completion.

anchor: 118.36 — Experiment 17 ... Finding: forbidden VM deployment exists. Remediation: deploy container. Verification: container starts. Does this prove remediation? Not necessarily. We need Rule→Verification. The test must establish that the VM is no longer the active deployment. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: a container merely 'starting' does not prove a forbidden VM deployment has actually been remediated; verification must specifically target the rule (VM no longer active), not just the remediation action; result PASS.

anchor: 118.37 — Finding closure ... A finding should only become Closed when closure criteria are satisfied. Closed⇒RemediationVerified.
statement: States Closed⇒RemediationVerified as the closure invariant for findings.

invariants.name: I_ClosedRequiresVerified
invariants.statement: A finding may be marked Closed only when Closed⇒RemediationVerified holds.

anchor: 118.38 — Experiment 18 ... Finding is marked closed after a developer comments 'Fixed.' No verification evidence exists. Expected: potential invalid closure. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: closure based on an unverified developer 'Fixed' comment is a potential invalid closure; result PASS.

anchor: 118.39 — Re-observation ... After remediation: Runtime→Observation_2. We need to compare Observation_2 against the original violation.
statement: States post-remediation re-observation (Observation_2) must be compared against the original violation.

anchor: 118.40 — Experiment 19 ... Original: VMActive=True. After remediation: VMActive=False. Expected: strong remediation evidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: VMActive shifting from True to False post-remediation is strong remediation evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 118.41 — Knowledge update ... Once verified: Finding→ResolvedKnowledge. The organization now knows the previous architecture deviation has been remediated. This should not merely disappear from the system.
statement: States a verified finding produces Finding->ResolvedKnowledge, a persisted organizational fact, not merely disappearing from the system.

anchor: 118.42 — Historical preservation ... The system should retain Finding_original and Resolution. History≠CurrentState.
statement: States History≠CurrentState: both the original finding and its resolution must be retained.

anchor: 118.43 — Experiment 20 ... Finding is deleted after closure. Expected: historical traceability is lost. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 20: deleting a finding after closure loses historical traceability, classified OBS.

anchor: 118.44 — Closure loop ... Runtime→Observation→Finding→Governance→Decision→Remediation→Verification→Knowledge. This is the reverse counterpart to Step 117.
statement: Presents the full closure loop as the reverse counterpart to Step 117's forward trace.

anchor: 118.45 — Full bidirectional loop ... INTENT→DECISION→ACTION→RUNTIME→OBSERVATION→FINDING→GOVERNANCE→[back to]DECISION. And evidence/provenance surround the loop.
statement: Combines Step 117 and 118 into a full bidirectional loop diagram from Intent through Governance back to Decision, surrounded by evidence/provenance.

anchor: 118.46 — This is stronger than a knowledge graph ... A conventional knowledge graph may represent A→B. KnowledgeOS requires more: A→B→Action→Observation→Evidence. The graph participates in an operational control cycle.
statement: States KnowledgeOS requires more than a conventional knowledge graph's static A->B relation, requiring participation in an operational control cycle.

anchor: 118.47 — Control-loop interpretation ... ReferenceState versus ObservedState. The difference produces Error. Then Error→CorrectiveAction. KnowledgeOS≈SemanticControlLoop for engineering knowledge and governance.
statement: Introduces the control-loop interpretation KnowledgeOS≈SemanticControlLoop (ReferenceState vs ObservedState producing Error->CorrectiveAction).

anchor: 118.48 — But not autonomous control by default ... This does not imply that KnowledgeOS should automatically modify production systems. The control loop can stop at Recommendation or GovernanceDecision. Automation depth must be governed.
statement: States the control loop does not imply autonomous production modification by default; it may stop at Recommendation or GovernanceDecision, with automation depth governed.

anchor: 118.49 — Automation levels ... L0 Detect: Observation→Finding. L1 Recommend: Finding→Recommendation. L2 Decide: Finding→Decision. L3 Execute: Decision→Action. L4 Closed-loop automation: Action→Observation→Verification with automated remediation. The appropriate level depends on risk.
statement: Defines a five-level automation-depth taxonomy L0 (Detect) through L4 (Closed-loop automation), risk-dependent.

anchor: 118.50 — Experiment 21 ... A low-risk formatting issue is automatically corrected. Expected: potential L4 automation. A production security-policy change should not necessarily receive the same autonomy. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: low-risk formatting auto-correction may reach L4, while production security-policy changes warrant lower autonomy; result PASS.

anchor: 118.51 — AI autonomy boundary ... AgentCapability⊆DelegatedAuthority. An agent should never gain authority simply because it has technical credentials.
statement: States AgentCapability⊆DelegatedAuthority: an agent must never gain authority merely from technical credentials.

invariants.name: I_AgentCapabilitySubsetDelegatedAuthority
invariants.statement: AgentCapability⊆DelegatedAuthority: an agent's technical capability must never exceed its delegated authority.

anchor: 118.52 — Experiment 22 ... Agent can technically execute production deployment. Governance policy allows only staging deployment. Expected: TechnicalCapability>DelegatedAuthority. This is a dangerous asymmetry. Result: GOVERNANCE GAP
statement: Experiment 22: an agent technically capable of production deployment despite staging-only policy is a dangerous TechnicalCapability>DelegatedAuthority asymmetry, classified GOVERNANCE GAP.

anchor: 118.53 — Deterministic enforcement ... Policy→MachineCheck→Allow/Deny. Not Policy→AgentInstruction alone.
statement: States deterministic enforcement Policy->MachineCheck->Allow/Deny is required, not Policy->AgentInstruction alone.

anchor: 118.54 — Experiment 23 ... Agent instructions say never deploy directly to production. But the credentials permit it and no enforcement exists. Expected: policy is advisory rather than deterministic. Result: WEAK ASSURANCE
statement: Experiment 23: an unenforced 'never deploy to production' instruction with permissive credentials is merely advisory, classified WEAK ASSURANCE.

anchor: 118.55 — Evidence accumulation ... E1=InitialObservation, E2=Finding, E3=Decision, E4=Remediation, E5=Verification, E6=PostRemediationObservation. EvidenceChain=(E1,...,E6).
statement: Defines the six-stage EvidenceChain=(E1..E6) for the closure loop.

anchor: 118.56 — Experiment 24 ... Only final state is stored. Expected: current state may be known, historical reasoning is weak. Result: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 24: storing only the final state leaves historical reasoning weak, classified PARTIAL.

anchor: 118.57 — Evidence lineage ... Strong KnowledgeOS semantics should preserve E6→E5→E4→E3→E2→E1. Then an agent can explain why is this finding now closed?
statement: States full evidence lineage E6->E5->E4->E3->E2->E1 should be preserved, enabling an agent to explain finding closure.

anchor: 118.58 — Experiment 25 ... Agent is asked why was this architecture violation closed? It can traverse Finding→Decision→Remediation→Verification. Expected: explainable closure. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: an agent traversing Finding->Decision->Remediation->Verification can explain closure; result PASS.

anchor: 118.59 — Reopening ... A finding that was closed may become relevant again. Remediated but later DeviationReappears. Then Closed→Reopened.
statement: Defines reopening semantics Closed->Reopened for findings whose deviation reappears.

anchor: 118.60 — Experiment 26 ... Runtime again violates the same architecture rule. Expected: a new observation should be distinguishable from the historical finding. Result: PASS. The system should not simply erase the old history.
statement: Experiment 26: a recurring violation's new observation must be distinguishable from the historical finding, preserving old history; result PASS.

anchor: 118.61 — Recurrence semantics ... Finding_1 and Finding_2 as separate occurrences, potentially related by recurrenceOf. This allows detection of systemic problems.
statement: Defines recurrenceOf linking separate Finding occurrences, enabling systemic-problem detection.

anchor: 118.62 — Experiment 27 ... Same violation occurs five times. Expected: KnowledgeOS can potentially derive RecurringProblem. This becomes higher-level organizational knowledge. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: five recurrences of the same violation can be derived as a RecurringProblem, higher-level organizational knowledge; result PASS.

anchor: 118.63 — From individual findings to organizational knowledge ... Findings→Pattern→Knowledge. 'Our deployment process repeatedly bypasses the architecture approval gate.' That is organizational knowledge derived from multiple observations.
statement: Defines Findings->Pattern->Knowledge, illustrated by a derived systemic-cause statement about repeated approval-gate bypass.

anchor: 118.64 — Experiment 28 ... Ten independent findings reveal the same underlying cause. Expected: potential systemic finding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: ten independent findings sharing an underlying cause reveal a potential systemic finding; result PASS.

anchor: 118.65 — Governance learning ... OperationalEvidence→GovernanceLearning. The organization can then modify policy, architecture, tooling, controls, agent behavior.
statement: Defines OperationalEvidence->GovernanceLearning enabling changes to policy/architecture/tooling/controls/agent behavior.

anchor: 118.66 — Experiment 29 ... Repeated manual exceptions occur. The organization changes the architecture rule. Expected: OperationalEvidence→GovernanceDecision→NewRule. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: repeated manual exceptions leading to a rule change demonstrates OperationalEvidence->GovernanceDecision->NewRule; result PASS.

anchor: 118.67 — The true closed loop ... Intent→Decision→Action→Reality→Observation→Finding→Governance→Decision' where Decision' may modify the previous understanding. This is an actual learning/control loop.
statement: Presents the true closed loop Intent->Decision->Action->Reality->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision', an actual learning/control loop where Decision' may revise prior understanding.

anchor: 118.68 — KnowledgeOS as organizational memory ... The loop means KnowledgeOS does not merely remember what we decided. It can remember what we decided, what happened, what went wrong, what we learned, and how the decision evolved.
statement: States the loop enables KnowledgeOS to remember not just decisions but outcomes, failures, learning, and decision evolution -- a substantially richer organizational-memory model.

anchor: 118.69 — Architecture implication ... the fundamental KnowledgeOS unit may ultimately not be Document. It may be TraceableKnowledgeEpisode where Episode=Intent+Decision+Action+Observation+Evidence+Learning. Again, this is a conceptual candidate, not yet an implementation claim.
statement: Proposes TraceableKnowledgeEpisode=Intent+Decision+Action+Observation+Evidence+Learning as a candidate replacement for Document as KnowledgeOS's fundamental unit, explicitly a conceptual candidate, not an implementation claim.

anchor: 118.70 — Step 118 verdict ... Runtime→Observation→Finding→Governance→Decision→Remediation→Verification→Knowledge. Combined with Step 117: Intent↔Decision↔Action↔Reality↔Evidence↔Knowledge. STEP 118 — GOVERNANCE-TO-ENGINEERING CLOSURE MODEL: PASS. The actual implementation still needs to be tested ag
statement: Records the Step 118 verdict PASS for the combined bidirectional forward/reverse loop model, with the actual implementation still needing to be tested against it.

anchor: Step 119 — KnowledgeOS Control-Loop Evidence Test preview ... Expected→Observed→Detected→Classified→Governed→Remediated→Verified→Recorded. When KnowledgeOS discovers that reality differs from authoritative knowledge, what actually happens next? observation capability vs assurance capability (Observa
statement: Previews Step 119: testing the eight-stage Expected->Observed->Detected->Classified->Governed->Remediated->Verified->Recorded loop against one real deviation, classifying the current implementation's capability tier from mere observation up to full closed-loop organizational engineering knowledge.

anchor: We now leave the abstract graph model and perform the first end-to-end architectural experiment. Can one real engineering change be reconstructed from organizational intent all the way to verified runtime reality and back into authoritative knowledge? Intent→Decision→Authority→Implementation→Verific
statement: Frames Step 117 as the first end-to-end architectural experiment: reconstructing one real change across the target chain Intent->Decision->Authority->Implementation->Verification->Runtime->Evidence->Knowledge.

anchor: 117.1 — Why one change is enough ... If we can trace one representative change completely, we establish that the architecture has the mechanisms necessary for a closed loop. Conversely, if the chain breaks, the exact break tells us where the architecture currently stops.
statement: States tracing one representative change suffices to establish closed-loop mechanisms, or to pinpoint exactly where the chain breaks.

anchor: 117.2 — The canonical engineering-change object ... EC=(Intent,Decision,Authority,Change,Verification,Runtime,Evidence,Knowledge). This is not a proposal for a new domain entity. It is a reconstruction structure for one real historical change.
statement: Defines EC=(Intent,Decision,Authority,Change,Verification,Runtime,Evidence,Knowledge) as a reconstruction structure, explicitly not a new domain entity.

type_signature.codomain: Intent x Decision x Authority x Change x Verification x Runtime x Evidence x Knowledge

anchor: 117.3 — Stage 1: Intent ... BusinessNeed, Risk, ComplianceRequirement, TechnicalDebt, ArchitectureEvolution, SecurityNeed. Can the reason for the change be reconstructed?
statement: Lists six candidate intent motivations, asking whether the reason for a change can be reconstructed.

anchor: 117.4 — Experiment 1 ... A Git commit exists: upgrade Nexus. Can we conclude why the change happened? No. The commit establishes ChangeOccurred. It does not establish WhyChangeWasRequired. Result: technical evidence only
statement: Experiment 1: a bare commit message establishes ChangeOccurred, not WhyChangeWasRequired; result technical evidence only.

anchor: 117.5 — Intent evidence ... Business requirement→Change request→Architecture discussion. Now Intent→ChangeRequest.
statement: Defines a stronger intent-evidence chain Business requirement->Change request->Architecture discussion, yielding Intent->ChangeRequest.

anchor: 117.6 — Experiment 2 ... A Jira ticket explicitly states Current Nexus version is no longer supported and must be upgraded. Expected: Intent is now evidenced. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 2: an explicit Jira ticket rationale evidences Intent; result PASS.

anchor: 117.7 — Stage 2: Decision ... Intent does not automatically create a decision. We need Intent→Decision. 'Upgrade Nexus OSS 3.69 to Nexus Pro using a parallel containerized deployment' is materially different from 'Nexus needs modernization.'
statement: States Intent does not automatically create Decision, illustrated by a specific upgrade decision differing materially from a vague modernization intent.

anchor: 117.8 — Experiment 3 ... Change request exists. No explicit decision exists. Expected: Intent=Known but Decision=Unknown. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: a change request without an explicit decision leaves Intent=Known, Decision=Unknown; result PASS.

anchor: 117.9 — Decision evidence ... Architecture Board record, ADR, approved change, governance decision, documented authorization. But Document≠Decision. The document must actually establish the decision.
statement: States Document≠Decision: a document must actually establish the decision, not merely reference it.

anchor: 117.10 — Stage 3: Authority ... Decision→Authority. Who or what had the authority to make this decision? This is where KnowledgeOS must distinguish Actor from Authority.
statement: Introduces the Actor≠Authority distinction for the Decision->Authority stage.

anchor: 117.11 — Experiment 4 ... A Domain Architect recommends 'We should migrate Nexus.' Expected: Recommendation. This does not establish AuthorizedDecision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 4: a domain architect's recommendation is not an AuthorizedDecision; result PASS.

anchor: 117.12 — Experiment 5 ... Architecture Board formally approves the architecture direction. Expected: Authority-authorizes->Decision. Result: PASS assuming the approval record can be evidenced.
statement: Experiment 5: formal Architecture Board approval evidences Authority-authorizes->Decision, conditional on the approval record being evidenced; result PASS.

anchor: 117.13 — Authority scope ... AuthorityScope. An Architecture Board may have authority over Architecture. It may not automatically have authority over ProductionOperations.
statement: States AuthorityScope must be checked separately: architecture authority does not automatically extend to production operations authority.

anchor: 117.14 — Experiment 6 ... Architecture Board approves target architecture. Operations team performs production deployment. Expected: these are potentially two separate authority boundaries. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 6: architecture approval and production deployment execution are potentially two separate authority boundaries; result PASS.

anchor: 117.15 — Stage 4: Implementation ... Decision→Implementation. Decision→ADR→Commit→BuildArtifact.
statement: Defines the Decision->Implementation stage via Decision->ADR->Commit->BuildArtifact.

anchor: 117.16 — Experiment 7 ... Decision says containerize Nexus. Git contains a commit introducing Containerfile, Podman configuration, deployment configuration. Expected: potential implementation evidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: a commit introducing containerization artifacts matching a decision is potential implementation evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 117.17 — Strong implementation relationship ... commit references decision; PR references ADR; implementation record references change request; deployment references build artifact. Then Decision-implementedBy->Change.
statement: Defines strong Decision-implementedBy->Change evidence via explicit cross-references between commit/PR/implementation-record/deployment and decision/ADR/change-request/build-artifact.

anchor: 117.18 — Experiment 8 ... Commit message explicitly references the approved change. Expected: ImplementationTrace=Strong. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 8: a commit explicitly referencing the approved change yields ImplementationTrace=Strong; result PASS.

anchor: 117.19 — Stage 5: Verification ... Implementation→Verification. unit tests, integration tests, architecture tests, security tests, deployment checks, smoke tests, operational validation.
statement: Defines Implementation->Verification across seven possible verification types.

anchor: 117.20 — Experiment 9 ... Container starts successfully. Does that prove the architecture is correct? No. It proves RuntimeStartup=True. Not ArchitectureConformance=True. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: a successfully starting container proves RuntimeStartup=True, not ArchitectureConformance=True; result PASS.

anchor: 117.21 — Verification dimensions ... FunctionalVerification, ArchitectureVerification, SecurityVerification, OperationalVerification. One successful test cannot represent all four.
statement: Separates verification into four dimensions (Functional/Architecture/Security/Operational), stating one test cannot represent all four.

anchor: 117.22 — Experiment 10 ... Nexus container responds on port 8081. Expected: OperationalVerification. But not necessarily ArchitectureVerification. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 10: a responding container evidences OperationalVerification but not necessarily ArchitectureVerification; result PASS.

anchor: 117.23 — Deterministic assurance ... Rule→DeterministicCheck→Result. NoForbiddenDependency can be mechanically tested.
statement: Connects to the deterministic-assurance principle Rule->DeterministicCheck->Result, illustrated by mechanically testable NoForbiddenDependency.

anchor: 117.24 — Experiment 11 ... Architecture rule says service must not access production database directly. A static architecture test proves the dependency graph complies. Expected: VerificationEvidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 11: a static dependency-graph architecture test proving compliance with a no-direct-DB-access rule is VerificationEvidence; result PASS.

anchor: 117.25 — Stage 6: Runtime ... Verification→Runtime. Did the actual deployed system become what the implementation intended?
statement: Defines the Verification->Runtime stage, asking whether the deployed system matches implementation intent.

anchor: 117.26 — Experiment 12 ... Build artifact says Nexus:v2. Runtime actually runs Nexus:v1. Expected: Implementation≠Runtime. Result: DRIFT. This is exactly the type of problem a KnowledgeOS should eventually be able to represent.
statement: Experiment 12: a build-artifact-vs-runtime version mismatch (v2 vs v1) is Implementation≠Runtime, classified DRIFT.

anchor: 117.27 — Runtime identity ... RuntimeInstance connected to ArtifactVersion. Potentially DeploymentID.
statement: Defines runtime identity as RuntimeInstance connected to ArtifactVersion and potentially DeploymentID.

anchor: 117.28 — Experiment 13 ... Runtime reports artifact=nexus-pro:2.1, deployment=D-42. Expected: strong runtime identity evidence. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a runtime report including artifact version and deployment ID is strong runtime identity evidence; result PASS.

anchor: 117.29 — Stage 7: Observation ... Runtime state produces Observation. Nexus reachable, Repository count=43, Blob stores=40, Data size=256 GB. These are observations, not conclusions.
statement: States raw runtime observations (reachability, counts, sizes) are observations, not conclusions.

anchor: 117.30 — Experiment 14 ... Monitoring says Nexus container is healthy. Expected: Observation. It is not automatically ArchitectureConformant. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 14: a 'healthy' monitoring status is an Observation, not automatically ArchitectureConformant; result PASS.

anchor: 117.31 — Observation → Evidence ... Observation: ContainerRunning=True supports Claim: DeploymentIsOperational. Observation-supports->Claim.
statement: Defines Observation-supports->Claim, illustrated by ContainerRunning=True supporting DeploymentIsOperational.

anchor: 117.32 — Experiment 15 ... Health check passes. Architecture Board decision required Nexus must run with rootless Podman. Runtime evidence confirms rootless operation. Expected: Observation→Evidence→Claim. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: runtime evidence confirming a required rootless-Podman condition demonstrates Observation->Evidence->Claim; result PASS.

anchor: 117.33 — Stage 8: Updated knowledge ... Evidence→Knowledge. The result of the change should become part of the organization's current knowledge. This is more than a deployment log.
statement: Defines Evidence->Knowledge: the result of a change should become part of current organizational knowledge, more than a deployment log.

anchor: 117.34 — Experiment 16 ... Deployment completes. KnowledgeOS does not update the architecture state. Expected: RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState. Result: Knowledge synchronization gap
statement: Experiment 16: a completed deployment with no corresponding architecture-state update leaves RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState, a knowledge synchronization gap.

anchor: 117.35 — Closed-loop condition ... Intent→Decision→Authority→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Evidence→Knowledge. A genuine KnowledgeOS should eventually be able to reconstruct this path.
statement: Restates the complete forward chain as the closed-loop condition a genuine KnowledgeOS should eventually reconstruct.

anchor: 117.36 — The traceability matrix ... Intent/Decision/Authority/Implementation/Verification/Deployment/Runtime/Observation/Evidence/Knowledge, each with a Question and Evidence column. This becomes the canonical Engineering Traceability Record.
statement: Presents the canonical ten-row Engineering Traceability Record template (stage x question x evidence).

anchor: 117.37 — Four possible outcomes ... Outcome A Complete: EndToEndTraceability. Outcome B Technically complete: TechnicalTraceability. Outcome C Governance complete: GovernanceTraceability. Outcome D Fragmented: TraceabilityFragmentation.
statement: Defines four possible traceability outcomes: Complete, Technically complete, Governance complete, Fragmented.

anchor: 117.38 — Why this matters for KnowledgeOS ... KnowledgeOS should not merely answer 'Where is the architecture document?' It should answer 'Why does the current architecture exist, who authorized it, what implementation realizes it, and what evidence demonstrates that the deployed system still confor
statement: Reframes KnowledgeOS's value proposition from document lookup to a full why/who/what/evidence-of-conformance capability.

anchor: 117.39 — Agent use case ... An agent should be able to retrieve CurrentDecision, Authority, RelevantArchitecture, ImplementationConstraints, ExistingEvidence, KnownFindings. Then it can reason within an authoritative context.
statement: States an agent handling a change request should retrieve six categories of authoritative context before reasoning.

anchor: 117.40 — Experiment 17 ... Agent retrieves only Nexus migration documentation. Expected: useful contextual information, but not enough to establish CurrentAuthority. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: documentation-only retrieval is useful context but insufficient to establish CurrentAuthority; result PASS.

anchor: 117.41 — Agent recommendation ... Agent can then produce Recommendation based on AuthoritativeKnowledge. But the recommendation remains AgentInference.
statement: States agent recommendations remain AgentInference even when based on authoritative knowledge.

anchor: 117.42 — Experiment 18 ... Agent recommends 'Use parallel deployment.' Expected: Recommendation. If the Architecture Board approves: Recommendation→Decision. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: an agent recommendation becomes Decision only upon Architecture Board approval (Recommendation->Decision); result PASS.

anchor: 117.43 — Agent action ... Decision→DelegatedAuthority→AgentAction. This creates the bridge between governance and AI engineering.
statement: Defines Decision->DelegatedAuthority->AgentAction as the bridge between governance and AI engineering.

anchor: 117.44 — Experiment 19 ... Codex creates a pull request implementing an approved decision. Expected trace: Decision→CodexAction→PullRequest→Commit. Result: PASS provided the references are preserved.
statement: Experiment 19: a Codex-implemented decision traces as Decision->CodexAction->PullRequest->Commit, conditional on preserved references; result PASS.

anchor: 117.45 — Verification by agent ... The agent can then run Verification. But it must not simply report 'Looks good.' Instead Tool→DeterministicResult→Evidence.
statement: Requires agent-run verification to follow Tool->DeterministicResult->Evidence, not a prose summary.

anchor: 117.46 — Experiment 20 ... Codex runs architecture tests. All pass. Expected: VerificationEvidence. The agent's prose summary is secondary. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: agent-run passing architecture tests are VerificationEvidence, with the agent's prose summary secondary; result PASS.

anchor: 117.47 — The agent assurance chain ... Authoritative Knowledge→Agent Context→Reasoning→Recommendation→Authorized Action→Deterministic Verification→Evidence→KnowledgeOS Update. This is the architecture we have been progressively reconstructing.
statement: Presents the ideal agent assurance chain from Authoritative Knowledge through Agent Context/Reasoning/Recommendation/Authorized Action/Deterministic Verification/Evidence to KnowledgeOS Update.

anchor: 117.48 — Failure experiment ... Agent reads stale memory, proposes a change, implements it, tests it, never checks current architecture authority. The technical result might be correct. But GovernanceTrace=Broken.
statement: Presents a failure experiment: an agent acting on stale memory without checking current authority produces GovernanceTrace=Broken even if technically correct.

anchor: 117.49 — Experiment 21 ... Agent's implementation passes all tests but violates an Architecture Board decision. Expected: TechnicalVerification=PASS but GovernanceConformance=FAIL. Result: PASS. Technical correctness does not imply organizational correctness.
statement: Experiment 21: a test-passing but board-decision-violating implementation is TechnicalVerification=PASS/GovernanceConformance=FAIL, crystallizing the principle that technical correctness does not imply organizational correctness.

anchor: 117.50 — Two-dimensional assurance ... TechnicalConformance and GovernanceConformance. Overall: Conformance=Technical∩Governance.
statement: Defines two-dimensional assurance Conformance=Technical∩Governance.

anchor: 117.51 — Experiment 22 ... Implementation is technically valid but not authorized. Expected: Technical=PASS, Governance=FAIL. Overall: FAIL. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: a technically-valid-but-unauthorized implementation yields overall FAIL under Conformance=Technical∩Governance; result PASS.

anchor: 117.52 — Conversely ... A decision may be fully authorized but technically incorrectly implemented. Then Governance=PASS, Technical=FAIL. Again Overall=FAIL.
statement: Presents the converse case: a fully-authorized but technically-incorrect implementation also yields overall FAIL.

anchor: 117.53 — KnowledgeOS assurance model ... Assurance=Evidence+Verification+Authority+Traceability rather than Assurance=TestResult.
statement: Defines the KnowledgeOS assurance model Assurance=Evidence+Verification+Authority+Traceability, explicitly rejecting Assurance=TestResult.

anchor: 117.54 — Traceability completeness ... T=verified links/required links. For important architecture decisions, a single missing critical edge can invalidate the trace. Therefore CriticalPath must be assessed separately.
statement: Defines traceability completeness T=verified-links/required-links, requiring CriticalPath to be assessed separately since one missing edge can invalidate the trace.

anchor: 117.55 — Critical path ... Authority→Decision→Action→Verification→Evidence is the minimal governance-assurance path.
statement: Defines the critical path Authority->Decision->Action->Verification->Evidence as the minimal governance-assurance path.

anchor: 117.56 — Experiment 23 ... All implementation artifacts exist. But no authority can be established. Expected: CriticalPath=Broken. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: complete implementation artifacts with no establishable authority yield CriticalPath=Broken; result PASS.

anchor: 117.57 — Temporal reconstruction ... t_intent, t_decision, t_implementation, t_verification, t_deployment, t_observation. Then verify temporal consistency.
statement: Defines temporal reconstruction across six timestamped stages, requiring consistency verification.

anchor: 117.58 — Experiment 24 ... Verification timestamp t_v occurs before implementation t_i. Expected: potential invalid evidence or clock/data problem. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 24: a verification timestamp preceding its implementation timestamp is a potential invalid-evidence or clock/data problem; result PASS.

anchor: 117.59 — Version reconstruction ... DecisionVersion must be connected to ImplementationVersion. Decision D42→Commit c81→Artifact v2.4.
statement: Defines version reconstruction DecisionVersion->ImplementationVersion, illustrated by Decision D42->Commit c81->Artifact v2.4.

anchor: 117.60 — Experiment 25 ... Commit implements an older superseded decision. Expected: potential governance mismatch. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 25: a commit implementing an already-superseded decision is a potential governance mismatch, classified OBS.

anchor: 117.61 — Knowledge update ... KnowledgeOS should ideally record DecisionStatus and ImplementationStatus. The exact representation is implementation-specific.
statement: States KnowledgeOS should ideally record DecisionStatus and ImplementationStatus alongside verification/runtime/knowledge status.

anchor: 117.62 — Experiment 26 ... Decision remains Approved with no indication whether implementation occurred. Expected: governance state and engineering state are disconnected. Result: OBS
statement: Experiment 26: a decision remaining 'Approved' with no implementation-status indication leaves governance and engineering state disconnected, classified OBS.

anchor: 117.63 — The state reconciliation problem ... DeclaredState, ImplementationState, DeploymentState, RuntimeState, KnowledgeState. KnowledgeOS's role is potentially to reconcile these.
statement: Defines five potentially divergent state realities, proposing KnowledgeOS's role as reconciling them.

anchor: 117.64 — The reconciliation model ... Declared→Implemented→Deployed→Observed→Verified→Authoritative Knowledge. Every transition should have evidence.
statement: Defines the reconciliation chain Declared->Implemented->Deployed->Observed->Verified->Authoritative Knowledge, every transition requiring evidence.

anchor: 117.65 — Experiment 27 ... Declared, implementation, deployment, runtime all use PostgreSQL. Expected: strong conformance chain. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 27: PostgreSQL used consistently across declared/implementation/deployment/runtime is a strong conformance chain; result PASS.

anchor: 117.66 — Experiment 28 ... Declared and implementation use PostgreSQL. Runtime uses MySQL. Expected: ArchitectureDrift. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 28: PostgreSQL declared/implemented but MySQL at runtime is ArchitectureDrift; result PASS.

anchor: 117.67 — Finding generation ... When the graph detects Expected≠Observed, we can generate Finding. But Detection≠Finding until the system interprets the discrepancy according to a rule.
statement: Reiterates Detection≠Finding: a rule must interpret Expected≠Observed before a Finding is generated.

anchor: 117.68 — Experiment 29 ... Runtime differs from architecture. System creates ArchitectureDriftFinding with rule, observed state, expected state, evidence. Expected: strong semantic finding. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 29: a fully-fielded ArchitectureDriftFinding (rule/observed/expected/evidence) is a strong semantic finding; result PASS.

anchor: 117.69 — Finding lifecycle ... Open→Investigating→Remediating→Verified→Closed. This connects the loop back to governance.
statement: Defines the finding lifecycle Open->Investigating->Remediating->Verified->Closed, connecting back to governance.

anchor: 117.70 — Experiment 30 ... Finding is marked Closed. No verification evidence exists. Expected: potential lifecycle integrity violation. Result: PASS
statement: Experiment 30: a Closed finding with no verification evidence is a potential lifecycle integrity violation; result PASS.

anchor: 117.71 — The complete KnowledgeOS loop ... INTENT→DECISION→AUTHORITY→ENGINEERING ACTION→IMPLEMENTATION→DETERMINISTIC VERIFICATION→RUNTIME→OBSERVATION→EVIDENCE→KNOWLEDGE UPDATE→future INTENT. The cycle is Intent→Decision→Action→Reality→Evidence→Knowledge.
statement: Presents the complete target-architecture cycle diagram from Intent through Knowledge Update back to future Intent.

anchor: 117.72 — The decisive distinction ... A repository or knowledge base primarily stores State. An operating system manages State+Transitions+Control+Feedback. KnowledgeOS=Knowledge+StateTransitions+Governance+Evidence+Feedback is a much stronger architectural definition than 'AI knowledge platform.'
statement: States the decisive distinction: a repository stores State, an operating system manages State+Transitions+Control+Feedback, formalized as KnowledgeOS=Knowledge+StateTransitions+Governance+Evidence+Feedback.

anchor: 117.73 — Step 117 verdict ... Can one real change be traversed from intent to authoritative post-change knowledge? If yes, KnowledgeOS demonstrates operating-system characteristics. If the chain breaks, the missing edge identifies an architectural gap. STEP 117 — TRACEABILITY EXPERIMENT: DEFINED. Th
statement: Records the Step 117 verdict DEFINED (not PASS/FAIL), with the actual implementation verdict explicitly left evidence-dependent.

anchor: Step 118 — Governance-to-Engineering Closure Test preview ... We now test the reverse direction. When reality changes unexpectedly, can KnowledgeOS propagate that observation back into governance and authoritative knowledge? Runtime→Observation→Finding→Governance→Decision→Remediation→Verification. T
statement: Previews Step 118: testing the reverse direction Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification, moving from traceability to closed-loop engineering control.

anchor: We now have the complete target model. The next step is to test whether the actual KnowledgeOS/EKS ecosystem closes the loop in practice. Expected→Observed→Detected→Classified→Governed→Remediated→Verified→Recorded.
statement: Frames Step 119 as testing whether the actual ecosystem closes the loop via the target Expected->Observed->Detected->Classified->Governed->Remediated->Verified->Recorded.

anchor: 119.1 — The control-loop hypothesis ... KnowledgeOS=ReferenceState+Observation+Comparison+Governance+Action+Verification+Learning. The essential operation is Compare(Expected,Observed) followed by a controlled response.
statement: States the control-loop hypothesis KnowledgeOS=ReferenceState+Observation+Comparison+Governance+Action+Verification+Learning centered on Compare(Expected,Observed).

anchor: 119.2 — Reference state ... architecture, ADR, implementation constitution, coding standard, policy, approved configuration, governance decision, security rule, deployment specification. The reference state is R_t.
statement: Defines R_t as the reference state drawn from nine possible authoritative sources.

anchor: 119.3 — Experiment 1: Is there a reference? ... Component A differs from expected state. Expected according to what? If no authoritative source can be identified: ExpectedState=Unknown. Verdict: Reference missing
statement: Experiment 1: a 'differs from expected state' report with no identifiable authoritative source yields ExpectedState=Unknown, verdict Reference missing.

anchor: 119.4 — Reference hierarchy ... EnterprisePolicy, ArchitectureDecision, DomainRule, ImplementationRule, RuntimeExpectation. These may conflict. Therefore the system needs precedence semantics.
statement: Defines a five-level reference hierarchy that may conflict, requiring precedence semantics.

anchor: 119.5 — Experiment 2: conflicting references ... Architecture: PostgreSQL required. Team documentation: MySQL allowed. Which one governs? If KnowledgeOS cannot determine authority: GovernanceAmbiguity. Verdict: AMBIGUOUS. This is a semantic problem, not a search problem.
statement: Experiment 2: conflicting PostgreSQL-vs-MySQL references with no determinable authority yield GovernanceAmbiguity, verdict AMBIGUOUS, explicitly a semantic problem not a search problem.

anchor: 119.6 — Expected-state provenance ... ExpectedState→Source→Authority→Validity. Without this, agents can retrieve outdated or non-authoritative expectations.
statement: Defines ExpectedState->Source->Authority->Validity as required provenance, without which agents risk retrieving outdated or non-authoritative expectations.

anchor: 119.7 — Experiment 3 ... Agent retrieves a Markdown document describing the desired architecture. The document has no approval status. Expected: useful information, but Authority=Unknown. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 3: an unapproved Markdown architecture document is useful but leaves Authority=Unknown; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.8 — Observation ... Expected→Observed. Observation may come from Git, CI, deployment, Kubernetes, Podman, monitoring, filesystem, API, security scanner, architecture checker. The observation needs identity and timestamp.
statement: Defines Expected->Observed across ten possible observation sources, requiring identity and timestamp.

anchor: 119.9 — Experiment 4 ... Scanner produces component=X, dependency=Y. No timestamp or environment exists. Expected: observation exists but contextual provenance is incomplete. Verdict: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 4: a scanner result with no timestamp/environment has incomplete contextual provenance; verdict PARTIAL.

anchor: 119.10 — Comparison ... Compare(R_t,O_t). This must be deterministic wherever possible. ExpectedDependency(A,B)=false, ObservedDependency(A,B)=true, therefore Violation=True.
statement: Defines the central Compare(R_t,O_t) operation, required to be deterministic wherever possible, illustrated by a dependency-existence violation.

anchor: 119.11 — Experiment 5 ... A human reviewer visually compares two architecture diagrams. Expected: potentially useful review, but it is not deterministic assurance. Verdict: Human verification rather than Deterministic control
statement: Experiment 5: human visual diagram comparison is Human verification, not Deterministic control.

anchor: 119.12 — Deterministic comparison ... expected.json, observed.json → deterministic comparator → DIFF. This produces reproducible results.
statement: Describes a deterministic comparator pipeline (expected.json/observed.json->comparator->DIFF) producing reproducible results.

anchor: 119.13 — Experiment 6 ... Same inputs produce different compliance results depending on which agent evaluates them. Expected: weak assurance. Verdict: NON-DETERMINISTIC
statement: Experiment 6: identical inputs yielding different compliance results across evaluating agents is weak assurance, verdict NON-DETERMINISTIC.

anchor: 119.14 — Classification ... A difference is not automatically a governance violation. Difference→Classification. ExpectedChange, ApprovedException, TemporaryDrift, Violation, Unknown.
statement: Defines Difference->Classification across five categories, stating a difference is not automatically a violation.

anchor: 119.15 — Experiment 7 ... Deployment differs from architecture because an approved emergency exception is active. Expected: Difference≠Violation. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 7: a deployment difference covered by an approved emergency exception is Difference≠Violation; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.16 — Governance routing ... Classification→GovernancePath. Architecture violation→Architecture Governance. Security violation→Security Governance. Operational failure→Operations.
statement: Defines Classification->GovernancePath with three example routing mappings.

anchor: 119.17 — Experiment 8 ... All findings are routed to one generic queue. Expected: basic issue management exists, but governance semantics are weak. Verdict: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 8: routing all findings to one generic queue has weak governance semantics; verdict PARTIAL.

anchor: 119.18 — Governance decision ... Finding→Decision. Remediate, AcceptRisk, GrantException, ChangeRule, RejectFinding.
statement: Lists five possible Finding->Decision outcomes.

anchor: 119.19 — Experiment 9 ... Finding disappears after a human clicks Resolved. No decision exists. Expected: issue lifecycle exists, governance decision semantics are not proven. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 9: a finding resolved by a human click with no decision record proves issue lifecycle but not governance decision semantics; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.20 — Remediation ... If Decision=Remediate then Decision→RemediationAction. The action must retain DecisionID.
statement: States remediation actions must retain DecisionID for traceability.

anchor: 119.21 — Experiment 10 ... Engineer fixes the problem but the commit contains no reference to the finding or decision. Expected: remediation occurred, traceability weak. Verdict: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 10: a fix commit with no finding/decision reference is weak traceability; verdict PARTIAL.

anchor: 119.22 — Agent remediation ... For AI agents, Agent→Action must include AgentIdentity and DelegatedAuthority.
statement: States agent remediation actions must include AgentIdentity and DelegatedAuthority.

anchor: 119.23 — Experiment 11 ... Agent creates a pull request. Git identifies the user account, but not which agent or session performed the action. Expected: human account provenance may exist, agent-level provenance unknown. Verdict: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment 11: a PR identified only by a human account, not agent/session, leaves agent-level provenance unknown; verdict PARTIAL.

anchor: 119.24 — Verification ... After remediation: Action→Verification. The verification must address the original condition.
statement: States post-remediation verification must address the original violated condition.

anchor: 119.25 — Experiment 12 ... Original finding: unauthorized dependency exists. Remediation: code formatting changed. Verification: unit tests pass. Expected: verification does not address the finding. Verdict: INVALID CLOSURE
statement: Experiment 12: an unauthorized-dependency finding remediated by unrelated formatting and verified by unrelated unit tests is INVALID CLOSURE.

anchor: 119.26 — Closure condition ... FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding. Potentially FindingClosed⇒ObservedState conforms.
statement: States FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding (potentially also ⇒ObservedState conforms) as a closure invariant.

invariants.name: I_FindingClosedRequiresAddressed
invariants.statement: FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding, and potentially FindingClosed⇒ObservedState conforms.

anchor: 119.27 — Experiment 13 ... Finding is closed. New runtime observation still shows the violation. Expected: ClosureInvalid or FindingReopened. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 13: a closed finding whose violation persists in a new observation should be ClosureInvalid or FindingReopened; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.28 — Knowledge update ... Once the remediation is verified: VerifiedState→KnowledgeState'. The current organizational knowledge should now reflect reality.
statement: States verified remediation should update organizational knowledge (VerifiedState->KnowledgeState') to reflect reality.

anchor: 119.29 — Experiment 14 ... Runtime is corrected. The architecture repository still describes the old state. Expected: RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState. Verdict: KNOWLEDGE DRIFT
statement: Experiment 14: corrected runtime with a stale architecture repository is RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState, verdict KNOWLEDGE DRIFT.

anchor: 119.30 — This is a critical distinction ... Implementation drift: Code≠Architecture. Runtime drift: Runtime≠Deployment. Knowledge drift: Knowledge≠Reality. KnowledgeOS potentially needs to detect all three.
statement: Defines a three-way drift taxonomy (Implementation/Runtime/Knowledge drift), stating KnowledgeOS potentially needs to detect all three.

anchor: 119.31 — Experiment 15 ... Code is correct. Runtime is correct. Knowledge documentation is stale. Expected: KnowledgeDrift. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 15: correct code and runtime with stale documentation is KnowledgeDrift; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.32 — Knowledge synchronization ... RuntimeEvidence→KnowledgeUpdateCandidate. But this should not necessarily automatically overwrite authoritative knowledge.
statement: States RuntimeEvidence->KnowledgeUpdateCandidate should not automatically overwrite authoritative knowledge.

anchor: 119.33 — Important boundary ... ObservedTruth from AuthoritativeKnowledge. A runtime observation tells us this is what happened. It does not automatically tell us this is what the organization has decided should happen.
statement: States the ObservedTruth≠AuthoritativeKnowledge boundary: observation reports what happened, not what was decided should happen.

anchor: 119.34 — Experiment 16 ... Runtime changes from PostgreSQL to MySQL. Agent proposes updating architecture documentation to MySQL. Expected: it should first determine whether the change was authorized. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 16: an agent must check authorization before proposing to update documentation to match an observed database engine change; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.35 — Knowledge update proposal ... Observation→KnowledgeChangeProposal rather than Observation→AutomaticAuthority. This preserves governance.
statement: States Observation->KnowledgeChangeProposal (not AutomaticAuthority) preserves governance.

anchor: 119.36 — Human-in-the-loop boundary ... For low-risk derived metadata, automatic update may be acceptable. For architecture authority, approval may be required.
statement: States a risk-based human-in-the-loop boundary: low-risk metadata may auto-update, architecture-authority changes require approval.

anchor: 119.37 — Experiment 17 ... Runtime metadata last_seen=2026-08-28 updates automatically. Expected: reasonable. Architecture decision 'production architecture is now officially changed' should not necessarily be automatically generated. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 17: low-risk metadata auto-update is reasonable while an architecture-authority statement should not be auto-generated; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.38 — Control-loop levels ... C0 Observe: Runtime→Observation. C1 Detect: Observation→Difference. C2 Assure: Difference→Finding. C3 Govern: Finding→Decision. C4 Remediate: Decision→Action. C5 Verify: Action→Verification. C6 Learn: Verification→Knowledge.
statement: Defines a seven-level control-loop maturity model C0 (Observe) through C6 (Learn).

anchor: 119.39 — The complete level ... A complete KnowledgeOS control loop therefore satisfies C0+C1+C2+C3+C4+C5+C6. The current implementation should be evaluated level by level rather than given one vague maturity label.
statement: States a complete control loop requires all seven levels, evaluated individually rather than via one vague maturity label.

anchor: 119.40 — Control-loop integrity ... A control loop is only as strong as its weakest critical transition. C0=5, C1=5, C2=5 but C3=0. Then the system detects problems but cannot govern them.
statement: States a control loop is only as strong as its weakest critical transition, illustrated by strong detection undermined by zero governance.

anchor: 119.41 — Experiment 18 ... Excellent runtime monitoring exists. Findings are generated. But no connection to governance exists. Expected: DetectionSystem not ClosedLoopKnowledgeOS. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 18: excellent detection with no governance connection is a mere DetectionSystem, not a ClosedLoopKnowledgeOS; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.42 — Conversely ... Governance is excellent C3=5. But no runtime observations exist C0=0. Then the system cannot detect reality drift. It becomes GovernanceRepository. Not a closed engineering feedback system.
statement: Presents the converse case: excellent governance with zero observation is a GovernanceRepository, not a closed engineering feedback system.

anchor: 119.43 — Experiment 19 ... Architecture Board decisions are perfectly recorded. No implementation/runtime feedback reaches KnowledgeOS. Expected: GovernedKnowledge but ClosedLoop=False. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 19: perfectly recorded decisions with no runtime feedback are GovernedKnowledge but ClosedLoop=False; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.44 — The two-sided architecture ... Top-down: Governance→Engineering. Bottom-up: Engineering→Governance. KnowledgeOS becomes interesting at their intersection: Governance↔Engineering.
statement: Defines the two-sided architecture with KnowledgeOS positioned at the Governance<->Engineering intersection.

anchor: 119.45 — Top-down path ... Policy→Architecture→Decision→Authorization→Implementation→Deployment.
statement: Defines the top-down path Policy->Architecture->Decision->Authorization->Implementation->Deployment.

anchor: 119.46 — Bottom-up path ... Runtime→Observation→Verification→Finding→Governance→Decision. Together: GOVERNANCE ↕ KNOWLEDGEOS ↕ ENGINEERING.
statement: Defines the bottom-up path Runtime->Observation->Verification->Finding->Governance->Decision, together forming the Governance<->KnowledgeOS<->Engineering stack.

anchor: 119.47 — Why the agent layer belongs in the middle ... They consume GovernedKnowledge. They produce Recommendations. They may execute AuthorizedActions. They generate Observations and Evidence. Agent=Participant in the Knowledge Loop, not the owner of organizational truth.
statement: States agents are Participants in the Knowledge Loop (consuming governed knowledge, producing recommendations, executing authorized actions, generating observations/evidence), never the owner of organizational truth.

anchor: 119.48 — Experiment 20 ... Agent discovers a discrepancy. It creates FindingCandidate. A governance mechanism validates it. Then Finding→Decision. Expected: strong agent integration. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 20: an agent-created FindingCandidate validated by governance and driving Finding->Decision is strong agent integration; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.49 — Agent as evidence producer ... Agent→Tool→Result→Evidence. The evidence must identify agent/session, tool, input, output, timestamp.
statement: Defines Agent->Tool->Result->Evidence, requiring five identifying fields (agent/session, tool, input, output, timestamp).

anchor: 119.50 — Experiment 21 ... Agent says 'I checked the repository.' No tool execution record exists. Expected: Evidence=Weak. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 21: an unbacked agent claim with no tool execution record is Evidence=Weak; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.51 — Agent hallucination boundary ... AgentAssertion≠Evidence unless evidence provenance exists. AgentRecommendation≠Decision. AgentCapability≠Authority. These three distinctions should become central to the AI engineering platform.
statement: States three central agent-boundary distinctions: AgentAssertion≠Evidence, AgentRecommendation≠Decision, AgentCapability≠Authority.

invariants.name: I_AgentAssertionNeqEvidence
invariants.statement: AgentAssertion≠Evidence unless evidence provenance exists.

invariants.name: I_AgentRecommendationNeqDecision
invariants.statement: AgentRecommendation≠Decision.

invariants.name: I_AgentCapabilityNeqAuthority
invariants.statement: AgentCapability≠Authority.

anchor: 119.52 — Deterministic assurance boundary ... LLMReasoning from DeterministicAssurance. The agent may reason probabilistically. The final compliance assertion should, where feasible, rely on deterministic evidence.
statement: Separates LLMReasoning from DeterministicAssurance, requiring compliance assertions to rely on deterministic evidence where feasible.

anchor: 119.53 — Experiment 22 ... LLM concludes the architecture is compliant. A deterministic checker says FAIL. Expected: Compliance=FAIL. The LLM conclusion cannot override the deterministic result. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 22: an LLM's compliant conclusion cannot override a deterministic checker's FAIL; Compliance=FAIL; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.54 — Evidence priority ... DeterministicVerifiedEvidence > ToolObservedEvidence > HumanAssertion > AgentAssertion > Inference. This does not mean human evidence is unimportant. It means the epistemic status differs.
statement: Defines the evidence-priority hierarchy DeterministicVerifiedEvidence>ToolObservedEvidence>HumanAssertion>AgentAssertion>Inference as an epistemic-status ordering, not a value judgment.

anchor: 119.55 — Epistemic status ... WhatIsKnown versus WhatIsInferred. Observed, Verified, Asserted, Inferred, Proposed, Authoritative.
statement: Defines a six-value epistemic status vocabulary (Observed/Verified/Asserted/Inferred/Proposed/Authoritative) preserving WhatIsKnown vs WhatIsInferred.

anchor: 119.56 — Experiment 23 ... Agent infers 'This service probably owns the database.' Expected: Inferred. It should not silently become Authoritative. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 23: an agent's probabilistic inference must remain Inferred, not silently become Authoritative; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.57 — KnowledgeOS epistemic boundary ... KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status. This is arguably one of the most important architectural properties discovered in the reconstruction.
statement: States KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status, self-identified as one of the most important architectural properties discovered in the reconstruction.

anchor: 119.58 — Closed-loop learning ... After verification: Evidence→Knowledge. But not all evidence should become permanent organizational knowledge. We need Evidence→CandidateKnowledge→Validation→AuthoritativeKnowledge.
statement: Requires Evidence->CandidateKnowledge->Validation->AuthoritativeKnowledge rather than a direct Evidence->Knowledge jump.

anchor: 119.59 — Experiment 24 ... One transient runtime event occurs. Expected: it should not automatically become an architecture rule. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 24: a single transient runtime event should not automatically become an architecture rule; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.60 — Knowledge promotion ... Raw→Observed→Supported→Validated→Authoritative. This is a knowledge promotion pipeline.
statement: Defines the five-stage knowledge promotion pipeline Raw->Observed->Supported->Validated->Authoritative.

anchor: 119.61 — Promotion authority ... Validated→Authoritative may require explicit authority. Promotion→Authority.
statement: States the final Validated->Authoritative transition may require explicit Promotion->Authority.

anchor: 119.62 — Experiment 25 ... Agent discovers a recurring architecture pattern. It automatically declares 'New enterprise architecture standard.' Expected: governance violation unless the agent has delegated authority to create such standards. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment 25: an agent unilaterally declaring a discovered pattern a new enterprise standard is a governance violation absent delegated authority; verdict PASS.

anchor: 119.63 — The control-loop invariant ... No authoritative knowledge change without valid authority. No governance closure without verification evidence. No evidence claim without provenance. Together these form a semantic assurance constitution.
statement: States three synthesizing invariants (authority-required change, verification-required closure, provenance-required evidence) forming a semantic assurance constitution.

invariants.name: I_NoAuthoritativeChangeWithoutAuthority
invariants.statement: No authoritative knowledge change without valid authority.

invariants.name: I_NoClosureWithoutVerification
invariants.statement: No governance closure without verification evidence.

invariants.name: I_NoEvidenceWithoutProvenance
invariants.statement: No evidence claim without provenance.

anchor: 119.64 — Candidate KnowledgeOS Constitution ... K1 Provenance: KnowledgeObject→Provenance. K2 Authority: AuthoritativeChange→Authority. K3 Verification: ClosedFinding→VerificationEvidence. K4 Temporal validity: CurrentKnowledge→Validity. K5 Epistemic separation: Inference≠Fact. K6 Agent boundary: Ag
statement: Defines a candidate seven-principle KnowledgeOS Constitution K1-K7 (Provenance/Authority/Verification/TemporalValidity/EpistemicSeparation/AgentBoundary/Traceability).

anchor: 119.65 — The deeper architectural conclusion ... KnowledgeOS≠KnowledgeGraph. Nor RAG. Nor AgentPlatform. Nor GovernanceRepository. The stronger model is KnowledgeOS=Governed Knowledge+Engineering State+Evidence+Agents+Feedback.
statement: Rejects four insufficient KnowledgeOS equivalences (KnowledgeGraph/RAG/AgentPlatform/GovernanceRepository), stating KnowledgeOS=GovernedKnowledge+EngineeringState+Evidence+Agents+Feedback.

anchor: 119.66 — Step 119 verdict ... Expected→Observed→Detected→Classified→Governed→Remediated→Verified→Recorded and the reverse learning path Evidence→ValidatedKnowledge→FutureDecision. STEP 119 — CONTROL-LOOP MODEL: PASS. Again, this is the architectural test model, not yet a claim that every stage exist
statement: Records Step 119 verdict PASS for the control-loop test model, explicitly not a claim that every stage exists in the current implementation.

anchor: Step 120 — KnowledgeOS Constitutional Invariants preview ... consolidate everything discovered so far into a small set of non-negotiable architectural invariants. What are the few invariants that, if violated, fundamentally change KnowledgeOS into something else? Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus
