statement: Previews Step 120: consolidating discovered rules into a small non-negotiable invariant set (Provenance/Authority/EpistemicStatus/TemporalValidity/DeterministicVerification/Traceability/Feedback), to be tested and de-duplicated into the KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution for use by Claude, Codex and other agents.

anchor: We now move from architectural principles to implementation conformance. The decisive question is now: Where is each constitutional invariant actually enforced? Not merely mentioned. Not merely intended. Enforced.
statement: Frames Step 121's shift from architectural principle (candidate constitution C1-C7) to implementation-conformance testing: where is each invariant actually enforced.

anchor: 121.1 — The conformance chain ... Constitution→Architecture→Mechanism→Implementation→Verification→Runtime. A rule becomes operationally real only when this chain exists. C1→ProvenanceModel→ProvenanceService→Code→Test→RuntimeEvidence.
statement: Defines the conformance chain Constitution->Architecture->Mechanism->Implementation->Verification->Runtime, a rule becoming operationally real only when the full chain exists.

anchor: 121.2 — The conformance matrix ... Rule x Architecture mechanism/Implementation/Enforcement/Test/Runtime/Verdict for C1-C7, all cells '?'. This becomes the constitutional conformance register.
statement: Presents the seven-rule constitutional conformance register template across six columns, all cells '?'.

anchor: 121.3 — Four possible verdicts ... CONFORMANT, PARTIAL, DECLARED, ABSENT, UNKNOWN. We should avoid a simplistic pass/fail model.
statement: Defines five conformance verdicts (CONFORMANT/PARTIAL/DECLARED/ABSENT/UNKNOWN), avoiding a simplistic pass/fail model.

anchor: 121.4 — C1: Provenance ... AuthoritativeKnowledge→Provenance. Where does provenance live? source_id, created_by, created_at, origin, lineage, version. But individual metadata fields are not automatically a provenance model.
statement: States C1 Provenance (AuthoritativeKnowledge->Provenance), warning individual metadata fields are not automatically a provenance model.

anchor: 121.5 — Provenance enforcement test ... Create(K). Can an authoritative knowledge object be created without provenance? If yes: C1=NotEnforced. If no: C1=Enforced.
statement: Defines the provenance enforcement test via Create(K): whether an authoritative object can be created without provenance determines C1=Enforced/NotEnforced.

anchor: 121.6 — Experiment C1.1 ... createAuthoritativeKnowledge without source metadata. A: Creation rejected → C1 Strong. B: Creation succeeds but marked provisional → C1 Partial. C: Creation succeeds as authoritative → C1 Violation.
statement: Experiment C1.1: attempting to create authoritative knowledge without source metadata yields three possible outcomes (rejected/Strong, provisional/Partial, accepted-as-authoritative/Violation).

anchor: 121.7 — Provenance inheritance ... A derived object should ideally preserve lineage: K2-derivedFrom->K1. This is particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.
statement: States derived objects should preserve lineage (K2-derivedFrom->K1), particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.

anchor: 121.8 — Experiment C1.2 ... Agent summarizes ten source documents. Summary has no source references. Expected: DerivedKnowledge has weak provenance. Verdict: C1 PARTIAL/VIOLATED depending on whether it can still be treated as authoritative.
statement: Experiment C1.2: an agent summary with no source references has weak provenance, verdict C1 PARTIAL/VIOLATED depending on authoritative treatment.

anchor: 121.9 — C2: Authority ... AuthoritativeChange→Authority. We test the promotion operation Proposed→Authoritative. What prevents unauthorized promotion?
statement: States C2 Authority tested via the Proposed->Authoritative promotion operation and what prevents unauthorized promotion.

anchor: 121.10 — Experiment C2.1 ... Agent creates Proposal P. Then attempts P→Approved without an authorized actor. Expected: Reject.
statement: Experiment C2.1: an unauthorized attempt to approve a proposal should be rejected.

anchor: 121.11 — Strong authority enforcement ... Proposal→Authorization check→Authority validation→Approval→Authoritative state. The important part is that the authority check is machine-enforced.
statement: Presents the strong authority-enforcement pipeline, emphasizing the authority check must be machine-enforced.

anchor: 121.12 — Weak authority enforcement ... If the system simply stores approved_by='Nab' without validating whether that actor had authority, then AuthorityRepresentation=True but AuthorityEnforcement=False.
statement: States the AuthorityRepresentation≠AuthorityEnforcement gap: recording an approver's name without validating actual authority.

anchor: 121.13 — C3: Epistemic separation ... Inference≠Observation≠Verification≠Authority. Now we test whether these states are represented.
statement: States C3 Epistemic separation (Inference≠Observation≠Verification≠Authority) tested by whether these states are represented.

anchor: 121.14 — Experiment C3.1 ... Agent produces 'I believe service A owns database B.' System stores status=AUTHORITATIVE. Expected: C3=VIOLATED.
statement: Experiment C3.1: an agent's belief statement stored as status=AUTHORITATIVE is C3=VIOLATED.

anchor: 121.15 — Strong epistemic model ... Agent inference→Proposed claim→Evidence→Verification→Approval→Authoritative knowledge. This preserves the epistemic journey.
statement: Presents the strong epistemic-journey model Agent inference->Proposed claim->Evidence->Verification->Approval->Authoritative knowledge.

anchor: 121.16 — Why this is particularly important for KnowledgeOS ... Traditional systems can often tolerate Record=Fact. AI systems cannot. Because an LLM constantly produces PlausibleStatements. KnowledgeOS therefore needs to distinguish Plausibility from Evidence.
statement: Argues traditional systems can tolerate Record=Fact but AI systems, constantly producing PlausibleStatements, cannot, requiring KnowledgeOS to distinguish Plausibility from Evidence.

anchor: 121.17 — C4: Temporal validity ... CurrentKnowledge≠HistoricalKnowledge. We test Supersede(K1,K2). Can the system establish that K2 replaces K1?
statement: States C4 Temporal validity (CurrentKnowledge≠HistoricalKnowledge) tested via Supersede(K1,K2).

anchor: 121.18 — Experiment C4.1 ... Two architecture decisions exist. No supersession relationship exists. Agent retrieves both. Expected: potential ambiguity. Verdict: C4 PARTIAL
statement: Experiment C4.1: two unlinked architecture decisions retrieved together is potential ambiguity, verdict C4 PARTIAL.

anchor: 121.19 — Temporal enforcement ... ValidAt(K,t). ValidAt(K1,t1)=True but ValidAt(K1,t2)=False.
statement: Defines the temporal-validity query primitive ValidAt(K,t).

anchor: 121.20 — Experiment C4.2 ... A decision is marked superseded. Agent requests current architecture. System still returns superseded decision as authoritative. Expected: C4=VIOLATED.
statement: Experiment C4.2: a system returning a superseded decision as authoritative is C4=VIOLATED.

anchor: 121.21 — C5: Deterministic assurance ... DeterministicallyTestableClaim→ReproducibleVerification. This is one of the strongest connections to the existing KnowledgeOS assurance architecture.
statement: States C5 Deterministic assurance (DeterministicallyTestableClaim->ReproducibleVerification).

anchor: 121.22 — Verification contract ... Rule+Input→Result. We want Result to be reproducible.
statement: Defines the verification reproducibility contract Rule+Input->Result.

anchor: 121.23 — Experiment C5.1 ... Architecture check runs twice against identical inputs. Results R1≠R2. Expected: verification mechanism is not deterministic. Verdict: C5 FAIL
statement: Experiment C5.1: identical inputs yielding different results across runs is a non-deterministic verification mechanism, verdict C5 FAIL.

anchor: 121.24 — Evidence-backed verification ... Rule, Input, Tool, Version, Timestamp, Result, Evidence. This enables reproduction.
statement: Defines a seven-field evidence-backed verification record schema enabling reproduction.

anchor: 121.25 — Experiment C5.2 ... Checker says PASS but no rule, input or version is recorded. Expected: weak assurance. Verdict: C5 PARTIAL
statement: Experiment C5.2: a bare PASS with no recorded rule/input/version is weak assurance, verdict C5 PARTIAL.

anchor: 121.26 — C6: Traceability ... MaterialAction→Authorization. PullRequest→ChangeRequest. Deployment→ApprovedChange.
statement: States C6 Traceability (MaterialAction->Authorization), illustrated by PullRequest->ChangeRequest and Deployment->ApprovedChange.

anchor: 121.27 — Experiment C6.1 ... Production deployment exists. No corresponding approved change can be identified. Expected: TraceabilityGap. Verdict: C6 FAIL for a governance-controlled deployment.
statement: Experiment C6.1: a production deployment with no identifiable approved change is a TraceabilityGap, verdict C6 FAIL for governance-controlled deployments.

anchor: 121.28 — Traceability granularity ... ActionClass→TraceabilityRequirement. Read repository: Low. Run local test: Low. Create PR: Medium. Merge protected branch: High. Production deployment: High. Change architecture rule: Very high.
statement: Defines a traceability-granularity table mapping six action classes to required traceability levels (Low through Very high).

anchor: 121.29 — C7: Feedback ... MaterialDeviation→Governance/KnowledgeFeedback. This is the hardest invariant to establish.
statement: States C7 Feedback (MaterialDeviation->Governance/KnowledgeFeedback), called the hardest invariant to establish.

anchor: 121.30 — Experiment C7.1 ... Runtime detects Expected≠Observed. System creates an alert. But no Finding or GovernancePath. Expected: observation capability, not closed-loop governance. Verdict: C7 PARTIAL
statement: Experiment C7.1: an alert with no Finding or GovernancePath is mere observation capability, not closed-loop governance, verdict C7 PARTIAL.

anchor: 121.31 — Strong feedback ... Observation→Finding→Classification→Governance→Decision. Then Decision→Action→Verification. Finally Verification→Knowledge.
statement: Presents the strong feedback sequence Observation->Finding->Classification->Governance->Decision->Action->Verification->Knowledge.

anchor: 121.32 — The enforcement gap ... Documented, Modeled, Checked, Enforced, Governed. These are different maturity states.
statement: Defines a five-level rule-maturity taxonomy: Documented, Modeled, Checked, Enforced, Governed.

anchor: 121.33 — Example ... Architecture Constitution says agents must not bypass KnowledgeOS: Documented. If AGENTS.md points to KnowledgeOS: Modeled/Directed. If a hook blocks direct access: Enforced. If violations generate findings: Governed.
statement: Illustrates the five-level rule-maturity taxonomy via a worked agent-bypass-prevention example.

anchor: 121.34 — This distinction matters for Claude/Codex ... The earlier pointer-layer principle can now be tested properly. A local memory file should not become an independent authority.
statement: States the maturity taxonomy allows properly testing the pointer-layer principle for Claude/Codex.

anchor: 121.35 — Experiment 1: Claude ... .claude/memory/ says rule X. KnowledgeOS says rule Y. Strong implementation: Agent resolves conflict via KnowledgeOSAuthority>LocalMemory. Weak implementation: agent uses whichever text is retrieved first.
statement: Experiment: tests conflict resolution between local Claude memory and KnowledgeOS, distinguishing strong (KnowledgeOSAuthority>LocalMemory) from weak (first-retrieved-wins) implementations.

anchor: 121.36 — Experiment 2: Codex ... The same test must work for .codex/. Therefore GovernanceRule(Claude)=GovernanceRule(Codex). This is the symmetry principle.
statement: States the symmetry principle GovernanceRule(Claude)=GovernanceRule(Codex), requiring the same conflict-resolution test for both agents.

anchor: 121.37 — The pointer-layer invariant ... A1: Agent-local operating artifacts MUST NOT silently become an alternative authority for organizational knowledge. Cache≠Authority.
statement: Formalizes agent-architecture invariant A1: agent-local operating artifacts must not silently become an alternative authority; Cache≠Authority.

invariants.name: A1
invariants.statement: Agent-local operating artifacts MUST NOT silently become an alternative authority for organizational knowledge. Cache≠Authority.

anchor: 121.38 — Agent cache requirements ... SourceID, Version, RetrievedAt, Freshness. Then Cache→AuthoritativeSource.
statement: Defines legitimate agent-cache requirements (SourceID/Version/RetrievedAt/Freshness) linking Cache->AuthoritativeSource.

anchor: 121.39 — Experiment A1.1 ... Agent memory says source=KnowledgeOS, version=47. KnowledgeOS current version=48. Expected: agent recognizes Cache=STALE. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment A1.1: an agent recognizing a version-47 cache as stale against a version-48 current source demonstrates Cache=STALE detection; verdict PASS.

anchor: 121.40 — Constitutional enforcement architecture ... CONSTITUTION→ARCHITECTURE RULES→{Runtime Checks, CI Checks, Agent Controls}→Evidence→Findings→Governance→Decision. This is the architecture of enforceable knowledge.
statement: Presents the constitutional enforcement architecture diagram, called the architecture of enforceable knowledge.

anchor: 121.41 — Governance record ... Violation=(Rule,Observed,Expected,Evidence,Actor,Time,Scope). This prevents governance from becoming an informal conversation.
statement: Defines the structured Violation=(Rule,Observed,Expected,Evidence,Actor,Time,Scope) record schema, preventing governance from becoming informal conversation.

type_signature.codomain: Rule x Observed x Expected x Evidence x Actor x Time x Scope

anchor: 121.42 — Experiment C8.1 ... Checker detects a violation. Only console output exists: FAILED. Expected: technical signal, not yet GovernanceEvidence. Verdict: PARTIAL
statement: Experiment C8.1: a bare console FAILED output is a technical signal, not yet GovernanceEvidence, verdict PARTIAL.

anchor: 121.43 — Constitutional evidence chain ... Rule→Check→Result→Evidence→Finding. This is the deterministic assurance chain.
statement: Defines the constitutional evidence chain Rule->Check->Result->Evidence->Finding, the deterministic assurance chain.

anchor: 121.44 — Constitutional promotion ... Proposal→Review→Decision→Authority→Rule. Thus even the constitution itself must be governed.
statement: States even new constitutional rules must follow Proposal->Review->Decision->Authority->Rule; the constitution itself must be governed.

anchor: 121.45 — Bootstrap paradox ... Who governs the KnowledgeOS Constitution? If the constitution is itself mutable without authority, then Authority can be bypassed by simply changing the rule. Therefore ConstitutionChange→HigherOrderAuthority.
statement: Surfaces the bootstrap paradox of constitutional self-governance, formalized as ConstitutionChange->HigherOrderAuthority.

anchor: 121.46 — Experiment C9.1 ... Developer modifies C1: Provenance is no longer required. No approval process exists. Expected: constitution can be silently weakened. Verdict: CRITICAL GOVERNANCE GAP
statement: Experiment C9.1: a developer silently weakening C1 with no approval process is a CRITICAL GOVERNANCE GAP.

anchor: 121.47 — Constitutional versioning ... KOS Constitution v0.1. A new version v0.2 must have change rationale, authority, effective date, superseded version, verification.
statement: Requires constitutional versioning with five mandatory fields (rationale/authority/effective date/superseded version/verification).

anchor: 121.48 — Constitution as governed knowledge ... Constitution⊂AuthoritativeKnowledge. Therefore the constitution itself obeys Provenance, Authority, TemporalValidity, Traceability.
statement: States Constitution⊂AuthoritativeKnowledge, so the constitution itself obeys Provenance/Authority/TemporalValidity/Traceability.

anchor: 121.49 — Recursive governance ... Governance→Knowledge. But also Knowledge→Governance. The constitution defines the rules by which authoritative knowledge evolves.
statement: States the recursive property: Governance->Knowledge and Knowledge->Governance, since the constitution defines the rules by which knowledge evolves.

anchor: 121.50 — The constitutional conformance model ... Conformance(C_i)=Architecture∩Implementation∩Verification∩Evidence. A rule is genuinely conformant only if all four are present.
statement: Defines Conformance(C_i)=Architecture∩Implementation∩Verification∩Evidence, requiring all four for genuine conformance.

anchor: 121.51 — Preliminary matrix ... Without inventing repository facts, our current reconstruction status is: all seven rules 'To verify' except C5 'Strong conceptual evidence; implementation to verify.' This is deliberately conservative.
statement: Presents a deliberately conservative preliminary status matrix marking all seven rules as needing verification.

anchor: 121.52 — What we can already establish ... strong support for the design intent around DeterministicAssurance, Governance, Evidence, AgentBehavior, Traceability. But design intent is not equivalent to implementation conformance.
statement: States strong design-intent support exists for five areas, but design intent is not equivalent to implementation conformance.

anchor: 121.53 — The evidence principle ... ArchitectureClaim≠ImplementationFact until implementation evidence establishes the relationship. This protects the entire reconstruction from becoming architecture fiction.
statement: States the methodological rule ArchitectureClaim≠ImplementationFact, protecting the reconstruction from becoming architecture fiction.

invariants.name: I_ArchitectureClaimNeqImplementationFact
invariants.statement: ArchitectureClaim≠ImplementationFact until implementation evidence establishes the relationship.

anchor: 121.54 — Three truth layers ... T1 Historical evidence. T2 Architectural interpretation. T3 Target architecture. They must never be silently mixed.
statement: Defines three truth layers (T1 Historical evidence, T2 Architectural interpretation, T3 Target architecture) that must never be silently mixed.

anchor: 121.55 — This is particularly important for old sessions ... accumulated KnowledgeOS discussions contain a mixture of existing implementation, planned architecture, experimental concepts, rejected ideas, and future target architecture.
statement: States the accumulated KnowledgeOS discussions mix five different statement kinds, requiring every statement to be classified.

anchor: 121.56 — Proposed classification ... Status∈{Observed,Implemented,Verified,Proposed,Target,Rejected,Unknown}. This should become part of the reconstruction methodology.
statement: Defines a seven-value statement-classification vocabulary as part of the reconstruction methodology.

anchor: 121.57 — Example ... 'KnowledgeOS should provide evidence lineage' could mean Target. 'Evidence lineage is implemented in service X' requires ImplementationEvidence. 'Evidence lineage passed test Y' requires VerificationEvidence.
statement: Illustrates the statement-classification vocabulary with three worked example statements.

anchor: 121.58 — Architectural hallucination prevention ... Instead of 'KnowledgeOS has X' we say 'X — Target architecture; implementation evidence not yet established.' That is much stronger engineering documentation.
statement: States the classification scheme functions as an anti-hallucination mechanism for architecture reconstruction, replacing unqualified 'has X' claims with explicit status-qualified statements.

anchor: 121.59 — Conformance evidence packet ... Rule→Interpretation→Implementation location→Mechanism→Test→Runtime evidence→Verdict→Gap→Recommendation. This becomes the authoritative audit artifact.
statement: Specifies the nine-stage Conformance Evidence Packet as the authoritative audit artifact.

anchor: 121.60 — The final conformance equation ... C_i^actual=Evidence(Architecture_i,Implementation_i,Verification_i,Runtime_i). Not C_i^actual=Documentation_i.
statement: States the final conformance equation C_i^actual=Evidence(Architecture_i,Implementation_i,Verification_i,Runtime_i), explicitly not Documentation_i.

anchor: 121.61 — Step 121 verdict ... Constitution→Mechanism→Implementation→Enforcement→Verification→Runtime. The reconstruction must classify every rule as Conformant | Partial | Declared | Absent | Unknown rather than assuming compliance.
statement: Records the Step 121 verdict establishing the Constitution-to-Implementation Conformance Method, requiring every rule classified rather than assumed compliant.

anchor: Step 122 — KnowledgeOS Evidence Execution Protocol preview ... a standard protocol that Claude, Codex, and eventually other agents can use to inspect a KnowledgeOS repository without contaminating the result with assumptions. Claim→Locate→Inspect→Trace→Test→Observe→Classify→Report. FACT | INFERENCE
statement: Previews Step 122: an agent-executable Claim->Locate->Inspect->Trace->Test->Observe->Classify->Report protocol with FACT|INFERENCE|TARGET|GAP output separation, toward a self-verifying engineering knowledge system.

anchor: We now consolidate the previous experiments. The objective is to identify the smallest set of invariants whose violation would fundamentally change the nature of KnowledgeOS. Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus+TemporalValidity+DeterministicVerification+Traceability+Feedback.
statement: Frames Step 120's objective: identifying the smallest invariant set whose violation would fundamentally change KnowledgeOS, starting from a seven-part candidate.

anchor: 120.1 — What makes an invariant constitutional? A constitutional invariant says: if this property is violated, the system no longer has the intended semantic character. ConstitutionalInvariant≠CodingConvention. 'Use PostgreSQL' is not necessarily constitutional. 'Authoritative knowledge must have id
statement: Defines ConstitutionalInvariant≠CodingConvention: a constitutional invariant's violation changes the system's intended semantic character, illustrated by contrasting a technology preference with a provenance requirement.

anchor: 120.2 — Invariant K1: Provenance ... Every authoritative knowledge object MUST have provenance. Provenance should answer where did it originate, when, through which process, who/what produced it, from which source material.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K1: every authoritative knowledge object must have provenance answering five questions (origin/when/process/producer/source material).

anchor: 120.3 — Why provenance is constitutional ... Without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText. That destroys the ability to answer: Why should I trust this?
statement: Argues without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText, destroying trust justification.

anchor: 120.4 — Experiment K1.1 ... KnowledgeOS contains 'The architecture requires rootless containers.' No source, author, decision, timestamp or provenance exists. Can the system establish that it is authoritative? No. Verdict: K1 VIOLATED
statement: Experiment K1.1: a sourceless/authorless/timestampless architecture statement cannot be established as authoritative; verdict K1 VIOLATED.

anchor: 120.5 — Provenance does not equal source URL ... SourceURL does not tell us WhoApproved or WhenDidItBecomeValid. Source≠CompleteProvenance.
statement: States Source≠CompleteProvenance: a URL alone does not establish approval or validity onset.

anchor: 120.6 — Invariant K2: Authority ... Every authoritative governance change MUST have identifiable authority. Decision→Authority.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K2: every authoritative governance change must have identifiable authority (Decision->Authority).

anchor: 120.7 — Why authority is constitutional ... Without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision. And AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth. That is unacceptable.
statement: Argues without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision and AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth.

anchor: 120.8 — Experiment K2.1 ... Agent generates 'Architecture standard changed to X.' No authorized decision exists. Expected: Status=Proposed. Not Status=Authoritative. Verdict: K2 VIOLATION if promoted
statement: Experiment K2.1: an unauthorized agent-declared standard change must remain Status=Proposed; K2 VIOLATION if promoted to Authoritative.

anchor: 120.9 — Authority is not identity ... Actor≠Authority. Credential≠Authority. Role≠Authority unless the governance model explicitly establishes the mapping.
statement: States Actor≠Authority, Credential≠Authority, Role≠Authority unless the governance model explicitly maps them.

anchor: 120.10 — Invariant K3: Epistemic status ... KnowledgeOS MUST distinguish observed, verified, inferred, proposed and authoritative information. This is perhaps the most important AI-specific invariant.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K3, called perhaps the most important AI-specific invariant: distinguishing observed/verified/inferred/proposed/authoritative information.

anchor: 120.11 — Why epistemic status matters ... 'The service probably owns this database' versus 'The Architecture Board decided that this service owns this database.' The textual similarity may be high. Their epistemic status is radically different.
statement: Illustrates why epistemic status matters via a textually-similar but epistemically-radically-different sentence pair.

anchor: 120.12 — Experiment K3.1 ... LLM generates Inference(X). System stores it identically to AuthoritativeDecision(X). Expected: K3 VIOLATION
statement: Experiment K3.1: storing an LLM inference identically to an authoritative decision is K3 VIOLATION.

anchor: 120.13 — Candidate epistemic states ... Observed, Imported, Asserted, Inferred, Proposed, Verified, Approved, Superseded. But we should only implement states that have real semantic value.
statement: Lists an eight-value candidate epistemic vocabulary, cautioning only states with real semantic value should be implemented.

anchor: 120.14 — Invariant K4: Temporal validity ... Authoritative knowledge MUST have determinable temporal validity. At minimum Current versus Superseded.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K4: authoritative knowledge must have determinable temporal validity, at minimum Current vs Superseded.

anchor: 120.15 — Why time is constitutional ... An architecture decision from 2024 may not represent the current architecture in 2026. Therefore HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth.
statement: Argues HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth, illustrated by a 2024 decision potentially not representing 2026's current architecture.

anchor: 120.16 — Experiment K4.1 ... Two decisions exist: D1 use architecture A, D2 use architecture B. No relationship identifies which supersedes which. Expected: agent cannot safely determine current architecture. Verdict: K4 VIOLATION
statement: Experiment K4.1: two competing, unlinked decisions leave an agent unable to safely determine current architecture; verdict K4 VIOLATION.

anchor: 120.17 — Creation time versus validity ... We must explicitly distinguish CreatedAt from ValidFrom. And potentially ValidUntil.
statement: States CreatedAt must be distinguished from ValidFrom (and potentially ValidUntil).

anchor: 120.18 — Experiment K4.2 ... Decision created 2026-08-01 but effective 2026-09-01. If the system only knows created_at, it cannot correctly answer is this decision currently effective. Verdict: K4 PARTIAL
statement: Experiment K4.2: a decision created before its effective date cannot be correctly evaluated by a created_at-only system; verdict K4 PARTIAL.

anchor: 120.19 — Invariant K5: Deterministic verification ... Where a claim is deterministically testable, authoritative assurance MUST be based on reproducible verification evidence. This does not eliminate human judgment. It prevents LLMConfidence from becoming Verification.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K5: deterministically testable claims must be assured via reproducible evidence, preventing LLMConfidence from becoming Verification.

anchor: 120.20 — Experiment K5.1 ... Static checker returns FAIL. LLM says the architecture looks compliant. Expected: Compliance=FAIL. Verdict: K5 PASS
statement: Experiment K5.1: a static-checker FAIL overrides an LLM's compliant assessment, Compliance=FAIL; verdict K5 PASS.

anchor: 120.21 — Why 'where deterministically testable' matters ... Is this architecture strategically appropriate may require human judgment. K5 should not become EverythingMustBeAutomated. It should be DeterministicWherePossible.
statement: Scopes K5 to DeterministicWherePossible, not EverythingMustBeAutomated, since some questions (e.g. strategic appropriateness) require judgment.

anchor: 120.22 — Invariant K6: Traceability ... Material engineering actions MUST be traceable to their governing intent, decision or authorization where governance requires it. Action→Decision.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K6: material engineering actions must be traceable to governing intent/decision/authorization where required.

anchor: 120.23 — Experiment K6.1 ... Agent changes production architecture. No decision, authorization or change record can be identified. Expected: TraceabilityGap. Verdict: K6 VIOLATION
statement: Experiment K6.1: an untraceable production architecture change is a TraceabilityGap; verdict K6 VIOLATION.

anchor: 120.24 — Traceability does not mean bureaucracy ... Not every action requires Architecture Board approval. RequiredTraceability(Action) depends on Risk+Scope+GovernanceClass. The invariant concerns required traceability, not universal approval.
statement: Scopes K6 to required traceability (function of Risk+Scope+GovernanceClass), not universal bureaucratic approval.

anchor: 120.25 — Invariant K7: Feedback ... Material deviations between authoritative expected state and observed engineering reality MUST be capable of feeding back into governance and knowledge. This is what makes the platform an operating system rather than a static repository.
statement: Proposes candidate invariant K7: material deviations must be capable of feeding back into governance and knowledge, distinguishing an operating system from a static repository.

anchor: 120.26 — Experiment K7.1 ... Runtime violates an architecture rule. System detects it. But the finding never reaches Governance and does not update Knowledge. Expected: observation capability exists, closed-loop capability does not. Verdict: K7 VIOLATION
statement: Experiment K7.1: a detected runtime violation that never reaches governance or updates knowledge shows observation without closed-loop capability; verdict K7 VIOLATION.

anchor: 120.27 — Are seven invariants really necessary? Could Provenance be absorbed into Traceability? Not completely. Traceability asks how are objects connected. Provenance asks where did this object come from. They are related but distinct.
statement: Tests whether Provenance can be absorbed into Traceability, concluding they are related but distinct (connection vs origin).

anchor: 120.28 — Could authority be part of provenance? Partially. A decision may have AuthoritativeSource. But authority is a governance relationship: Actor-authorizedBy->Decision. Therefore it deserves separate treatment.
statement: Tests whether Authority can fold into Provenance, concluding authority is a distinct governance relationship deserving separate treatment.

anchor: 120.29 — Could temporal validity be part of provenance? Again, partially. Provenance answers when was this created. Validity asks when is this considered applicable. CreatedAt≠Validity. Keep it separate.
statement: Tests whether Temporal validity can fold into Provenance, concluding CreatedAt≠Validity requires separate treatment.

anchor: 120.30 — Could epistemic status be part of provenance? No. A source can be known while the statement remains Inference. Provenance≠EpistemicStatus.
statement: Tests whether Epistemic status can fold into Provenance, concluding Provenance≠EpistemicStatus since a known source does not resolve inference-vs-fact status.

anchor: 120.31 — Could deterministic verification be part of evidence? Yes conceptually. But it deserves explicit treatment because KnowledgeOS has a specific architectural goal: AIReasoning→DeterministicAssurance. Therefore retain it as a constitutional principle.
statement: Tests whether Deterministic verification can fold into Evidence, retaining it separately due to the specific AIReasoning->DeterministicAssurance architectural goal.

anchor: 120.32 — Could feedback be part of traceability? No. Traceability can be completely static: Decision→Commit. Feedback requires Reality→Knowledge. Different property.
statement: Tests whether Feedback can fold into Traceability, concluding they are different properties (static connection vs reality-driven update).

anchor: 120.33 — Minimal constitutional set ... After reduction, the seven candidates remain justified. KOS Constitution={K1,K2,K3,K4,K5,K6,K7}.
statement: Concludes the reduction analysis: all seven candidates remain justified, forming KOS Constitution={K1..K7}.

anchor: 120.34 — Constitutional Rule K1: Provenance. Authoritative knowledge MUST have provenance. Minimum meaning: every authoritative knowledge object must be traceable to an identifiable source/process and origin context.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K1 (Provenance) with its minimum-meaning gloss.

anchor: 120.35 — Constitutional Rule K2: Authority. Authoritative changes MUST have identifiable authority. Minimum meaning: a recommendation, inference, or agent output cannot become organizationally authoritative merely because it exists.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K2 (Authority) with its minimum-meaning gloss.

anchor: 120.36 — Constitutional Rule K3: Epistemic separation. Inference, observation, verification, proposal, and authority MUST remain distinguishable. This is the core anti-hallucination architecture.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K3 (Epistemic separation), called the core anti-hallucination architecture.

anchor: 120.37 — Constitutional Rule K4: Temporal validity. Current knowledge MUST be distinguishable from historical or superseded knowledge.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K4 (Temporal validity).

anchor: 120.38 — Constitutional Rule K5: Deterministic assurance. Deterministically testable claims SHOULD be assured through reproducible evidence. We deliberately use SHOULD rather than MUST because some verification domains inherently require judgment.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K5 (Deterministic assurance) deliberately using SHOULD rather than MUST, since some verification domains require judgment.

anchor: 120.39 — Constitutional Rule K6: Traceability. Material governed actions MUST be traceable to their authorization.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K6 (Traceability).

anchor: 120.40 — Constitutional Rule K7: Feedback. Material deviations MUST be capable of feeding back into governance and authoritative knowledge. This does not mean every deviation must automatically change knowledge. It means the architecture must provide the pathway.
statement: States Constitutional Rule K7 (Feedback), clarifying the requirement is the pathway's existence, not automatic knowledge change.

anchor: 120.41 — Constitutional Rule K8? A tempting additional invariant is Identity. But perhaps identity is foundational infrastructure rather than a KnowledgeOS-specific constitutional principle.
statement: Considers and declines Identity as an eighth constitutional rule, reclassifying it as foundational infrastructure.

anchor: 120.42 — Foundation invariant F1 ... Semantically significant objects MUST have stable identity. This applies to decisions, evidence, findings, rules, actions, knowledge objects.
statement: Defines Foundation Invariant F1: semantically significant objects must have stable identity, applying to six object types.

anchor: 120.43 — Foundation invariant F2: Immutability/history ... Historical authoritative records must not silently disappear. This follows from provenance and temporal validity. F2⊂K1+K4.
statement: Defines Foundation Invariant F2 (immutability/history preservation) as following from and subsumed by K1+K4, not a separate constitutional rule.

anchor: 120.44 — Foundation invariant F3: Versioning ... Versioning is required for many objects but is an implementation mechanism supporting TemporalValidity. No need to elevate it separately.
statement: States versioning is an implementation mechanism supporting TemporalValidity (K4), not elevated to a separate constitutional rule.

anchor: 120.45 — Constitution versus implementation ... The constitution says K1: Provenance. Implementation may choose relational tables, event store, graph database, metadata, signed records, Git, immutable object storage. The constitution should not prescribe the technology.
statement: Distinguishes Constitution (invariant) from Implementation (technology choice), stating the constitution must not prescribe technology.

anchor: 120.46 — Constitution versus architecture ... KOS Constitution defines invariants. Architecture determines How. Implementation determines Exactly how. Constitution→Architecture→Implementation.
statement: Defines the layering Constitution->Architecture->Implementation, each answering a progressively more concrete question.

anchor: 120.47 — Constitution versus agent instructions ... Agent instructions should say: Follow KnowledgeOS constitutional constraints. They should not duplicate the entire KnowledgeOS knowledge base. AGENTS.md→Operating contract→KnowledgeOS→Authoritative knowledge.
statement: Extends the constitution/implementation separation to agent instructions: AGENTS.md should reference constitutional constraints, not duplicate the knowledge base.

anchor: 120.48 — Symmetry with Claude ... .claude/ owns AgentBehavior. It should not become AuthoritativeEngineeringKnowledge.
statement: States .claude/ owns AgentBehavior, not AuthoritativeEngineeringKnowledge.

anchor: 120.49 — Symmetry with Codex ... .codex/ owns CodexBehavior. Not KnowledgeOSReplacement. This preserves the pointer-layer architecture.
statement: States .codex/ owns CodexBehavior, not KnowledgeOSReplacement, preserving the pointer-layer architecture symmetrically with Claude.

anchor: 120.50 — Experiment K8.1 ... Claude local memory says Architecture Board approved X. KnowledgeOS says Architecture Board approved Y. If .claude/ has no explicit authority to override KnowledgeOS: KnowledgeOS>LocalMemory. Verdict: PASS
statement: Experiment K8.1: absent explicit override authority, KnowledgeOS>LocalMemory resolves a Claude-memory-vs-KnowledgeOS conflict; verdict PASS.

anchor: 120.51 — Agent cache exception ... Local knowledge can still exist as a projection: KnowledgeOS→AgentCache. But it must preserve Source, Version, Freshness. Therefore Cache≠Authority.
statement: States legitimate agent-cache projections must preserve Source/Version/Freshness, but Cache≠Authority regardless.

anchor: 120.52 — Constitution and deterministic assurance ... Claim→Evidence→Verification. Action→Decision→Authority. Knowledge→Validity. Inference→EpistemicStatus. This is a coherent system.
statement: Connects the constitution to four short governing chains, called a coherent system.

anchor: 120.53 — Constitutional dependency graph ... Provenance feeds Authority, Epistemic, Validity, which feed Traceability, Evidence, which feed Deterministic Verification, which feeds Feedback.
statement: Presents the constitutional dependency graph rooted at Provenance, flowing through Authority/Epistemic/Validity to Traceability/Evidence to Deterministic Verification to Feedback.

anchor: 120.54 — Constitutional failure propagation ... NoProvenance causes EvidenceTrust↓ which causes VerificationTrust↓ which causes DecisionTrust↓.
statement: Defines the provenance-failure propagation chain: NoProvenance->EvidenceTrust down->VerificationTrust down->DecisionTrust down.

anchor: 120.55 — Authority failure propagation ... NoAuthority causes DecisionStatus=Ambiguous which causes ActionAuthorization=Ambiguous. Therefore authority is not merely administrative metadata.
statement: Defines the authority-failure propagation chain, concluding authority is not merely administrative metadata.

anchor: 120.56 — Epistemic failure propagation ... If Inference=Authority then AIOutput→OrganizationalTruth. That is the fundamental AI governance failure.
statement: Defines the epistemic-failure propagation chain (Inference=Authority->AIOutput->OrganizationalTruth), called the fundamental AI governance failure.

anchor: 120.57 — Temporal failure propagation ... If SupersededKnowledge=CurrentKnowledge then AgentContext may be wrong even when retrieval is technically perfect. RetrievalAccuracy≠KnowledgeCorrectness.
statement: Defines the temporal-failure propagation chain, yielding RetrievalAccuracy≠KnowledgeCorrectness.

anchor: 120.58 — Verification failure propagation ... If LLMAssertion=Verification then deterministic assurance disappears. Therefore AIReasoning must remain distinct from Assurance.
statement: Defines the verification-failure propagation chain, requiring AIReasoning to remain distinct from Assurance.

anchor: 120.59 — Traceability failure propagation ... If Action-not->Decision then after an incident we may know what changed but not why it was allowed. That is a governance blind spot.
statement: Defines the traceability-failure propagation chain, yielding a post-incident governance blind spot.

anchor: 120.60 — Feedback failure propagation ... If Runtime-not->Knowledge then KnowledgeOS gradually becomes stale. Therefore KnowledgeDecay is unavoidable without feedback.
statement: Defines the feedback-failure propagation chain, yielding unavoidable KnowledgeDecay absent feedback.

anchor: 120.61 — The constitutional equation ... KnowledgeOSIntegrity=P∩A∩E∩T∩V∩R∩F. The intersection matters. A platform satisfying six of seven is not necessarily constitutionally sound.
statement: Defines KnowledgeOSIntegrity=P∩A∩E∩T∩V∩R∩F, stating the intersection matters: six of seven satisfied is not necessarily constitutionally sound.

anchor: 120.62 — The most important invariant ... If we had to choose only one, EpistemicStatus is perhaps the most important for the AI layer. Because it prevents AIInference→Fact→Authority without an explicit promotion process.
statement: Identifies EpistemicStatus as the single most important invariant for the AI layer, preventing unpromoted AIInference->Fact->Authority.

anchor: 120.63 — The most important governance invariant ... For governance, Authority is fundamental.
statement: Identifies Authority as the most important invariant for governance.

anchor: 120.64 — The most important assurance invariant ... For engineering assurance, Evidence+DeterministicVerification is fundamental.
statement: Identifies Evidence+DeterministicVerification as the most important invariant for engineering assurance.

anchor: 120.65 — The most important operating-system invariant ... For the OS concept, Feedback is fundamental. Without feedback, KnowledgeOS can remain a sophisticated static knowledge system.
statement: Identifies Feedback as the most important invariant for the operating-system concept, without which KnowledgeOS remains a sophisticated static knowledge system.

anchor: 120.66 — The resulting architecture constitution: KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution v0.1. C1 Provenance, C2 Authority, C3 Epistemic Separation, C4 Temporal Validity, C5 Deterministic Assurance, C6 Traceability, C7 Feedback.
statement: Freezes the KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution v0.1 (C1-C7), restating each rule in final form.

anchor: 120.67 — What we deliberately did NOT put into the constitution: use a graph database, PostgreSQL, vector embeddings, RAG, Kafka, MCP, Claude, Codex, a specific framework/UI/API. These are architectural/implementation choices. The constitution must survive technology changes.
statement: Enumerates eleven deliberately excluded technology/tool choices, stating the constitution must survive technology changes.
